He is sitting upright, leaning forward with his mouth open and drooling, and he has soft inspiratory stridor. He has received none of the recommended childhood vaccinations. Blood culture grows small gram-negative coccobacilli that grow on chocolate agar but not on sheep blood agar alone. Vaccination with which of the following antigens would most likely have prevented this illness?

options.label: A
options.html: Capsular polysaccharide conjugated to a protein carrier

options.label: B
options.html: Detoxified exotoxin (toxoid) adsorbed to aluminum salt

options.label: C
options.html: Inactivated whole bacterial cells given with an adjuvant

options.label: D
options.html: Live attenuated bacteria given by mouth

items.explanationHtml:
This is acute epiglottitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus that needs factors X (hemin) and V (NAD), supplied by chocolate agar. The Hib vaccine contains the type b capsular polysaccharide, polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP), conjugated to a protein carrier. Conjugation converts a T-cell-independent antigen into a T-cell-dependent one, so infants under 2 years make protective, boostable IgG.

Takeaway: The Hib vaccine is a PRP capsule conjugated to protein, which lets infants respond.

whyNot.B: Toxoid vaccines protect against toxin-mediated diseases such as diphtheria and tetanus; Hib disease is not toxin-mediated.
whyNot.C: Whole-cell inactivated vaccines are not used for Hib; the protective antigen is the capsule.
whyNot.D: There is no live attenuated Hib vaccine.
whyNot.E: Lipooligosaccharide is not the vaccine antigen, and nontypeable H influenzae lacks a capsule and is not covered by the vaccine.

items.objective: Relate the Hib conjugate vaccine antigen to prevention of epiglottitis.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at night because of a harsh, barking cough and noisy breathing that began after 2 days of runny nose and low-grade fever. He has inspiratory stridor when crying, but not at rest, and is alert and playful between coughing spells. Narrowing at which of the following sites best explains his symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), most often caused by parainfluenza virus, inflames and swells the larynx and the subglottic trachea. In young children the subglottis, surrounded by the complete cricoid ring, is the narrowest part of the airway, so edema there causes the barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor. On an AP neck film this narrowing appears as the steeple sign.

Takeaway: Croup narrows the subglottic airway, giving a barking cough and inspiratory stridor (steeple sign).

whyNot.A: Supraglottic swelling is epiglottitis, which causes drooling, toxicity and a muffled voice rather than a barking cough.
whyNot.B: Nasopharyngeal obstruction (adenoids, choanal atresia) causes mouth breathing or cyanosis relieved by crying, not barking cough.
whyNot.C: Retropharyngeal swelling (abscess) causes fever, neck stiffness and drooling in a toxic child.
whyNot.D: Bronchiolar narrowing (bronchiolitis, asthma) causes expiratory wheeze, not inspiratory stridor.

items.objective: Localize the airway narrowing responsible for the signs of croup.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. On the second day he has right-sided facial pain and swelling, nasal congestion and blurred vision in the right eye. Nasal endoscopy shows black, necrotic tissue on the right middle turbinate. Biopsy of this tissue is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Broad non-septate hyphae with wide-angle branching invading vessels

options.label: B
options.html: Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae on the mucosal surface

options.label: C
options.html: Encapsulated yeasts with narrow-based budding and a clear halo

options.label: D
options.html: Large thick-walled spherules filled with endospores

options.label: E
options.html: Narrow septate hyphae branching at acute angles in necrotic tissue

items.explanationHtml:
Rapidly progressive necrotizing sinusitis with black eschar in a patient with ketoacidosis is mucormycosis (Rhizopus, Mucor and related molds). Tissue shows broad, ribbon-like, non-septate (pauci-septate) hyphae branching at wide angles. The fungi invade arteries, causing thrombosis and infarction, which produces the black necrotic tissue and allows spread to the orbit and brain. Acidosis and increased free iron favor their growth.

Takeaway: Mucormycosis: DKA plus black necrotic sinus tissue; broad non-septate hyphae that invade vessels.

whyNot.B: Budding yeast with pseudohyphae is Candida, which causes mucosal thrush, not angioinvasive necrotizing sinusitis.
whyNot.C: Encapsulated yeast with narrow-based budding is Cryptococcus, which causes meningitis and pneumonia.
whyNot.D: Spherules with endospores are Coccidioides, a dimorphic fungus causing pulmonary and disseminated disease.
whyNot.E: Narrow septate hyphae with acute-angle branching are Aspergillus, which causes invasive sinusitis mainly in profound neutropenia.

items.objective: Recognize the histology of rhinocerebral mucormycosis in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old girl has had a cough for 3 weeks. It began as a mild cold, then progressed to bouts of 10–15 rapid coughs followed by a high-pitched gasp and sometimes vomiting. Between episodes she feels well and has a normal examination. She received her childhood vaccinations but no adolescent booster. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?

options.label: B
options.html: Atypical lymphocytes with a positive heterophile test

items.explanationHtml:
Paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting after a catarrhal phase is pertussis. Waning immunity from childhood acellular vaccine is a common reason for infection in adolescents. Pertussis toxin inhibits lymphocyte homing to lymphoid tissue, so lymphocytes stay in the blood and an absolute lymphocytosis results, often striking in infants.

Takeaway: Pertussis causes lymphocytosis; adolescents lose vaccine immunity and need a Tdap booster.

whyNot.B: Atypical lymphocytes with a positive heterophile test indicate infectious mononucleosis.
whyNot.C: Cold agglutinins suggest Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which causes a prolonged cough but without whoops and post-tussive vomiting.
whyNot.D: Eosinophilia suggests parasitic infection, allergy or drug reaction, not pertussis.
whyNot.E: Neutropenia is not a feature of pertussis; the total leukocyte count is often raised.

items.objective: Recognize the lymphocytosis of pertussis in an adolescent with waning immunity.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has had sneezing, nasal itching and clear rhinorrhea every spring for several years. Symptoms begin within minutes of being outdoors on windy days. Examination shows pale, swollen nasal turbinates and dark discoloration under both eyes. Which of the following is the initial event in the reaction that causes his symptoms within minutes of exposure?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of complement by antigen–antibody complexes

options.label: B
options.html: Binding of allergen-specific IgG to Fc receptors on neutrophils

options.label: C
options.html: Cross-linking of IgE bound to mast cells by the allergen

options.label: D
options.html: Recognition of allergen by sensitized CD8+ T cells

options.label: E
options.html: Release of interleukin-1 from activated macrophages in the airway wall

items.explanationHtml:
Seasonal allergic rhinitis is a type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction. After sensitization, allergen-specific IgE is bound to FcεRI on mucosal mast cells. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules, triggering degranulation and release of histamine and newly made leukotrienes and prostaglandins within minutes. A late phase hours later is driven by eosinophils and Th2 cytokines.

Takeaway: Allergic rhinitis begins with allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells (type I hypersensitivity).

whyNot.A: Complement activation by immune complexes defines type III hypersensitivity (serum sickness, glomerulonephritis).
whyNot.B: IgG-mediated reactions involve type II or III mechanisms; the immediate allergic response is IgE-mediated.
whyNot.D: T-cell recognition drives delayed (type IV) reactions over 48–72 hours, not symptoms within minutes.
whyNot.E: Interleukin-1 mediates fever and acute-phase responses, not the immediate allergic reaction.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of the immediate phase of allergic rhinitis.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy who recently arrived from a country with low vaccination coverage has had fever, sore throat and painful swallowing for 3 days. He has marked swelling of the anterior neck. A gray membrane covers the tonsils and posterior pharynx and bleeds when the clinician tries to lift it. He has never been vaccinated. Gram stain of material from beneath the membrane shows club-shaped gram-positive rods. Without treatment, he is at greatest risk of which of the following complications during the next 1–2 weeks?
items.explanationHtml:
Pharyngeal diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) forms a gray, adherent pseudomembrane with bull-neck swelling. The organism stays local, but its exotoxin, which stops protein synthesis by inactivating elongation factor 2, is absorbed and injures distant tissues. Myocarditis, often with AV block or arrhythmias, typically appears in the first 1–2 weeks and is the main cause of death; cranial and peripheral neuropathies follow later. Treatment is antitoxin plus antibiotics; prevention is the toxoid vaccine.

Takeaway: Diphtheria: gray adherent pseudomembrane, and its toxin causes myocarditis and neuropathy.

whyNot.A: Glomerulonephritis is a sequel of group A streptococcal infection, not diphtheria.
whyNot.B: Erythema nodosum follows streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis and other triggers, not diphtheria.
whyNot.C: Diphtheria is a toxin-mediated disease and does not typically cause lung abscess.
whyNot.E: Splenic rupture complicates infectious mononucleosis.

items.objective: Recognize myocarditis as the major toxin-mediated complication of pharyngeal diphtheria.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl has had fever, neck pain and refusal to eat for 3 days after a sore throat. She holds her neck stiffly and cries when it is extended. A lateral neck radiograph shows marked widening of the prevertebral soft tissue. Contrast CT confirms a fluid collection between the posterior pharyngeal wall and the prevertebral fascia. If untreated, the infection can extend through which of the following spaces directly into the posterior mediastinum?

options.label: A
options.html: The danger space behind the alar layer

options.label: B
options.html: The parapharyngeal space beside the pharynx

options.label: C
options.html: The peritonsillar space around the tonsil

options.label: D
options.html: The pretracheal space in front of the trachea

options.label: E
options.html: The submandibular space below the mandible

items.explanationHtml:
This is a retropharyngeal abscess. Directly behind the retropharyngeal space, between the alar and prevertebral layers of deep cervical fascia, is the danger space, which runs uninterrupted from the skull base to the posterior mediastinum at the level of the diaphragm. Pus that breaks into it can track down and cause descending necrotizing mediastinitis.

Takeaway: The danger space links retropharyngeal infection to the posterior mediastinum.

whyNot.B: The parapharyngeal space connects to the carotid sheath and retropharyngeal space, but the direct route to the posterior mediastinum is the danger space.
whyNot.C: The peritonsillar space lies around the tonsillar capsule and is the site of peritonsillar abscess.
whyNot.D: The pretracheal space lies in front of the trachea and leads to the anterior (superior) mediastinum, not the posterior mediastinum.
whyNot.E: The submandibular space is the site of Ludwig angina, which spreads mainly to the parapharyngeal space and floor of mouth.

items.objective: Trace the fascial pathway by which retropharyngeal infection reaches the mediastinum.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had 2 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She is otherwise healthy, takes no medications and has not taken antibiotics in the past year. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. She is alert. Crackles are heard at the right base. A chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Serum urea nitrogen is 12 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin

options.label: B
options.html: Admission for intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam

options.label: E
options.html: Symptomatic treatment only, with review in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
She has community-acquired pneumonia with a CURB-65 score of 0 and normal oxygenation, so she can be treated at home. For a healthy adult without comorbidities or recent antibiotics, high-dose oral amoxicillin (or doxycycline) is recommended; a macrolide alone is used only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is low. Treatment lasts at least 5 days and until clinically stable.

Takeaway: Healthy outpatient with CAP and no risk factors: oral amoxicillin (or doxycycline); keep fluoroquinolones for patients with comorbidities.

whyNot.A: Admission and IV combination therapy are for patients with higher severity scores, hypoxemia or inability to take oral drugs.
whyNot.B: Broad MRSA and antipseudomonal coverage is for patients with prior isolation of these organisms or hospital-acquired infection, not a healthy outpatient.
whyNot.D: A respiratory fluoroquinolone is reserved for outpatients with comorbidities or beta-lactam allergy, given its adverse effects and resistance pressure.
whyNot.E: Radiographically confirmed bacterial pneumonia needs antibiotics; withholding them risks progression.

items.objective: Choose outpatient empiric therapy for low-risk community-acquired pneumonia.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of fever, cough and increasing dyspnea. He is confused. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 34/min and blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg despite 30 mL/kg of intravenous crystalloid; norepinephrine is started. Oxygen saturation is 86% on a non-rebreather mask, and he is intubated. A chest x-ray shows dense left lower lobe consolidation. He has not been in hospital or received antibiotics in the past year, and no resistant organisms have been isolated from him before. Blood and sputum cultures are sent. In addition to supportive care, which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
items.explanationHtml:
Septic shock and respiratory failure make this severe community-acquired pneumonia. Empiric therapy must cover S pneumoniae, H influenzae, S aureus (MSSA) and Legionella, so a beta-lactam plus a macrolide (or a beta-lactam plus a respiratory fluoroquinolone) is recommended. Monotherapy is not adequate in severe disease. Without prior MRSA or Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics, routine MRSA and antipseudomonal coverage is not added; cultures guide escalation. Current guidance also suggests systemic glucocorticoids in severe CAP.

Takeaway: Severe CAP: beta-lactam plus macrolide (or plus fluoroquinolone); add MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage only for specific risk factors.

whyNot.A: Ampicillin-sulbactam alone also misses atypical organisms.
whyNot.B: A beta-lactam alone leaves atypical organisms, notably Legionella, uncovered in severe disease.
whyNot.D: Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is acceptable for non-severe inpatients but not for septic shock and ventilation.
whyNot.E: This triple regimen is for patients with risk factors for MRSA and resistant Pseudomonas, which he lacks; unnecessary broad therapy adds toxicity and resistance.

items.objective: Choose empiric antibiotics for severe community-acquired pneumonia without resistance risk factors.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman has been intubated in the intensive care unit for 7 days after a subarachnoid hemorrhage. She received intravenous cefepime 3 weeks ago for a urinary tract infection. She now has a temperature of 38.9°C (102°F), purulent endotracheal secretions, a rising oxygen requirement and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg. In the unit, about 25% of S aureus isolates are methicillin-resistant. Endotracheal aspirate and blood cultures are obtained. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
items.explanationHtml:
New fever, purulent secretions, worsening oxygenation and a new infiltrate more than 48 hours after intubation define ventilator-associated pneumonia. Likely organisms include Pseudomonas, other resistant gram-negative rods and MRSA. IV antibiotics within the past 90 days, septic shock and a unit with a high MRSA rate are risk factors for resistant organisms, so empiric therapy should combine MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem); with septic shock and recent IV antibiotics, a second antipseudomonal agent of another class is often added. Narrow therapy when cultures return; 7 days suffices for most responders.

Takeaway: VAP with resistance risk: MRSA coverage plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, then de-escalate by cultures.

whyNot.A: Ampicillin-sulbactam plus a macrolide covers community pathogens but neither Pseudomonas nor MRSA.
whyNot.B: This is a community-acquired regimen; it misses Pseudomonas and MRSA.
whyNot.C: Linezolid covers MRSA, but ceftriaxone has no reliable activity against Pseudomonas.
whyNot.D: Vancomycin covers MRSA, but ceftriaxone leaves Pseudomonas and other resistant gram-negative rods untreated.

items.objective: Select empiric therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia with risk factors for resistant organisms.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old man is admitted with 4 days of fever, cough, watery diarrhea and new confusion. He returned 9 days ago from a hotel stay where he used the hot tub daily. Temperature is 39.7°C (103.5°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 26/min and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. A chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. A sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils and no predominant organism. Laboratory results:

TestResult
Sodium128 mEq/L
Potassium3.6 mEq/L
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL
AST92 U/L
ALT88 U/L
Leukocytes14,800/mm3

Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis rapidly?
items.explanationHtml:
Pneumonia with high fever, diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia and raised aminotransferases after hot-tub exposure suggests Legionella. The urine antigen test is rapid and specific; it detects serogroup 1, which causes most cases, so a negative result does not fully exclude infection and respiratory culture or PCR can be added. Treat with a respiratory fluoroquinolone or azithromycin.

Takeaway: Severe pneumonia with hyponatremia, diarrhea and water exposure: send a Legionella urine antigen.

whyNot.A: Cold agglutinins suggest Mycoplasma but are non-specific and slow; Mycoplasma rarely causes this severe systemic picture with hyponatremia.
whyNot.B: Beta-D-glucan supports invasive fungal infection or Pneumocystis, which do not fit an acute lobar pneumonia in an immunocompetent man.
whyNot.C: Antistreptolysin O detects prior group A streptococcal infection and plays no role in pneumonia diagnosis.
whyNot.D: An acid-fast smear is for suspected TB, a subacute illness with weeks of symptoms.

items.objective: Order the rapid confirmatory test for suspected Legionella pneumonia.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who moved to the United States from a country with a high tuberculosis burden 2 years ago comes to the emergency department with 2 months of cough, intermittent blood-streaked sputum, night sweats and a 6-kg weight loss. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. A chest x-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. HIV testing is pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Airborne isolation and sputum testing for mycobacteria

options.label: B
options.html: CT-guided needle biopsy of the cavity

options.label: C
options.html: Interferon-gamma release assay and outpatient follow-up

options.label: D
options.html: Start isoniazid alone pending culture results

options.label: E
options.html: Start oral levofloxacin and repeat the chest x-ray in 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Weeks of cough, hemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss with an upper-lobe cavity in a person from a high-burden country is active pulmonary TB until proven otherwise. He must be placed in airborne isolation (negative-pressure room, N95 respirators) and three sputum samples collected for acid-fast smear and culture, with a NAAT on at least one sample for rapid confirmation and rifampin-resistance testing. Four-drug therapy usually starts after samples are taken when suspicion is high.

Takeaway: Suspected active TB: isolate first, then three sputum samples for smear, culture and NAAT before therapy.

whyNot.B: Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when sputum is easily obtained; it does not address infection control.
whyNot.C: An IGRA cannot distinguish latent from active TB and can be negative in active disease; discharging him would expose others.
whyNot.D: Monotherapy for possible active TB selects resistant mutants; active disease needs a four-drug regimen.
whyNot.E: Empiric fluoroquinolones are active against M tuberculosis, can mask TB, delay diagnosis and select resistance.

items.objective: Manage suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis with isolation and sputum testing.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old nurse has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on routine employee screening; her test 1 year ago was negative. She has no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss, and her examination is normal. A chest x-ray is normal. HIV test is negative, and liver tests are normal. She takes no medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat the interferon-gamma release assay in 12 months without treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Three sputum samples for acid-fast smear and culture before any decision

items.explanationHtml:
A new positive IGRA in an asymptomatic healthcare worker with a normal chest x-ray means latent TB infection with recent conversion, which carries the highest risk of progression. Treat it. Shorter rifamycin-based regimens are preferred because more people complete them: 4 months of daily rifampin, 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, or 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin; 6–9 months of isoniazid is an alternative.

Takeaway: Positive IGRA + no symptoms + normal x-ray = latent TB; treat with a short rifamycin-based regimen.

whyNot.A: BCG does not treat existing infection and is not used for adults in the United States.
whyNot.C: Four-drug therapy is for active disease; there is no evidence of active TB here.
whyNot.D: Recent conversion carries a high risk of progression in the first 2 years; observation forgoes effective prevention.
whyNot.E: Sputum testing is needed only with symptoms or an abnormal chest x-ray; with neither, active TB is adequately excluded.

items.objective: Treat latent tuberculosis infection with a preferred short rifamycin-based regimen.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago has 3 weeks of progressive dyspnea, dry cough and low-grade fever. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 60/mm3. Respirations are 26/min. Arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 61 mm Hg and PaCO2 30 mm Hg. A chest x-ray shows bilateral diffuse interstitial opacities. Direct fluorescent antibody staining of induced sputum confirms Pneumocystis jirovecii. He has no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Pneumocystis pneumonia is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 21 days. Because his room-air PaO2 is below 70 mm Hg (and his A–a gradient is well above 35 mm Hg), adjunctive prednisone started with the antibiotic is indicated: it blunts the inflammatory worsening that follows organism death and lowers the risk of respiratory failure and death. Antiretroviral therapy is started within about 2 weeks.

Takeaway: PJP with PaO2 < 70 mm Hg or A–a gradient ≥ 35: TMP-SMX plus prednisone.

whyNot.A: Echinocandins are not standard therapy for Pneumocystis pneumonia.
whyNot.B: Amphotericin targets ergosterol, which Pneumocystis lacks, and is not effective.
whyNot.C: Atovaquone is a second-line choice for mild disease in patients who cannot take TMP-SMX.
whyNot.D: TMP-SMX is correct, but omitting steroids in moderate-to-severe hypoxemia raises the risk of respiratory failure and death.

items.objective: Treat moderate-to-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia with TMP-SMX and adjunctive glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old woman who lives in a nursing home has had 4 days of fever, myalgia, headache and cough during a regional influenza outbreak. She has heart failure and type 2 diabetes. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 20/min and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. The lungs are clear. A chest x-ray shows no infiltrate. A rapid molecular test of a nasopharyngeal swab is positive for influenza A. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Influenza vaccination now, without antiviral therapy

options.label: E
options.html: Supportive care only, because symptoms began more than 48 hours ago

items.explanationHtml:
Antiviral treatment is recommended for anyone with influenza who is hospitalized, severely ill or at high risk of complications, such as adults 65 or older, nursing-home residents and people with heart disease or diabetes, regardless of how long they have had symptoms. Oseltamivir, a neuraminidase inhibitor, is the usual choice. The 48-hour window applies to otherwise healthy outpatients. Residents of the facility are also given antiviral prophylaxis during an outbreak.

Takeaway: High-risk patients with influenza get oseltamivir even after 48 hours of symptoms.

whyNot.A: Vaccination does not treat active infection; she needs antiviral therapy now.
whyNot.B: There is no bacterial pneumonia on x-ray; antibiotics would be indicated only if secondary bacterial pneumonia developed.
whyNot.C: Circulating influenza A strains are resistant to the adamantanes, so amantadine is not used.
whyNot.E: The 48-hour limit applies to low-risk outpatients; high-risk and hospitalized patients still benefit after 48 hours.

items.objective: Treat influenza in high-risk patients with a neuraminidase inhibitor regardless of symptom duration.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy born at term has had 2 days of rhinorrhea followed by 1 day of cough and fast breathing in January. He is feeding a little less than usual but has had six wet diapers today. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 150/min, respirations are 52/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. There is mild subcostal retraction, with diffuse wheezes and fine crackles bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Chest x-ray to look for consolidation

options.label: B
options.html: Nasal suctioning and supportive care at home

options.label: D
options.html: Oral amoxicillin for presumed bacterial infection

items.explanationHtml:
This is bronchiolitis, usually from RSV: an infant under 2 years with coryza followed by cough, tachypnea, wheeze and crackles in winter. The diagnosis is clinical. Because he is well oxygenated, hydrated and only mildly distressed, he can be cared for at home with nasal suctioning, feeding support and clear return precautions. Bronchodilators, glucocorticoids and antibiotics do not improve outcomes. Admission is for hypoxemia, apnea, dehydration or severe distress.

Takeaway: Bronchiolitis is diagnosed clinically and treated supportively; no routine x-ray, bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Routine chest imaging is not needed in typical bronchiolitis; it often shows atelectasis that leads to unnecessary antibiotics.
whyNot.C: Bronchodilators have not shown benefit in bronchiolitis and are not recommended routinely.
whyNot.D: This is a viral illness; antibiotics are only for a proven bacterial coinfection such as acute otitis media.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoids do not shorten illness or prevent admission in bronchiolitis.

items.objective: Manage mild bronchiolitis in an infant with supportive care.

items.stemHtml: A 37-year-old man has 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss. A chest x-ray shows a cavity in the left upper lobe. He is placed in airborne isolation. Sputum acid-fast smear is positive, and a nucleic acid amplification test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis without the rifampin-resistance mutation. HIV test is negative. Baseline liver tests are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Isoniazid and rifampin, with pyridoxine, for 6 months

options.label: B
options.html: Isoniazid with pyridoxine alone for 9 months

options.label: C
options.html: Levofloxacin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide, each given daily

options.label: D
options.html: Rifampin alone, taken daily, for 4 months

items.explanationHtml:
Drug-susceptible active pulmonary TB is treated with an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then a continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months (longer if the cavity's cultures remain positive at 2 months). Ethambutol can be dropped once full susceptibility is confirmed. Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy. Directly observed therapy and public health reporting follow.

Takeaway: Active drug-susceptible TB: 2 months of four drugs, then 4 months of isoniazid plus rifampin, with pyridoxine.

whyNot.A: Two drugs from the start are insufficient for the high bacillary load of cavitary disease; pyrazinamide makes 6 months enough.
whyNot.B: Isoniazid monotherapy is a latent TB regimen; in active disease it selects resistance.
whyNot.C: Fluoroquinolone-based regimens are second-line options for resistance or intolerance, not initial therapy for susceptible TB.
whyNot.D: Rifampin alone is a latent TB regimen and would breed resistance in active disease.

items.objective: Start standard four-drug therapy for drug-susceptible active pulmonary tuberculosis.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) The patient was started on isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol with pyridoxine. Five weeks later he has nausea, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort. His sclerae are icteric. Serum AST is 410 U/L, ALT 520 U/L and total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL. Hepatitis A, B and C serologies are negative. He has no fever and his cough has improved. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue all drugs and add N-acetylcysteine

options.label: B
options.html: Continue all four drugs and repeat liver tests in 2 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Stop all antituberculous treatment until the liver tests normalize, then restart all four drugs together

options.label: D
options.html: Stop ethambutol only and continue the other three drugs

options.label: E
options.html: Stop the three hepatotoxic drugs, then reintroduce them one by one

items.explanationHtml:
He has drug-induced hepatitis: symptoms with aminotransferases above 3 times the upper limit (and jaundice). Isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide are all hepatotoxic, so all three must be stopped. In cavitary disease that is still infectious, a temporary non-hepatotoxic regimen (for example ethambutol with a fluoroquinolone and/or an injectable) can bridge the gap. When the liver tests return toward normal, the drugs are reintroduced one at a time, usually rifampin first, then isoniazid, while monitoring liver tests; the drug that causes a recurrence is permanently stopped. Restarting all at once makes the culprit impossible to identify.

Takeaway: TB drug hepatitis: stop the hepatotoxic drugs (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide), then rechallenge one at a time.

whyNot.A: N-acetylcysteine is not a substitute for stopping the offending drugs, and continuing them is unsafe.
whyNot.B: Continuing hepatotoxic drugs with symptomatic hepatitis and jaundice risks acute liver failure.
whyNot.C: Stopping everything may leave active cavitary TB untreated, and restarting all drugs together does not identify the cause.
whyNot.D: Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic; stopping only it leaves all three culprits in place.

items.objective: Manage hepatotoxicity during tuberculosis treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student has had 10 days of low-grade fever, headache, sore throat and a persistent dry cough. Several roommates have had similar symptoms. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). A few scattered crackles are heard. A chest x-ray shows patchy bilateral reticular opacities that look more extensive than the examination suggests. He took amoxicillin for 5 days without improvement. Which of the following features of the most likely causative organism best explains the treatment failure?

options.label: A
options.html: A polysaccharide capsule that blocks antibiotic entry

options.label: B
options.html: Absence of a peptidoglycan cell wall

options.label: C
options.html: Altered penicillin-binding proteins in the cell wall

options.label: E
options.html: Production of a beta-lactamase encoded on a plasmid

items.explanationHtml:
The story (young adult in close quarters, gradual dry cough, headache, x-ray worse than the examination) is classic for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Mycoplasma has a cell membrane containing sterols but no peptidoglycan wall, so beta-lactams, which inhibit cell-wall synthesis, have no target. It is invisible on Gram stain. Macrolides, doxycycline or fluoroquinolones are effective.

Takeaway: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so beta-lactams cannot work and Gram stain shows nothing.

whyNot.A: A capsule protects against phagocytosis, not against antibiotics, and is not the reason for treatment failure here.
whyNot.C: Altered penicillin-binding proteins cause penicillin resistance in pneumococci, which cause abrupt lobar pneumonia, not this pattern.
whyNot.D: Obligate intracellular growth describes Chlamydophila pneumoniae; Mycoplasma can grow on cell-free media.
whyNot.E: Beta-lactamase production explains amoxicillin failure in H influenzae or Moraxella, which do not fit this subacute atypical picture.

items.objective: Explain why beta-lactams fail against Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man who smokes is admitted with 3 days of high fever, cough, watery diarrhea and confusion. He works as a maintenance engineer servicing the air-conditioning cooling towers of an office building. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F). A chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Serum sodium is 127 mEq/L. A sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils and few organisms. Culture of the most likely pathogen requires which of the following media?
items.explanationHtml:
High fever, diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia with pneumonia after exposure to aerosolized water from a cooling tower point to Legionella pneumophila. It is a gram-negative rod that stains poorly with Gram stain (seen better with silver stain) and needs buffered charcoal yeast extract with cysteine and iron to grow. The urine antigen test is the quickest diagnostic test for serogroup 1.

Takeaway: Legionella: water source, hyponatremia, diarrhea; few organisms on Gram stain; grows on charcoal yeast extract with cysteine and iron.

whyNot.B: Factors X and V are needed by H influenzae; they do not support Legionella, which needs cysteine and iron.
whyNot.C: Löwenstein-Jensen medium grows M tuberculosis, which causes a subacute upper-lobe illness, not this acute picture.
whyNot.D: Sabouraud agar is for fungi.
whyNot.E: Thayer-Martin agar selects for Neisseria species, not a cause of this pneumonia.

items.objective: Identify Legionella pneumonia and its culture requirements.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man who lived alone is found dead at home. He had told a neighbor 3 days earlier that he had a fever, shaking chills and a cough with rusty sputum. At autopsy the entire left lower lobe is firm, airless and dusky, with a cut surface resembling liver. Microscopy shows alveoli filled with neutrophils, erythrocytes and fibrin. Which of the following stages of pneumonia is present?
items.explanationHtml:
This is lobar pneumonia, most likely pneumococcal, on about day 2–3. In red hepatization the alveoli are packed with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin, making the lobe red, firm and liver-like. Congestion comes first (day 1: vascular engorgement and fluid with bacteria); gray hepatization follows (days 4–6) as red cells break down and the exudate turns gray-brown.

Takeaway: Red hepatization = neutrophils + red cells + fibrin filling alveoli at about days 2–3 of lobar pneumonia.

whyNot.A: Congestion (first day) shows vascular engorgement and intra-alveolar fluid with many bacteria but few neutrophils and no fibrin-packed alveoli.
whyNot.B: Gray hepatization (days 4–6) has degenerating red cells and a gray-brown fibrinopurulent exudate.
whyNot.C: Organization replaces an uncleared exudate with fibroblasts and fibrous tissue, weeks later.
whyNot.E: In resolution the exudate is digested and cleared by macrophages, and the lung becomes aerated again.

items.objective: Recognize the histological stages of lobar pneumonia.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old girl who emigrated from a country where tuberculosis is common has a chest x-ray before school entry. It shows a small calcified nodule in the periphery of the right middle lobe and a calcified right hilar lymph node. She has no symptoms. Her interferon-gamma release assay is positive. Which of the following steps was most important for containing her infection?

options.label: A
options.html: Killing of free bacilli by complement membrane-attack complexes

options.label: B
options.html: Lysis of infected macrophages by natural killer cells alone

options.label: C
options.html: Neutralization of the bacilli by secretory IgA

options.label: D
options.html: Opsonization of bacilli by IgG with phagocytosis by neutrophils

options.label: E
options.html: Th1 cytokine signaling by CD4+ T cells that activates macrophages

items.explanationHtml:
The calcified peripheral nodule and hilar node form a healed Ghon complex (Ranke complex): primary tuberculosis contained by cell-mediated immunity. M tuberculosis survives inside alveolar macrophages by blocking phagolysosome maturation. Macrophages present antigen and secrete IL-12, which drives CD4 Th1 differentiation; Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill bacilli and to form caseating granulomas with TNF-alpha. People with IL-12 or interferon-gamma receptor defects get severe mycobacterial disease.

Takeaway: Containment of TB depends on the IL-12 → Th1 → interferon-gamma → activated macrophage axis, with TNF holding granulomas together.

whyNot.A: The waxy mycobacterial wall resists complement lysis, and complement does not contain intracellular infection.
whyNot.B: NK cells contribute early interferon-gamma, but the durable containment that leads to a calcified Ghon complex requires CD4 Th1 cells.
whyNot.C: Secretory IgA protects mucosal surfaces against extracellular organisms; antibodies cannot reach bacilli inside macrophages.
whyNot.D: Neutrophils and opsonizing antibody are central against extracellular pyogenic bacteria, not intracellular mycobacteria.

items.objective: Explain the cell-mediated immune response that contains primary tuberculosis.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman is being treated for latent tuberculosis infection with daily isoniazid. After 3 months she reports burning and numbness of both feet. Vibration sense is reduced at the toes. She drinks alcohol heavily and eats poorly. Supplementation with which of the following would most likely have prevented this complication?
items.explanationHtml:
Isoniazid forms an inactive complex with pyridoxine and increases its excretion, depleting vitamin B6, a cofactor for neurotransmitter synthesis. The result is a dose-related peripheral neuropathy. Risk is highest with malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, diabetes, kidney failure, HIV, pregnancy and in slow acetylators. Pyridoxine is given with isoniazid to prevent it.

Takeaway: Give pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in malnourished or alcohol-using patients.

whyNot.A: B12 deficiency also causes neuropathy, but isoniazid does not deplete B12 and supplementation would not prevent this drug effect.
whyNot.B: Folate is depleted by drugs such as methotrexate, trimethoprim and phenytoin, causing anemia rather than isoniazid neuropathy.
whyNot.C: Isoniazid can cause pellagra by depleting B6 needed for niacin synthesis, but niacin would not prevent the neuropathy.
whyNot.E: Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy in alcohol use disorder, but isoniazid neuropathy is a B6 effect.

items.objective: Link isoniazid neuropathy to pyridoxine depletion and its prevention.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man is in the second month of treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis with four drugs. He reports that colors look washed out and that he cannot tell red from green traffic lights. Visual acuity has fallen from 20/20 to 20/50 in both eyes. The drug most likely responsible acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of mycolic acid synthesis after activation by bacterial catalase-peroxidase

options.label: D
options.html: Disruption of membrane transport after conversion to an acid in phagolysosomes

items.explanationHtml:
Reduced acuity with loss of red-green color discrimination is optic neuritis from ethambutol, which inhibits mycobacterial arabinosyltransferase and so blocks arabinogalactan synthesis in the cell wall. Toxicity is dose-related and usually reversible if the drug is stopped early; acuity and color vision are checked at baseline and during therapy.

Takeaway: Ethambutol: arabinosyltransferase inhibitor; watch for optic neuritis with red-green color loss.

whyNot.A: Binding the 30S subunit describes streptomycin and other aminoglycosides, which cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.
whyNot.B: RNA polymerase inhibition is rifampin, which colors body fluids orange and induces CYP450 but does not cause optic neuritis.
whyNot.C: This describes isoniazid, which causes hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy; optic neuritis is rare.
whyNot.D: This describes pyrazinamide, which causes hepatitis and hyperuricemia.

items.objective: Match ethambutol optic neuritis to the drug's mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man from Ohio developed fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain 3 weeks after a camping trip near Phoenix, Arizona, during a dust storm. He also has painful red nodules on both shins and aching knees. A chest x-ray shows a left lower lobe infiltrate with hilar adenopathy. Biopsy of a lung lesion shows large, thick-walled round structures filled with many small endospores. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
items.explanationHtml:
Pneumonia with erythema nodosum and arthralgia after dust exposure in the southwestern United States is coccidioidomycosis ("valley fever"). In tissue, Coccidioides forms large spherules filled with endospores, unlike the yeasts of the other dimorphic fungi. Most infections resolve; dissemination (skin, bone, meninges) is more likely in immunosuppression and pregnancy.

Takeaway: Spherules with endospores + southwestern US dust + erythema nodosum = Coccidioides.

whyNot.A: Blastomyces is acquired in the Ohio/Mississippi valleys and Great Lakes and appears as large yeasts with broad-based budding, not spherules.
whyNot.C: Cryptococcus appears as narrow-budding yeasts with a thick polysaccharide capsule and classically causes meningitis in AIDS.
whyNot.D: Histoplasma is acquired from bird or bat droppings in river valleys and appears as small yeasts inside macrophages.
whyNot.E: Sporothrix enters through skin punctures (rose thorns) and causes ascending lymphocutaneous nodules, with cigar-shaped yeasts in tissue.

items.objective: Identify coccidioidomycosis by geography and tissue form.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old man is receiving induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia. His absolute neutrophil count has been below 100/mm3 for 16 days. He develops fever despite broad-spectrum antibacterial antibiotics, pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis. CT of the chest shows a nodule surrounded by a halo of ground-glass opacity. A biopsy of the nodule shows invasion of blood vessels by the causative organism. Which of the following best describes the organism in tissue?

options.label: B
options.html: Delicate beaded filaments that are weakly acid-fast

options.label: D
options.html: Thin septate hyphae with dichotomous branching at about 45°

options.label: E
options.html: Wide, ribbon-like, sparsely septate forms with right-angle branches

items.explanationHtml:
Prolonged profound neutropenia, fever unresponsive to antibacterials, hemoptysis and a nodule with a halo sign (hemorrhage around an infarct) indicate invasive aspergillosis. Aspergillus forms narrow septate hyphae that branch at acute (about 45°) angles and invade vessels. Serum galactomannan supports the diagnosis; voriconazole is first-line treatment.

Takeaway: Invasive aspergillosis: neutropenia + halo sign; septate hyphae branching at acute angles that invade vessels.

whyNot.A: Budding yeasts with pseudohyphae describe Candida, which rarely causes a primary lung nodule.
whyNot.B: Beaded, weakly acid-fast filaments describe Nocardia, a bacterium that causes lung abscess and brain abscess in immunosuppression.
whyNot.C: Small intracellular yeasts describe Histoplasma, which is not angioinvasive.
whyNot.E: Broad, pauciseptate hyphae branching at right angles describe the Mucorales (mucormycosis), seen mainly in diabetic ketoacidosis and also in neutropenia; voriconazole does not cover them.

items.objective: Recognize invasive aspergillosis in neutropenia and its tissue morphology.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 90/mm3. Oxygen saturation falls from 94% at rest to 85% after walking. A chest x-ray shows bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacities. Silver stain of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid shows cysts shaped like crushed spheres. The first-line drug for this infection acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding to ergosterol and forming pores in the fungal membrane

options.label: B
options.html: Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit to block translocation

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase in ergosterol synthesis

options.label: E
options.html: Sequential inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase

items.explanationHtml:
This is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: CD4 count below 200/mm3, subacute dyspnea with exertional desaturation, bilateral ground-glass opacities and cysts on silver stain. First-line treatment is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, two sequential steps in folate synthesis. Pneumocystis lacks ergosterol in its membrane, so amphotericin and azoles are ineffective.

Takeaway: Pneumocystis is treated with TMP-SMX (two sequential folate-synthesis steps); its membrane lacks ergosterol.

whyNot.A: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol, which Pneumocystis lacks, so it is ineffective.
whyNot.B: Macrolides and clindamycin act on the 50S subunit; clindamycin is used only with primaquine as a second-line regimen.
whyNot.C: Echinocandins inhibit beta-glucan synthesis and act on the cyst form, but they are not first-line treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia.
whyNot.D: Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis, which is irrelevant to an organism without ergosterol.

items.objective: Identify Pneumocystis pneumonia and the mechanism of its first-line drug.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive, lying on his back, after a night of heavy drinking. He has poor dentition. Two weeks later he has fever, night sweats and cough with foul-smelling sputum. A chest x-ray shows a thick-walled cavity with an air–fluid level. Which of the following is the most likely location of the cavity?

options.label: A
options.html: Anterior basal segment of the left lower lobe

options.label: B
options.html: Anterior segment of the left upper lobe

options.label: C
options.html: Lingula of the left upper lobe

options.label: D
options.html: Medial segment of the right middle lobe

options.label: E
options.html: Posterior segment of the right upper lobe

items.explanationHtml:
Aspiration of oral anaerobes during reduced consciousness, followed 1–2 weeks later by a cavity with an air–fluid level and putrid sputum, is a lung abscess. Where aspirated material goes depends on posture: supine, it runs into the posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes; upright, into the basal segments of the lower lobes. The right side is favored because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.

Takeaway: Supine aspiration lands in the posterior upper-lobe or superior lower-lobe segments, usually on the right.

whyNot.A: The basal lower-lobe segments receive material aspirated in the upright position.
whyNot.B: The anterior upper-lobe segments are not dependent when a person lies on the back.
whyNot.C: The lingula lies anteriorly and on the left; it is not a dependent site for supine aspiration.
whyNot.D: The right middle lobe is anterior and is a site of aspiration mainly when prone, not supine.

items.objective: Predict the site of aspiration lung abscess from the patient's position.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman comes to the emergency department after a fall. CT of the chest, done to exclude rib fractures, shows no fractures but a solitary 9-mm solid nodule with smooth margins in the right lower lobe. She smoked 1 pack a day for 25 years and quit 8 years ago. She reports that she had chest CT at another hospital 3 years ago during an admission for pneumonia. She feels well. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain and compare the previous CT

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat CT of the chest in 12 months

items.explanationHtml:
The first step for any newly found nodule is to compare it with prior imaging. If the nodule was present 3 years ago and has not grown, a solid nodule stable for 2 years or more is very likely benign and needs no further workup. If it is new or has grown, the probability of cancer rises and the next step changes to PET-CT or tissue sampling.

Takeaway: old images first: they are cheap, safe and often settle the question.

whyNot.A: Biopsy carries a risk of pneumothorax and is premature until prior imaging shows whether the nodule is new or growing.
whyNot.C: PET-CT may be appropriate later for a new or growing 9-mm solid nodule, but only after the prior CT is reviewed.
whyNot.D: A fixed surveillance interval ignores the available prior CT, which could show stability (no follow-up) or growth (urgent workup).
whyNot.E: Surgical resection is for high-probability nodules; the probability cannot be judged without knowing the nodule's history.

items.objective: Obtain prior imaging as the first step in evaluating an incidental pulmonary nodule.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man who has never smoked has CT of the abdomen for kidney stones. The lung bases show a 1.6-cm, well-circumscribed nodule in the left lower lobe. Dedicated chest CT shows that the nodule contains fat attenuation and coarse, clumped calcifications. He has no symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT-guided needle biopsy of the nodule

items.explanationHtml:
Macroscopic fat with popcorn calcification is diagnostic of a pulmonary hamartoma. A nodule with a benign pattern of calcification or fat needs no further imaging, biopsy or surgery.

Takeaway: benign calcification or fat in a nodule = reassure; no follow-up is needed.

whyNot.A: Bronchoscopy has a low yield for peripheral nodules and is unnecessary here.
whyNot.B: Biopsy adds the risk of pneumothorax and cannot add certainty to a diagnostic CT appearance.
whyNot.D: PET-CT is used to characterize indeterminate solid nodules; this nodule is already characterized as benign.
whyNot.E: Short-interval CT is used for indeterminate nodules, not those with diagnostic benign features.

items.objective: Recognize benign CT features of a pulmonary nodule that end the workup.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman who has never smoked has CT angiography of the chest for pleuritic chest pain after a long flight. There is no pulmonary embolism. A 4-mm solid nodule with smooth margins is seen in the right upper lobe. She has no history of cancer and no occupational exposures. Her pain resolves with ibuprofen. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding the nodule?

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat CT of the chest in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
A solid nodule under 6 mm in a patient at low risk has a probability of cancer well under 1%. Follow-up imaging would add radiation, cost and anxiety without benefit, so no routine follow-up is recommended.

Takeaway: tiny solid nodule + low-risk patient = no follow-up.

whyNot.A: Annual low-dose CT is lung cancer screening for older adults with a heavy smoking history, which she does not have.
whyNot.B: A 4-mm nodule is too small to biopsy safely or reliably.
whyNot.D: PET-CT cannot reliably characterize nodules this small and would not change management.
whyNot.E: Short-interval CT is reserved for larger or higher-risk nodules.

items.objective: Apply size and risk to decide that a tiny incidental nodule needs no follow-up.

items.stemHtml:
A 64-year-old man has a chest CT for persistent cough after a respiratory infection. The cough has resolved. The findings are shown:

FeatureFinding
Nodule1.2 cm, solid, smooth margin, right upper lobe
Calcification or fatNone
Prior imagingChest CT 2 years ago: no nodule
Mediastinal nodesNot enlarged
Smoking history30 pack-years; quit 10 years ago

His FEV1 is 82% of predicted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat CT of the chest in 12 months

options.label: E
options.html: Sputum cytology on three morning samples

items.explanationHtml:
A new 1.2-cm solid nodule without benign features in a former heavy smoker carries an intermediate probability of cancer. PET-CT is the usual next step: avid uptake favors cancer (and also stages the mediastinum), whereas absent uptake in a solid nodule of this size lowers the probability enough to allow surveillance. Tissue sampling is the alternative or follow-on step.

Takeaway: new solid nodule over 8 mm, intermediate risk: PET-CT and/or biopsy, not watchful waiting alone.

whyNot.A: A new solid nodule in a former heavy smoker cannot be dismissed.
whyNot.C: Waiting a year is too long for a new, enlarging nodule with intermediate probability of cancer.
whyNot.D: Tumor markers are neither sensitive nor specific for lung cancer and do not guide nodule evaluation.
whyNot.E: Sputum cytology has low sensitivity for peripheral nodules and is not used in nodule workup.

items.objective: Choose PET-CT for a new solid nodule with intermediate probability of malignancy.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man who smokes 1 pack a day and has smoked for 50 years has a 2.2-cm spiculated nodule in the right upper lobe. It measured 1.4 cm on CT 1 year ago. PET-CT shows intense uptake in the nodule and no uptake in mediastinal nodes or elsewhere. Brain MRI is normal. He walks 3 km daily, and pulmonary function tests show an FEV1 of 78% of predicted and a normal diffusing capacity. He wants treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: A 2-week course of antibiotics, then repeat CT

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat CT of the chest in 3 months

options.label: E
options.html: Surgical resection with lymph node evaluation

items.explanationHtml:
A growing, spiculated, PET-avid upper-lobe nodule in a heavy smoker has a high probability of cancer, staging shows no spread, and he is fit for surgery. Proceeding to resection (usually lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node evaluation, with intraoperative diagnosis) both confirms and treats early lung cancer. Preoperative biopsy is reasonable when surgical risk is high or a nonsurgical diagnosis would change the plan.

Takeaway: high-probability nodule + negative staging + fit patient = surgery.

whyNot.A: Nothing suggests infection; a nodule growing over a year with spiculation is not an acute pneumonia.
whyNot.B: Chemoradiation is for patients who cannot have surgery or have nodal disease, and treatment without tissue is not appropriate when surgery is possible.
whyNot.C: Further surveillance delays curative treatment of a nodule that is already growing and PET-avid.
whyNot.D: Sputum cytology is insensitive for peripheral tumors and a negative result would not change the plan.

items.objective: Refer a fit patient with a high-probability, negatively staged nodule for surgical resection.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man has had a hoarse voice for 6 weeks. He has no fever, cough or sore throat. He has smoked 1 pack a day for 40 years and drinks 3 beers daily. He has occasional heartburn. Examination of the neck shows no masses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: A 3-month trial of a proton pump inhibitor

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the neck with contrast

options.label: E
options.html: Voice rest and reassessment in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Hoarseness lasting more than about 4 weeks, especially in a heavy smoker and drinker, needs direct visualization of the larynx to look for carcinoma or a benign lesion. Empiric reflux treatment or voice therapy before laryngoscopy risks delaying a cancer diagnosis.

Takeaway: persistent hoarseness in a smoker: look at the vocal folds first.

whyNot.A: Empiric proton pump inhibitor therapy before laryngoscopy can delay the diagnosis of laryngeal cancer in a high-risk patient.
whyNot.B: CT is used to stage a lesion seen on laryngoscopy, not as the first test; it cannot assess mucosal lesions well.
whyNot.D: Voice therapy treats nodules and functional dysphonia, but only after laryngoscopy shows the cause.
whyNot.E: Watchful waiting is not appropriate after 6 weeks of hoarseness in a smoker.

items.objective: Order laryngoscopy for persistent hoarseness in a smoker before empiric therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a hoarse voice for 5 months. He plays on two hockey teams and his parents say he "shouts constantly". He has no breathing difficulty or swallowing problems. Laryngoscopy shows small, symmetric nodules on both vocal folds at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds, with normal vocal fold movement. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: A proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Voice therapy with a speech-language pathologist

items.explanationHtml:
Vocal fold nodules are reactive lesions caused by phonotrauma. Voice therapy to change how the voice is used is first-line and often curative, especially in children; surgery is reserved for persistent nodules after adequate therapy, because nodules recur if the vocal behavior does not change.

Takeaway: vocal fold nodules: voice therapy first.

whyNot.A: Systemic steroids do not resolve fibrotic nodules and carry avoidable adverse effects in a child.
whyNot.B: Reflux therapy has no role without reflux symptoms and does not treat phonotrauma nodules.
whyNot.C: Laser ablation is used for papillomas, not for reactive nodules in a child.
whyNot.D: Surgery is a last resort for nodules that persist despite voice therapy; without behavior change they recur.

items.objective: Treat vocal fold nodules first with voice therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a third episode in 2 months of heavy bleeding from the left nostril. The bleeding stopped with pressure. He has had left nasal stuffiness for 6 months. Pulse is 96/min and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Anterior rhinoscopy shows no bleeding point on the septum. Nasal endoscopy shows a smooth, reddish, lobulated mass in the posterior left nasal cavity. Hemoglobin is 11.6 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the skull base

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge with nasal saline and a humidifier

options.label: C
options.html: Endoscopic biopsy of the mass in the clinic

options.label: E
options.html: Silver nitrate cautery of the mass

items.explanationHtml:
The picture is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. The diagnosis is made by contrast imaging, which shows an enhancing mass centred on the sphenopalatine foramen and maps its extent for surgery. Biopsy is avoided because of the risk of severe hemorrhage. Treatment is preoperative embolization then (usually endoscopic) resection.

Takeaway: suspected angiofibroma: image, do not biopsy.

whyNot.B: Recurrent heavy unilateral bleeding with a posterior mass is not a minor nosebleed; discharging him misses a tumor.
whyNot.C: Office biopsy can cause life-threatening bleeding from this highly vascular tumor.
whyNot.D: Nothing suggests infection, and antibiotics do not address the mass.
whyNot.E: Cautery treats a visible anterior septal vessel, not a vascular tumor, and could provoke major bleeding.

items.objective: Image, rather than biopsy, a suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman has asthma controlled with an inhaled glucocorticoid. She has had nasal obstruction and loss of smell for a year, and twice she wheezed and became congested within an hour of taking naproxen. Examination shows bilateral pale, smooth polyps in the middle meatus. She has avoided NSAIDs since. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for her nasal polyps?
items.explanationHtml:
She has aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease with chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps. First-line treatment of polyps is a topical intranasal glucocorticoid with saline irrigation, together with strict avoidance of aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs. Short oral steroid bursts, leukotriene modifiers, sinus surgery, aspirin desensitization and type 2 biologics are escalation steps.

Takeaway: nasal polyps: intranasal steroid first; escalate to surgery or biologics when it fails.

whyNot.A: Long antibiotic courses do not treat type 2 eosinophilic polyps without bacterial sinusitis.
whyNot.B: Months of systemic glucocorticoids cause serious adverse effects and are not used as maintenance therapy for polyps.
whyNot.C: Surgery is for polyps that do not respond to adequate medical therapy, and they often regrow afterwards.
whyNot.E: Antihistamines help allergic rhinitis symptoms but do not shrink nasal polyps.

items.objective: Start intranasal glucocorticoids as first-line treatment for nasal polyps.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has had obstruction of the right nostril for 5 months and occasional blood-tinged nasal discharge. He worked for 30 years as a furniture maker. The left nasal cavity is normal. Endoscopy shows a single, irregular, polypoid mass arising from the right lateral nasal wall. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Intranasal glucocorticoid spray and reassessment in 3 months

options.label: C
options.html: Office polypectomy of the mass without histology

options.label: D
options.html: Sinus CT followed by tissue biopsy

items.explanationHtml:
A unilateral nasal mass in an older adult, with bleeding, is not an ordinary inflammatory polyp. It may be an inverted papilloma or a carcinoma; wood-dust exposure raises the risk of sinonasal adenocarcinoma. CT defines the extent and bone erosion, and biopsy gives the diagnosis.

Takeaway: unilateral nasal polyp in an adult: image and biopsy.

whyNot.A: Allergy testing addresses rhinitis and bilateral symptoms, not a unilateral bleeding mass.
whyNot.B: A steroid trial delays the diagnosis of a possible neoplasm; steroids shrink only inflammatory polyps.
whyNot.C: Removing the mass without histology could miss carcinoma or leave an inverted papilloma incompletely treated.
whyNot.E: Sweat chloride testing is for nasal polyps in children, in whom cystic fibrosis is likely.

items.objective: Image and biopsy a unilateral nasal mass in an adult to exclude neoplasm.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman who has never smoked has a 9-mm pure ground-glass nodule in the left upper lobe on CT done for chest pain. Follow-up CT 4 months later shows the same nodule, unchanged in size and still without a solid component. She has no symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Empiric antibiotics and repeat CT in 6 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
A pure ground-glass nodule that persists after a few months is not an infection; it may be adenocarcinoma in situ or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, which grows very slowly. These lesions are managed with prolonged CT surveillance (about 5 years), with resection if the nodule grows or develops a solid component.

Takeaway: persistent pure ground-glass nodule: long CT follow-up, not PET and not immediate surgery.

whyNot.B: Persistence after 4 months already argues against infection; antibiotics add nothing.
whyNot.C: Immediate lobectomy over-treats a lesion that may never progress; resection is reserved for growth or a new solid component.
whyNot.D: Stability over a few months does not exclude slow-growing adenocarcinoma, so follow-up is needed.
whyNot.E: PET-CT is often falsely negative in ground-glass lesions because their metabolic activity is low.

items.objective: Manage a persistent pure ground-glass nodule with prolonged CT surveillance.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has a chest CT after a motor vehicle collision. It shows a 1.8-cm, smoothly marginated nodule in the periphery of the left lower lobe. The nodule contains areas of fat attenuation and clumps of coarse calcification. A chest radiograph taken 6 years earlier showed a smaller nodule in the same place. The nodule is later removed during surgery for an unrelated reason. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on microscopic examination?

options.label: A
options.html: Atypical columnar cells spreading along intact alveolar walls

options.label: B
options.html: Islands of mature hyaline cartilage mixed with fat and clefts lined by respiratory epithelium

options.label: C
options.html: Necrotizing granulomas surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells

options.label: D
options.html: Nests of uniform cells with finely granular chromatin in a vascular stroma

options.label: E
options.html: Sheets of keratinizing squamous cells with intercellular bridges

items.explanationHtml:
A slowly growing, smooth peripheral nodule containing fat and popcorn calcification is a pulmonary hamartoma, the most common benign lung tumor. It is a disorganized mixture of mature cartilage, fat, smooth muscle and connective tissue with entrapped respiratory epithelium; the calcified cartilage produces the popcorn pattern.

Takeaway: fat plus popcorn calcification in a lung nodule means hamartoma: cartilage, fat and epithelial clefts.

whyNot.A: Lepidic growth of atypical columnar cells is adenocarcinoma in situ or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, which looks like ground glass, not fat and popcorn calcification.
whyNot.C: Necrotizing granulomas explain a calcified granuloma, but granulomas do not contain fat.
whyNot.D: Nests of uniform neuroendocrine cells describe a carcinoid tumor, which does not contain fat and is usually central.
whyNot.E: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma grows quickly, has irregular margins and contains no fat.

items.objective: Identify the histologic composition of a pulmonary hamartoma from its CT features.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a hoarse voice that has worsened over 8 months. For the past month her parents have heard noisy breathing when she runs. Her mother had anogenital warts during the pregnancy, and the girl was delivered vaginally. Flexible laryngoscopy shows multiple exophytic, wart-like masses on both vocal folds. Infection with which of the following is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is caused by the low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, the same types that cause anogenital warts. Juvenile disease follows exposure during vaginal birth and presents with progressive hoarseness, then stridor as papillomas narrow the glottis. Lesions recur because latent virus persists in adjacent mucosa.

Takeaway: wart-like laryngeal masses in a young child mean HPV 6/11 papillomatosis.

whyNot.A: Adenovirus causes pharyngitis, conjunctivitis and pneumonia but not papillomas.
whyNot.B: Epstein-Barr virus is linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma and lymphomas, not laryngeal papillomas.
whyNot.C: Herpes simplex causes vesicles and ulcers, not persistent exophytic masses.
whyNot.D: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types that drive carcinoma; papillomatosis is caused by the low-risk types.

items.objective: Identify HPV 6 and 11 as the cause of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy has had five episodes of heavy bleeding from the right nostril over 3 months, and he has had trouble breathing through the right side of his nose. He has no bleeding elsewhere and takes no medications. Endoscopy shows a smooth, red, lobulated mass filling the posterior right nasal cavity. Platelet count and coagulation studies are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent, heavy, unilateral epistaxis with nasal obstruction and a vascular-looking posterior nasal mass in an adolescent boy is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. The tumor arises near the sphenopalatine foramen and contains many thin-walled vessels without a normal muscle coat, so it bleeds readily.

Takeaway: teenage boy + recurrent unilateral epistaxis + posterior nasal mass = angiofibroma; image it, do not biopsy it in the office.

whyNot.A: An antrochoanal polyp is a pale, gray, nonvascular polyp that causes obstruction but not repeated heavy bleeding.
whyNot.B: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a rapidly growing malignancy of younger children that tends to cause proptosis or a fleshy mass, not years-long recurrent bleeds in a teen.
whyNot.C: Inverted papilloma occurs in older adults and arises from the lateral nasal wall; heavy bleeding is not typical.
whyNot.E: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma occurs mainly in adults, often presents with a neck mass or serous otitis media, and is linked to Epstein-Barr virus.

items.objective: Diagnose juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma from age, sex and recurrent unilateral epistaxis.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has asthma and has lost her sense of smell over 2 years. Examination shows bilateral pale, grape-like masses in the nasal cavities. Forty minutes after she takes ibuprofen for a headache she develops wheezing, nasal congestion, watery rhinorrhea and facial flushing. Serum IgE specific for ibuprofen is not detected. Which of the following best explains her reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Accumulation of bradykinin from inhibition of its breakdown

options.label: B
options.html: Activation of complement by circulating drug-antibody complexes

options.label: C
options.html: Direct histamine release caused by opioid receptor binding on mast cells

options.label: D
options.html: IgE-mediated mast cell activation by a drug-protein conjugate

options.label: E
options.html: Shunting of arachidonic acid toward overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes

items.explanationHtml:
This is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: asthma, nasal polyps and respiratory reactions to COX-1 inhibitors. Inhibiting COX-1 lowers protective prostaglandin E2, which normally restrains 5-lipoxygenase and mast cells, so arachidonic acid flows into the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and cysteinyl leukotrienes rise, causing bronchoconstriction and nasal symptoms. The reaction is pharmacologic, not IgE-mediated, and occurs with any nonselective NSAID.

Takeaway: asthma + nasal polyps + NSAID reaction = leukotriene overproduction after COX-1 inhibition.

whyNot.A: Bradykinin accumulation explains ACE inhibitor angioedema and cough, not NSAID-triggered bronchospasm with nasal polyps.
whyNot.B: Immune-complex reactions (serum sickness) appear days after exposure with fever, rash and arthralgia.
whyNot.C: Direct mast cell release by opioids causes flushing and itch but ibuprofen is not an opioid.
whyNot.D: A true IgE-mediated drug allergy is specific to one drug; this reaction is a class effect of COX-1 inhibitors and no drug-specific IgE is found.

items.objective: Explain the leukotriene mechanism of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for chronic nasal congestion and recurrent sinusitis. Examination shows bilateral nasal polyps. He has had two episodes of pneumonia and frequent bulky, foul-smelling stools. His height and weight are below the 5th percentile. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: B
options.html: Absent dynein arms in ciliary axonemes

options.label: C
options.html: Deficient secretory IgA at the mucosal surface

options.label: D
options.html: Impaired NADPH oxidase activity in neutrophils

options.label: E
options.html: Misfolded chloride channel retained in the endoplasmic reticulum

items.explanationHtml:
Nasal polyps in a child, with recurrent lung infections, steatorrhea and failure to thrive, indicate cystic fibrosis. The most common CFTR variant (F508del) produces a misfolded chloride channel that is degraded before it reaches the apical membrane, so secretions become thick and dehydrated. The sweat chloride test confirms it.

Takeaway: a child with nasal polyps needs a sweat chloride test.

whyNot.A: Chediak-Higashi syndrome causes albinism, neuropathy and pyogenic infections, not pancreatic insufficiency.
whyNot.B: Primary ciliary dyskinesia causes sinusitis and bronchiectasis, but not pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea, and polyps are less typical.
whyNot.C: Selective IgA deficiency causes sinopulmonary infections but not fat malabsorption from pancreatic failure or growth failure of this degree.
whyNot.D: Chronic granulomatous disease causes catalase-positive bacterial and fungal abscesses, not nasal polyps and steatorrhea.

items.objective: Link pediatric nasal polyps to cystic fibrosis and its CFTR defect.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman who teaches kindergarten has a hoarse, breathy voice that is worse at the end of each school week and improves during vacations. She does not smoke. Laryngoscopy shows small, symmetric, pale swellings on both vocal folds at the junction of their anterior and middle thirds. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of these lesions?

options.label: A
options.html: Clonal proliferation of squamous epithelium driven by viral oncoproteins

options.label: B
options.html: Extracellular deposition of misfolded light-chain protein

options.label: C
options.html: Granulomatous inflammation around an inhaled foreign material

options.label: D
options.html: Malignant invasion of the basement membrane by atypical squamous cells

options.label: E
options.html: Reactive edema and fibrosis of the lamina propria from repeated mechanical trauma

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral, symmetric swellings at the point of maximal vocal fold contact in a heavy voice user are vocal fold nodules. Repeated collision during phonation injures the superficial lamina propria, which responds with edema and then fibrosis. They are reactive and benign, and voice therapy is first-line.

Takeaway: nodules = bilateral, anterior-middle third junction, phonotrauma.

whyNot.A: Viral oncoproteins drive HPV papillomas, which are exophytic and wart-like rather than small symmetric swellings.
whyNot.B: Laryngeal amyloidosis is rare and produces waxy deposits, not lesions that fluctuate with voice use.
whyNot.C: Granulomas of the larynx occur at the posterior folds after intubation or reflux, not symmetric mid-fold swellings.
whyNot.D: Invasive carcinoma would not wax and wane with vacations, is usually unilateral and occurs mainly in smokers.

items.objective: Explain the phonotrauma pathogenesis and location of vocal fold nodules.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man who grew up in southern Ohio and spends weekends exploring caves has a chest radiograph before a job physical. It shows a 1.2-cm densely calcified nodule in the right middle lobe and calcified right hilar lymph nodes. He has no symptoms. If the nodule were examined microscopically, which of the following would most likely be found within the granulomas?

options.label: A
options.html: Budding yeasts surrounded by a thick polysaccharide capsule

options.label: C
options.html: Large yeasts with thick walls and broad-based budding

options.label: D
options.html: Septate hyphae branching at acute angles

options.label: E
options.html: Tiny oval yeasts packed inside histiocytes

items.explanationHtml:
Calcified nodules with calcified hilar nodes in someone from the Ohio River valley who explores caves (bat and bird droppings) are the healed scar of histoplasmosis. Histoplasma capsulatum appears as tiny yeasts packed inside macrophages. Calcified granulomas are the most common cause of a benign solitary nodule.

Takeaway: dense or central calcification in a nodule usually means an old granuloma; in the Ohio/Mississippi valleys think histoplasmosis.

whyNot.A: Cryptococcus has a thick polysaccharide capsule and is associated with pigeon droppings and meningitis.
whyNot.B: Spherules with endospores are Coccidioides, from the desert Southwest, not the Ohio River valley.
