whyNot.C: Broad-based budding yeasts are Blastomyces, which causes pulmonary and skin disease and is less often seen as an incidental calcified nodule.
whyNot.D: Acute-angle septate hyphae are Aspergillus, which forms fungus balls in cavities rather than calcified granulomas with calcified nodes.

items.objective: Recognize a calcified granuloma from histoplasmosis as a benign solitary nodule.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man has had blockage of the left side of his nose and occasional blood-streaked discharge for 6 months. Endoscopy shows a single fleshy, polypoid mass arising from the left lateral nasal wall. The mass is excised. Microscopy shows thickened squamous epithelium growing downward into the stroma as smooth-contoured nests with an intact basement membrane. Complete excision and close follow-up are needed mainly because this lesion has which of the following characteristics?

options.label: A
options.html: It belongs to an aspirin-sensitivity syndrome with asthma

options.label: B
options.html: It carries a risk of malignant transformation

options.label: C
options.html: It is the usual source of severe posterior epistaxis

options.label: D
options.html: It regresses with intranasal steroid treatment

options.label: E
options.html: It signals an underlying CFTR channel defect

items.explanationHtml:
A unilateral polypoid mass from the lateral nasal wall with epithelium that grows inward (endophytic) is a sinonasal inverted papilloma. It recurs if incompletely removed and is associated with squamous cell carcinoma in a minority of patients, either at presentation or later, so it is excised completely and followed.

Takeaway: unilateral nasal polyp in an adult = rule out inverted papilloma or carcinoma; inverted papilloma is removed completely because of its link to carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease causes bilateral inflammatory polyps, not a unilateral endophytic papilloma.
whyNot.C: Severe posterior epistaxis usually comes from branches of the sphenopalatine artery, not from inverted papillomas.
whyNot.D: Inflammatory polyps shrink with steroids; inverted papillomas are neoplasms and do not regress.
whyNot.E: CFTR defects cause bilateral inflammatory polyps in children, not unilateral inverted papillomas in older adults.

items.objective: Recognize inverted papilloma and its association with squamous cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman comes for a routine visit. She smoked 1 pack per day from age 20 until she quit at age 48. She has hypertension controlled with amlodipine and feels well. Her examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for lung cancer screening?

options.label: A
options.html: A single low-dose CT, repeated only if symptoms arise

options.label: D
options.html: No screening, because she no longer smokes

options.label: E
options.html: Yearly low-dose CT after shared decision-making

items.explanationHtml:
She is 57 with 28 pack-years and quit 9 years ago, so she meets the US Preventive Services Task Force criteria: age 50–80, ≥ 20 pack-years, currently smoking or quit within 15 years. Screening is annual low-dose CT, after a shared decision-making discussion of benefits and harms, until she has been smoke-free 15 years or her health limits curative treatment.

Takeaway: 50–80 years, ≥ 20 pack-years, quit < 15 years ago → annual low-dose CT.

whyNot.A: Screening is annual while she remains eligible, not a single scan.
whyNot.B: Sputum cytology is not recommended for screening.
whyNot.C: Chest radiography does not reduce lung cancer mortality and is not a screening test.
whyNot.D: Former smokers who quit within the past 15 years still qualify.

items.objective: Apply lung cancer screening eligibility criteria.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man who smokes has 2 weeks of facial swelling and fullness in his head that is worse when he bends forward. He is short of breath on exertion but has no stridor, and he is alert. Pulse is 96/min, blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. His face is plethoric, his neck veins are distended and do not pulsate, and there are dilated veins over the upper chest. Contrast CT shows a 7-cm right paratracheal mass compressing the superior vena cava, with no other lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Emergency radiation therapy to the mediastinum

options.label: B
options.html: Endovascular stent placement in the superior vena cava

items.explanationHtml:
He has superior vena cava syndrome from a mediastinal mass, but no stridor, laryngeal edema or confusion. Because treatment depends on histology (small cell carcinoma and lymphoma are treated with chemotherapy, other tumors with radiation or stenting), the next step is tissue diagnosis, for example by EBUS-guided aspiration or mediastinoscopy. Elevate the head of the bed meanwhile.

Takeaway: stable SVC syndrome → biopsy before treatment; stridor or cerebral edema → urgent stent.

whyNot.A: Radiation before a tissue diagnosis may obscure histology, and he is stable without airway or brain compromise.
whyNot.B: Stenting is first for stridor, laryngeal edema or confusion; this stable patient can have a diagnosis first.
whyNot.C: Steroids help mainly in steroid-responsive tumors such as lymphoma and can confound a lymphoma biopsy; they do not replace diagnosis.
whyNot.D: This obstruction is from extrinsic tumor compression, not primarily thrombus.

items.objective: Manage superior vena cava syndrome in a stable patient.

items.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old woman with a 50-pack-year history is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of confusion and vomiting. She takes no medications. Laboratory studies:

TestResult
Calcium, total14.1 mg/dL
Phosphorus2.4 mg/dL
Albumin3.8 g/dL
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.9)
Intact PTH6 pg/mL (normal 10–65)
PTH-related peptideElevated

Chest x-ray shows a 5-cm left hilar mass. Her mucous membranes are dry. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Severe symptomatic PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia (squamous cell carcinoma) with volume depletion and prerenal injury. Start with IV isotonic saline to restore volume and calciuresis, add calcitonin for a quick fall, and give a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid; dose-adjusted for kidney function) or denosumab for sustained control.

Takeaway: hypercalcemia of malignancy: IV saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate.

whyNot.A: Loop diuretics are used only after volume repletion, if at all; alone they worsen dehydration.
whyNot.B: Dialysis is reserved for very severe hypercalcemia with renal failure or heart failure that cannot take fluids.
whyNot.C: Thiazides raise serum calcium.
whyNot.E: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia needs active treatment.

items.objective: Treat severe hypercalcemia of malignancy.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man who smokes has a 3.2-cm spiculated left lower lobe mass on CT. PET-CT shows uptake in the mass and in an enlarged subcarinal lymph node; there is no other uptake. Brain MRI is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: CT-guided transthoracic biopsy of the lung mass

options.label: B
options.html: EBUS-guided needle aspiration of the subcarinal node

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat CT of the chest in 3 months

options.label: E
options.html: Sputum cytology on three morning samples

items.explanationHtml:
Sample the site that would give the highest stage, so one procedure provides both diagnosis and staging. A PET-positive subcarinal node (N2) is reached by EBUS-guided transbronchial needle aspiration. Positive N2 disease usually means chemoradiation-based therapy rather than upfront surgery.

Takeaway: in suspected lung cancer, biopsy the lesion that establishes the highest stage, often a mediastinal node by EBUS.

whyNot.A: Biopsying the primary diagnoses but does not stage; sampling the node does both.
whyNot.C: Surgery before mediastinal staging risks operating on N2 disease that is better treated nonsurgically.
whyNot.D: A PET-avid spiculated mass with a positive node needs tissue now, not surveillance.
whyNot.E: Sputum cytology has low sensitivity and gives no staging information.

items.objective: Choose the diagnostic procedure that both diagnoses and stages suspected lung cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman has a 2.4-cm peripheral right upper lobe nodule. CT-guided biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. PET-CT and EBUS show no nodal or distant disease, and brain MRI is normal. FEV1 and DLCO are 82% and 78% of predicted. She walks 3 km daily. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node sampling

options.label: D
options.html: Stereotactic body radiotherapy to the nodule

options.label: E
options.html: Surveillance CT of the chest every 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
This is stage I non-small cell lung cancer in a fit patient with adequate lung function. Curative treatment is anatomic resection (lobectomy, or segmentectomy for small peripheral tumors) with lymph node sampling. Molecular testing of the specimen guides any adjuvant therapy.

Takeaway: early-stage NSCLC in a fit patient → surgical resection; SBRT if inoperable.

whyNot.A: Chemoradiation is for unresectable stage III disease.
whyNot.B: Systemic therapy alone is for metastatic disease.
whyNot.D: SBRT is the alternative for medically inoperable patients; she is fit for surgery.
whyNot.E: A proven early-stage cancer in a fit patient should be treated with curative intent.

items.objective: Choose curative treatment for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with a 60-pack-year history has a 6-cm central left mass with bulky mediastinal nodes. Biopsy shows small cell carcinoma. Staging finds 3 liver metastases. His performance status is good. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Extensive-stage small cell lung cancer is treated with systemic therapy: a platinum drug with etoposide plus a PD-L1 inhibitor. The response is often dramatic but relapse is common. Brain imaging and early palliative care belong alongside.

Takeaway: SCLC is a systemic disease: chemoimmunotherapy (extensive) or chemoradiation (limited), not surgery.

whyNot.A: Targeted EGFR therapy is for EGFR-mutated adenocarcinoma, not small cell carcinoma.
whyNot.B: With good performance status, chemoimmunotherapy prolongs survival; palliative care should be added, not substituted, unless he declines.
whyNot.D: Surgery has no role in metastatic small cell carcinoma.
whyNot.E: Radiation alone does not treat liver metastases.

items.objective: Choose first-line treatment for extensive-stage small cell lung carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has had a hoarse voice for 7 weeks. He has smoked 1 pack per day for 40 years and drinks 4 beers daily. He has no fever, sore throat, dysphagia or weight loss. His neck examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: A 4-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor

options.label: E
options.html: Voice rest and reassessment in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Hoarseness lasting more than about 4 weeks, especially in a person who smokes and drinks, needs visualization of the larynx (flexible laryngoscopy) to look for glottic carcinoma, which causes early hoarseness. Empiric treatments and imaging should not come first.

Takeaway: persistent hoarseness in a smoker → laryngoscopy.

whyNot.A: Empiric acid suppression before visualizing the larynx can delay a cancer diagnosis.
whyNot.B: Imaging comes after the larynx has been visualized, not instead of it.
whyNot.D: Steroids are not indicated for undiagnosed hoarseness.
whyNot.E: Persistent hoarseness in a smoker and drinker needs prompt visualization.

items.objective: Evaluate persistent hoarseness in an adult at risk of laryngeal cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man has a 3-cm firm, nontender mass in the right upper neck for 6 weeks. It did not shrink after a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate. He has smoked for 35 years. He has no fever. The mass is mobile and lies anterior to the sternocleidomastoid. Flexible laryngoscopy shows no obvious mucosal lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: A second, longer course of antibiotics

options.label: C
options.html: Open excisional biopsy of the mass

items.explanationHtml:
A persistent firm neck mass in an adult smoker is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. After head and neck examination and laryngoscopy, obtain fine-needle aspiration (with p16/HPV testing) and contrast CT of the neck; look for an occult primary in the oropharynx and nasopharynx.

Takeaway: adult neck mass that persists → FNA, not open excision.

whyNot.A: A firm mass that persisted through antibiotics in a smoker needs tissue, not more antibiotics.
whyNot.C: Open excision of a possible metastatic squamous node can spill tumor and complicate definitive treatment; FNA comes first.
whyNot.D: The mass is lateral and anterior to the sternocleidomastoid, not in the thyroid.
whyNot.E: Observation delays diagnosis of a likely malignancy.

items.objective: Evaluate a persistent neck mass in an adult at risk for head and neck cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma has 2 days of worsening back pain and new leg weakness. He has difficulty walking and has not voided since last night. Strength is 3/5 in both legs, and there is a sensory level at the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.html: IV dexamethasone and urgent whole-spine MRI

options.label: D
options.html: Start a bisphosphonate and arrange physiotherapy

options.label: E
options.html: Technetium bone scan of the skeleton

items.explanationHtml:
Back pain with leg weakness, a sensory level and urinary retention in a patient with cancer is malignant spinal cord compression. Give high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and obtain an urgent MRI of the whole spine (multiple levels are common), then radiation and/or surgical decompression. Function at the start of treatment predicts outcome.

Takeaway: suspected cord compression: steroids now, whole-spine MRI now, then radiation or surgery.

whyNot.B: LP is not diagnostic and may worsen a compressive lesion.
whyNot.C: Outpatient imaging is too slow for suspected cord compression with deficits.
whyNot.D: This does not address an emergency that threatens permanent paralysis.
whyNot.E: A bone scan does not define cord compression.

items.objective: Manage malignant spinal cord compression.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with newly diagnosed metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (bone and liver) is beginning treatment. She has moderate pain, poor appetite and low mood, and her oncologist plans systemic therapy once molecular test results return. She asks whether starting palliative care means stopping cancer treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Palliative care begins only when no further cancer treatment is available

options.label: B
options.html: Palliative care can start now alongside cancer treatment and is linked to better quality of life

options.label: C
options.html: Palliative care is appropriate only when life expectancy is below 6 months

options.label: D
options.html: Palliative care requires her to stop systemic therapy

options.label: E
options.html: Palliative care will be considered after the first restaging scan

items.explanationHtml:
For patients with metastatic NSCLC, early palliative care integrated with oncologic care improves quality of life and mood, with no shortening of survival. It addresses pain, appetite, mood and goals of care while cancer treatment continues.

Takeaway: palliative care is for symptoms and goals at any stage, concurrent with cancer treatment; hospice is different.

whyNot.A: This outdated sequence delays symptom control; concurrent care is recommended.
whyNot.C: That describes hospice eligibility, not palliative care.
whyNot.D: Palliative care is compatible with active treatment; hospice enrolment is a separate decision.
whyNot.E: There is no reason to wait; her symptoms need attention now.

items.objective: Explain the role of early concurrent palliative care in metastatic lung cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has a 4-cm right lower lobe adenocarcinoma with metastases to bone and the adrenal gland. She has never smoked. Tissue testing shows an activating EGFR mutation, and PD-L1 is expressed in 60% of tumor cells. Her performance status is good. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line systemic therapy?

options.label: A
options.html: A PD-1 inhibitor alone, given the high PD-L1 expression

options.label: D
options.html: Cisplatin with etoposide and thoracic radiation

items.explanationHtml:
In metastatic NSCLC with a targetable driver, targeted therapy is first line regardless of PD-L1. An EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (a third-generation agent such as osimertinib) gives higher response rates and longer disease control than chemotherapy, and immunotherapy is of limited benefit in EGFR-mutant tumors.

Takeaway: driver mutation present → targeted therapy first, even with high PD-L1.

whyNot.A: Checkpoint inhibitors work poorly in EGFR-driven tumors and add toxicity before or with EGFR inhibitors; the driver takes priority over PD-L1.
whyNot.B: Anti-angiogenic therapy is not used alone as first-line treatment.
whyNot.D: This is the regimen for limited-stage small cell carcinoma.
whyNot.E: Chemotherapy alone is inferior when a targetable driver is present.

items.objective: Select first-line therapy for metastatic EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has 3 weeks of constipation, increased thirst and confusion. A chest x-ray shows a 4-cm right hilar mass with central cavitation. Serum calcium is 13.6 mg/dL, phosphorus is 2.6 mg/dL and PTH is low. A biopsy of the mass is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Glands lined by mucin-producing columnar cells

options.label: B
options.html: Large undifferentiated cells without glands or keratin

options.label: C
options.html: Nests of polygonal cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges

options.label: D
options.html: Sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding

options.label: E
options.html: Uniform cells in organoid nests with fine granular chromatin

items.explanationHtml:
A central, cavitating mass in a heavy smoker with hypercalcemia, low phosphate and suppressed PTH points to squamous cell carcinoma secreting PTH-related peptide. PTHrP acts on the PTH receptor, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption and lowering phosphate reabsorption, while the parathyroids switch off.

Takeaway: central + cavitation + PTHrP hypercalcemia = squamous cell carcinoma, recognized by keratin pearls.

whyNot.A: Adenocarcinoma is usually peripheral and is not the classic source of PTHrP hypercalcemia.
whyNot.B: Large cell carcinoma is usually peripheral and is not linked to PTHrP.
whyNot.D: Small cell carcinoma is central but causes SIADH or ectopic ACTH, not PTHrP hypercalcemia, and rarely cavitates.
whyNot.E: A carcinoid tumor is a central endobronchial polyp; it does not cause PTHrP hypercalcemia.

items.objective: Identify squamous cell lung carcinoma from location, cavitation and PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman who has never smoked has a 2.5-cm peripheral nodule in the right upper lobe. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. Tumor DNA sequencing finds an exon 19 deletion in a gene encoding a cell-surface receptor. The drug chosen for her acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding and neutralizing vascular endothelial growth factor

options.label: B
options.html: Blocking the PD-1 receptor on activated T lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibiting farnesylation and membrane localization of Ras

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibiting the receptor's intracellular tyrosine kinase activity

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibiting tubulin polymerization in dividing tumor cells

items.explanationHtml:
Exon 19 deletions activate the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), a receptor tyrosine kinase, most often in adenocarcinoma of people who never smoked. Small-molecule EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., osimertinib) compete at the ATP-binding site and shut off downstream signalling.

Takeaway: never-smoker adenocarcinoma with an EGFR mutation is treated with an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

whyNot.A: Anti-VEGF therapy targets angiogenesis, not the tumor's mutated receptor.
whyNot.B: Checkpoint blockade is used when no targetable driver is present; it does not target the mutated receptor.
whyNot.C: Farnesyltransferase inhibitors are not used for lung cancer, and the mutated gene here is a receptor, not Ras.
whyNot.E: Taxanes and vinca alkaloids are cytotoxic, not targeted at a driver mutation.

items.objective: Link an activating EGFR mutation in lung adenocarcinoma to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man who smokes has 2 months of weakness. He has trouble climbing stairs and getting up from a chair, and has a dry mouth. Proximal leg strength is reduced at first but improves over several seconds of sustained effort. Deep tendon reflexes are absent but appear after brief exercise. A chest CT shows a central mass with bulky mediastinal nodes. The weakness is most likely caused by antibodies against which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
This is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, usually paraneoplastic with small cell lung carcinoma. Antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce calcium entry and acetylcholine release. Repeated activation builds up residual calcium, so strength and reflexes improve briefly with effort; autonomic symptoms (dry mouth) are common.

Takeaway: proximal weakness that improves with use, areflexia and dry mouth in a smoker = Lambert-Eaton, from small cell carcinoma.

whyNot.A: MuSK antibodies cause a myasthenia variant with bulbar weakness; strength does not improve with effort.
whyNot.B: Anti-Hu causes sensory neuronopathy or encephalomyelitis with small cell cancer, not neuromuscular junction failure.
whyNot.C: Myasthenia gravis gives fatigable, not improving, weakness with ocular involvement and normal reflexes.
whyNot.E: These antibodies cause neuromyotonia or limbic encephalitis, not facilitating weakness.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome and its association with small cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man who smokes has severe right shoulder pain radiating down the inner arm for 4 months. He has wasting of the small muscles of the right hand. His right upper eyelid droops and the right pupil is smaller than the left; the difference is greatest in dim light. The forehead on the right is dry. Which structure is the tumor also most likely compressing?
items.explanationHtml:
An apical (superior sulcus, Pancoast) tumor invades the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1: medial arm pain, intrinsic hand wasting) and the cervical sympathetic chain, producing ipsilateral Horner syndrome: ptosis from loss of the superior tarsal muscle, miosis that is most obvious in the dark, and facial anhidrosis.

Takeaway: shoulder pain + hand wasting + Horner syndrome = superior sulcus tumor.

whyNot.B: A third nerve palsy causes ptosis with a dilated, not small, pupil and eye movement deficits.
whyNot.C: Phrenic involvement paralyses the hemidiaphragm; it does not affect the eye.
whyNot.D: Recurrent laryngeal involvement causes hoarseness, not ptosis and miosis; and the right nerve loops under the subclavian, not the apex.
whyNot.E: SVC obstruction causes facial and arm swelling with distended veins, not Horner syndrome.

items.objective: Localize a superior sulcus tumor from brachial plexus and sympathetic chain findings.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with a 45-pack-year history has 3 weeks of nausea, headache and confusion. Serum sodium is 121 mEq/L, serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg. She is clinically euvolemic. CT shows a large central mass. Immunohistochemistry of the tumor is most likely positive for which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine is SIADH. The classic lung source is small cell carcinoma, a central neuroendocrine tumor whose cells stain for chromogranin, synaptophysin and CD56.

Takeaway: SIADH with a central mass = small cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor (chromogranin, synaptophysin).

whyNot.A: Calretinin marks mesothelioma, a pleural tumor.
whyNot.C: These mark squamous cell carcinoma, which causes PTHrP hypercalcemia rather than SIADH.
whyNot.D: CD45 marks lymphoma, which can cause a mediastinal mass but not this paraneoplastic picture.
whyNot.E: Napsin A marks adenocarcinoma of lung origin, a peripheral tumor not classically linked to SIADH.

items.objective: Connect SIADH to small cell lung carcinoma and its neuroendocrine immunoprofile.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man has a 3-cm painless lump below the angle of the left jaw for 2 months. He has never smoked and drinks socially. Fine-needle aspiration shows squamous cell carcinoma with strong, diffuse p16 staining. A small primary tumor is found in the left tonsil. A viral protein in the tumor cells most likely contributes to cancer by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Activating a cellular tyrosine kinase by mimicking a growth factor receptor

options.label: B
options.html: Encoding a viral cyclin that drives Kaposi sarcoma cells

options.label: C
options.html: Expressing a latent membrane protein that mimics CD40

options.label: E
options.html: Integrating next to MYC and driving its transcription

items.explanationHtml:
HPV-related oropharyngeal carcinoma (tonsil, base of tongue) occurs in younger people with little tobacco exposure. E7 binds and inactivates Rb, releasing E2F and driving S-phase entry; loss of Rb feedback causes the overexpression of p16 used as a marker. E6 promotes degradation of p53.

Takeaway: p16-positive tonsil cancer is HPV-driven: E7 inactivates Rb, E6 degrades p53.

whyNot.A: This describes viral oncogenes such as v-erbB, not HPV.
whyNot.B: Viral cyclin is an HHV-8 product.
whyNot.C: LMP-1 is an EBV protein, relevant to nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not HPV-related tonsil cancer.
whyNot.E: MYC translocation drives Burkitt lymphoma; HPV does not act by insertional activation of MYC.

items.objective: Describe how HPV E6 and E7 cause oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man who emigrated from southern China 10 years ago has 2 months of a blocked left ear and a firm left upper neck node. Otoscopy shows a dull left tympanic membrane with an air-fluid level. He has no fever or ear pain. Biopsy of a nasopharyngeal mass shows undifferentiated carcinoma with many lymphocytes. Which infectious agent is most strongly associated with this tumor?
items.explanationHtml:
Nonkeratinizing (undifferentiated) nasopharyngeal carcinoma is associated with EBV and is common in southern China. Tumor near the eustachian tube opening causes a one-sided middle-ear effusion in an adult; early nodal spread to the upper neck is typical.

Takeaway: adult unilateral serous otitis + neck node + East Asian background = EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

whyNot.A: CMV is not an oncogenic cause of head and neck carcinoma.
whyNot.C: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma.
whyNot.D: HPV drives oropharyngeal (tonsil, base of tongue) carcinoma, not nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
whyNot.E: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

items.objective: Associate nasopharyngeal carcinoma with Epstein-Barr virus and its presenting signs.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with lung cancer has 6 weeks of weakness, hypertension (168/98 mm Hg) and leg edema. He has not gained weight and has no striae. Serum potassium is 2.6 mEq/L and bicarbonate 34 mEq/L. Morning cortisol and plasma ACTH are both markedly elevated, and cortisol does not fall after high-dose dexamethasone. Which histologic type of lung cancer most likely produced this syndrome?
items.explanationHtml:
Very high ACTH and cortisol that do not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone indicate ectopic ACTH. Small cell carcinoma secretes large amounts quickly, so hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypertension and weakness appear before the slow cushingoid body changes. (Bronchial carcinoid is the slower ectopic source.)

Takeaway: rapid ectopic ACTH syndrome with severe hypokalemia = small cell lung carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Adenocarcinoma is associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy and Trousseau syndrome rather than ectopic ACTH.
whyNot.B: Large cell carcinoma occasionally secretes hCG, not ACTH.
whyNot.C: Mesothelioma is a pleural tumor without endocrine syndromes.
whyNot.E: Squamous cell carcinoma secretes PTHrP, not ACTH.

items.objective: Recognize ectopic ACTH secretion by small cell lung carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with metastatic squamous cell lung carcinoma starts a monoclonal antibody against programmed death-1 (PD-1). Seven weeks later he has a dry cough and new dyspnea. Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. CT shows new bilateral ground-glass opacities, and infection is excluded. The mechanism of this complication is best described as which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct cytotoxic injury to type II pneumocytes

options.label: B
options.html: Drug-induced capillary leak from cytokine release by tumor lysis

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of peripheral T-cell tolerance to self antigens

items.explanationHtml:
PD-1 normally restrains activated T cells in peripheral tissues. Blocking it boosts antitumor immunity but also breaks peripheral self-tolerance, causing immune-related adverse events: pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, dermatitis. Pneumonitis is treated by holding the drug and giving glucocorticoids.

Takeaway: checkpoint inhibitor toxicity is autoimmune (loss of T-cell tolerance), treated with steroids.

whyNot.A: This describes drugs such as bleomycin; checkpoint inhibitors are not directly cytotoxic.
whyNot.B: Cytokine release syndrome is acute and systemic, not a delayed isolated pneumonitis.
whyNot.C: Type I reactions occur within minutes to hours of infusion, not weeks later.
whyNot.E: Lymphangitic carcinomatosis gives interlobular septal thickening, and timing after a new antibody points to a drug effect.

items.objective: Explain immune-related adverse events of PD-1 checkpoint blockade.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman who has never smoked has 6 months of recurrent right lower lobe pneumonia and two episodes of hemoptysis. Bronchoscopy shows a smooth, red, polypoid mass blocking the bronchus intermedius. Resection shows nests of uniform cells with round nuclei, finely stippled chromatin and rare mitoses, positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which of the following best describes the expected course after complete resection?

options.label: A
options.html: Early recurrence with liver and brain metastases in most patients

options.label: B
options.html: Excellent long-term survival in most patients

options.label: C
options.html: Lifelong carcinoid syndrome from residual tumor

options.label: D
options.html: Relapse within months that responds only to chemoradiation

items.explanationHtml:
A young nonsmoker with an endobronchial polyp causing obstruction, and low-grade neuroendocrine histology, has a typical carcinoid tumor. Surgical resection is usually curative, and long-term survival is excellent. It sits at the low-grade end of the neuroendocrine spectrum that ends in small cell carcinoma.

Takeaway: bronchial typical carcinoid: young nonsmoker, endobronchial polyp, cured by resection.

whyNot.A: This describes small cell carcinoma, which is high grade with many mitoses and necrosis.
whyNot.C: Carcinoid syndrome is uncommon with bronchial carcinoids and usually requires liver metastases.
whyNot.D: This again describes small cell carcinoma's behavior.
whyNot.E: Neuroendocrine tumors do not transform into squamous carcinoma.

items.objective: Distinguish the prognosis of bronchial carcinoid from small cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with a 40-pack-year history has a 3-cm right upper lobe mass. While being staged he notices that his finger ends have become bulbous, and he has aching, tender wrists and shins. Radiographs show new periosteal bone formation along the distal radius, ulna, tibia and fibula. Which tumor type is most often associated with this syndrome?
items.explanationHtml:
Clubbing with painful periostitis of long bones is hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy. In adults it is most often caused by non-small cell lung cancer, classically adenocarcinoma; it may improve after tumor resection.

Takeaway: clubbing plus periostitis in a smoker suggests NSCLC, especially adenocarcinoma.

whyNot.B: Mesothelioma can cause clubbing, but it is a pleural tumor and the mass here is parenchymal; NSCLC remains the commonest cause.
whyNot.C: RCC metastases can cause paraneoplastic polycythemia or hypercalcemia, not this classic lung association.
whyNot.D: Small cell carcinoma is associated with endocrine and neurologic syndromes, rarely with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.
whyNot.E: Carcinoids cause obstruction and, rarely, carcinoid syndrome.

items.objective: Associate hypertrophic osteoarthropathy with non-small cell lung cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman comes to the clinic with 3 weeks of progressive shortness of breath on exertion and a dry cough. Four years ago she was treated for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer with lumpectomy, radiation and endocrine therapy. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. There is dullness to percussion and absent breath sounds over the lower two-thirds of the right hemithorax. A chest radiograph shows a large right pleural effusion without mediastinal shift toward the effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Chest tube placement with intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy

options.label: B
options.html: CT-guided biopsy of the right lung

options.label: C
options.html: Oral furosemide and reassessment in 1 week

options.label: D
options.html: Talc pleurodesis through a chest tube

options.label: E
options.html: Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis with fluid analysis and cytology

items.explanationHtml:
A new, large, unexplained effusion should be sampled. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis is diagnostic (protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cells, microbiology and cytology) and, if a large volume is removed, therapeutic. Breast cancer is a leading cause of malignant effusion, but the cause must be proved.

Takeaway: new effusion in a cancer survivor: diagnostic and therapeutic thoracentesis first.

whyNot.A: Fibrinolytics with a chest tube treat complicated parapneumonic effusions or empyema, not an undiagnosed effusion in an afebrile patient.
whyNot.B: Lung biopsy targets a parenchymal lesion; the effusion itself is the easiest and safest source of diagnostic material.
whyNot.C: Diuretics treat transudates from heart failure, which nothing here suggests.
whyNot.D: Pleurodesis is for recurrent, proven malignant effusions after the lung has been shown to re-expand.

items.objective: Perform diagnostic thoracentesis for a new unexplained pleural effusion.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) The thoracentesis removes 1.2 L of blood-tinged fluid and her breathing improves. The fluid is an exudate with 82% lymphocytes, glucose 74 mg/dL and pH 7.36. Cytology shows clusters of adenocarcinoma cells that are positive for GATA3 and estrogen receptor and negative for TTF-1. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows pleural nodularity on the right, no lung mass and two small bone lesions in the spine. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: A new primary lung adenocarcinoma requiring lobectomy

options.label: B
options.html: Locally recurrent breast cancer requiring mastectomy

options.label: D
options.html: Metastatic breast cancer requiring systemic therapy

options.label: E
options.html: Reactive mesothelial cells requiring repeat cytology in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
Adenocarcinoma cells that are GATA3 and estrogen receptor positive and TTF-1 negative, with pleural nodularity and bone lesions, indicate metastatic (stage IV) breast cancer. Management is systemic therapy chosen by receptor status, plus control of the effusion; local surgery does not change the course of metastatic disease.

Takeaway: a malignant effusion means advanced disease, treated systemically.

whyNot.A: TTF-1 negativity and GATA3 and estrogen receptor positivity point to breast, not lung; there is also no lung mass.
whyNot.B: Pleural and bone disease is distant, not local, recurrence; mastectomy would not treat it.
whyNot.C: Mesothelioma is calretinin and WT1 positive and is not estrogen receptor positive adenocarcinoma.
whyNot.E: Reactive mesothelial cells do not express GATA3 and estrogen receptor as clusters of adenocarcinoma cells.

items.objective: Interpret malignant pleural fluid cytology as metastatic disease needing systemic therapy.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) She begins systemic therapy. Ten days later, her breathlessness returns. A chest radiograph shows the right effusion has re-accumulated to its previous size. The radiograph taken right after the first thoracentesis had shown that the right lung did not fully re-expand, and CT showed a thick rind of visceral pleural tumor. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the effusion?

options.label: E
options.html: Talc pleurodesis through a chest tube

items.explanationHtml:
A recurrent symptomatic malignant effusion needs a durable approach. Because the lung is trapped by a visceral pleural rind and cannot re-expand, pleurodesis would fail (the pleural surfaces cannot touch to fuse). An indwelling tunneled pleural catheter, drained at home, controls symptoms regardless of lung expansion and sometimes produces spontaneous pleurodesis.

Takeaway: recurrent malignant effusion: catheter or talc if the lung re-expands; catheter if it is trapped.

whyNot.B: Diuretics do not reduce a malignant exudate.
whyNot.C: Repeated thoracenteses expose her to repeated procedures and risks and suit only a very short life expectancy.
whyNot.D: Radical surgery is not appropriate for metastatic breast cancer with a malignant effusion.
whyNot.E: Talc pleurodesis needs apposition of visceral and parietal pleura; with a trapped lung it usually fails.

items.objective: Choose an indwelling pleural catheter for a recurrent malignant effusion with trapped lung.

items.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old man has had a right pleural effusion, fatigue and a 6-kg weight loss over 3 months. He is afebrile and has no edema or ascites. Pleural fluid and serum results are shown:

TestPleural fluidSerum
Protein4.4 g/dL6.6 g/dL
LDH310 U/L210 U/L
Glucose58 mg/dL96 mg/dL
pH7.29—
Nucleated cells2,400/mm3, 85% lymphocytes—
Gram stainNo organisms—
AppearanceBlood-tinged—

Which of the following is the most likely cause of the effusion?
items.explanationHtml:
The protein ratio (0.67) and LDH ratio (1.5) both exceed Light thresholds, so this is an exudate. A blood-tinged, lymphocytic exudate in an older man with weight loss is most consistent with malignancy; the low glucose and pH suggest a large tumor burden and a worse prognosis. Cytology, and pleural biopsy if cytology is negative, are the next steps.

Takeaway: bloody lymphocytic exudate + weight loss = malignant effusion until proved otherwise.

whyNot.A: Heart failure causes a transudate with low protein and LDH ratios.
whyNot.B: Hepatic hydrothorax is a transudate in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites.
whyNot.D: Nephrotic syndrome causes bilateral transudates from low oncotic pressure.
whyNot.E: Parapneumonic effusions follow pneumonia with fever and are neutrophil-predominant.

items.objective: Apply Light criteria and fluid features to identify a malignant effusion.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has 3 weeks of swelling of his face and both arms and a sense of fullness in his head when he bends over. He is alert and speaks normally, with no stridor. Pulse is 88/min, blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. His neck veins are distended and there are dilated veins over the upper chest. Contrast CT shows a 7-cm anterior mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava, with enlarged right supraclavicular lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Emergency radiation therapy to the mediastinal mass

options.label: C
options.html: Excisional or core biopsy of a neck node

options.label: D
options.html: High-dose IV glucocorticoids to shrink the mass

items.explanationHtml:
He has superior vena cava syndrome without airway or neurologic compromise, so there is time to make a tissue diagnosis first. An anterior mediastinal mass with supraclavicular nodes could be lymphoma, a germ cell tumor, thymoma or lung cancer, and each is treated differently. The least invasive route (here an accessible node) is preferred.

Takeaway: stable SVC syndrome: biopsy before treatment.

whyNot.A: He has no airway compromise, and sedation with a large anterior mediastinal mass can itself cause airway collapse.
whyNot.B: Radiation before diagnosis can obscure histology and is unnecessary when the patient is stable.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids before biopsy can partially treat a lymphoma and make the biopsy nondiagnostic.
whyNot.E: Thrombolysis is for catheter-related thrombosis, not for external compression by a tumor.

items.objective: Obtain tissue before treating a stable patient with malignant SVC syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with a newly found right hilar mass is brought to the emergency department because of increasing facial swelling over 2 days and noisy breathing. She is drowsy but answers questions. There is inspiratory stridor, marked facial and tongue swelling, and distended neck and chest-wall veins. Oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. CT shows near-complete occlusion of the superior vena cava by tumor. Biopsy results are pending. In addition to airway support, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Elective resection of the hilar mass

options.label: B
options.html: Endovascular stenting of the superior vena cava

options.label: D
options.html: Outpatient follow-up when biopsy results return

options.label: E
options.html: Warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3

items.explanationHtml:
Stridor (laryngeal edema) and reduced consciousness (cerebral venous congestion) make this life-threatening SVC syndrome. Endovascular stenting relieves the obstruction within hours and does not compromise a later tissue diagnosis; urgent radiation is an alternative. Definitive cancer treatment follows once histology is known.

Takeaway: SVC syndrome with stridor or confusion: stent now.

whyNot.A: Surgery is not an emergency treatment for SVC obstruction, and staging is incomplete.
whyNot.C: Discharge is unsafe, and steroids alone do not relieve a mechanical obstruction.
whyNot.D: Waiting is unsafe with stridor and altered consciousness.
whyNot.E: Anticoagulation alone does not relieve tumor compression and has no role in an emergency without thrombus.

items.objective: Treat life-threatening SVC syndrome with urgent endovascular stenting.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man had a sigmoid colectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy for stage III colon cancer 2 years ago. His CEA has risen from 2 to 9 ng/mL. CT shows two new 1-cm nodules in the right lower lobe and no disease in the liver, abdomen, colon or elsewhere; PET-CT confirms disease confined to the two nodules. Colonoscopy shows no recurrence. His FEV1 is 88% of predicted and he is active. Which of the following offers the best chance of long-term disease control?

options.label: D
options.html: Surgical resection of the lung nodules

items.explanationHtml:
Isolated, limited lung metastases from colorectal cancer, with the primary controlled, no other disease and good lung function, meet the criteria for pulmonary metastasectomy, which offers long-term survival in a meaningful proportion of patients. It is planned by a multidisciplinary team and often combined with systemic therapy.

Takeaway: controlled primary + few resectable lung metastases + adequate reserve = consider metastasectomy (colorectal, sarcoma, renal cell).

whyNot.A: Brushings have low yield for 1-cm peripheral nodules and do not treat them.
whyNot.B: Hospice is premature; he has potentially curable oligometastatic disease.
whyNot.C: Observation allows the metastases to grow and spread when they are still resectable.
whyNot.E: Whole-lung radiation is not a treatment for colorectal lung metastases and damages healthy lung.

items.objective: Recognize candidates for pulmonary metastasectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man who worked for 30 years as a boilermaker has had dull left chest pain and breathlessness for 4 months. CT shows a left pleural effusion with irregular, nodular pleural thickening along the lateral chest wall and mediastinal pleura. Two ultrasound-guided thoracenteses show an exudate with negative cytology. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
An exudative effusion with nodular pleural thickening after asbestos exposure suggests mesothelioma (or pleural metastases). Fluid cytology is often negative in mesothelioma and cannot assess invasion; after two negative cytologies, thoracoscopic biopsy provides tissue for histology and immunostains and allows drainage and pleurodesis at the same procedure.

Takeaway: suspected mesothelioma or persistently cytology-negative exudate: thoracoscopic pleural biopsy.

whyNot.A: The yield of a third cytology sample is low, especially for mesothelioma.
whyNot.B: Bronchoscopy looks inside the airways and has little yield for pleural disease without an endobronchial lesion.
whyNot.C: PET-CT can show active pleural disease but cannot provide the tissue diagnosis needed for treatment.
whyNot.D: Tumor markers cannot establish a pleural diagnosis.

items.objective: Choose thoracoscopic biopsy to diagnose suspected mesothelioma.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old woman had a stage II cutaneous melanoma excised from her back 3 years ago. She has smoked 1 pack a day for 35 years. Surveillance CT shows a single new 1.6-cm spiculated nodule in the left upper lobe; there are no other lesions, and brain MRI is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Start immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy for metastatic melanoma

options.label: E
options.html: Tissue sampling of the lung lesion

items.explanationHtml:
A single new lung nodule in a patient with a past cancer may be a metastasis or a new primary lung cancer; in a heavy smoker with a spiculated upper-lobe nodule, a primary lung cancer is quite possible. Treatment differs completely, so tissue is needed (biopsy, or resection that is both diagnostic and therapeutic).

Takeaway: solitary new nodule in a cancer survivor: obtain tissue before treating.

whyNot.A: Lavage has a low yield for a peripheral nodule.
whyNot.B: Waiting a year for a spiculated nodule in a heavy smoker risks progression.
whyNot.C: Treating as metastatic melanoma without tissue could miss a curable primary lung cancer.
whyNot.D: Radiation without tissue skips the diagnosis that decides between treatments.

items.objective: Obtain tissue for a solitary new lung nodule in a patient with a history of cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with metastatic gastric cancer has a large left pleural effusion. During ultrasound-guided thoracentesis, 2.4 L is removed; toward the end he reports chest tightness. Within an hour he develops a persistent cough with frothy sputum, his oxygen saturation falls from 95% to 86% on room air, and crackles are heard over the left lung. A chest radiograph shows that the left lung is re-expanded and filled with new, patchy alveolar opacities. There is no pneumothorax. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Rapid removal of a large volume of pleural fluid from a chronically collapsed lung can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema, with cough, hypoxemia and new opacities confined to the re-expanded lung within hours. Risk is reduced by stopping at about 1.5 L or when chest discomfort appears. Treatment is supportive with oxygen.

Takeaway: new opacities in the drained lung after a large-volume tap = re-expansion edema.

whyNot.A: Pulmonary embolism rarely produces new unilateral alveolar opacities within an hour of a procedure.
whyNot.B: Aspiration typically affects dependent segments after vomiting or impaired swallowing, not the whole drained lung after a tap.
whyNot.C: Hemothorax would show reaccumulating pleural fluid and falling hemoglobin, not alveolar opacities in a re-expanded lung.
whyNot.D: Lymphangitic spread develops over weeks and is not triggered by drainage.

items.objective: Recognize re-expansion pulmonary edema after large-volume thoracentesis.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man has a painless left testicular mass and cough. Serum hCG and AFP are markedly elevated. Orchiectomy shows a mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. CT shows retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and more than 20 nodules in both lungs; brain MRI and bone scan are normal. He asks about his outlook. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?

options.label: A
options.html: Cure is likely with cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy

options.label: B
options.html: Lung metastases make cure unlikely, so treatment aims only to relieve symptoms

options.label: C
options.html: Only resection of every lung nodule offers any chance of cure

options.label: D
options.html: Radiation to both lungs is the treatment most likely to cure him

options.label: E
options.html: Survival depends mainly on removing the retroperitoneal nodes first

items.explanationHtml:
Testicular germ cell tumors are among the most chemosensitive solid tumors. Even with many lung metastases, most men are cured with cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy; residual masses are resected afterwards, and tumor markers are used to follow response. Prognosis is graded by marker levels and the sites of metastasis (for example, metastases outside the lungs are worse).

Takeaway: lung metastases from a germ cell tumor are usually curable with chemotherapy.

whyNot.B: Lung metastases from germ cell tumors do not make cure unlikely; most patients are cured.
whyNot.C: Chemotherapy is the main treatment; surgery is used for residual masses afterwards, not first.
whyNot.D: Lung irradiation is not used for metastatic nonseminoma.
whyNot.E: Retroperitoneal node dissection is for residual disease after chemotherapy or for early-stage disease, not first-line in widespread disease.

items.objective: Counsel that metastatic germ cell tumors are usually curable with chemotherapy.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman had a sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma resected 3 years ago. She now has mild cough. Chest CT shows eight round, smoothly marginated nodules from 0.5 to 2.5 cm in both lungs, more numerous in the lower lobes and toward the periphery. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Aspiration of tumor cells into the airways

options.label: C
options.html: Hematogenous seeding from a distant primary

items.explanationHtml:
Multiple round nodules of different sizes, mainly peripheral and basal, in a patient with a known cancer are hematogenous metastases. Tumor cells reach the lung through systemic veins and lodge in the first capillary bed; the bases receive the most blood flow, so most nodules are there. Colorectal cancer reaches the lungs through the systemic veins (especially from the rectum) or after liver involvement.

Takeaway: multiple round basal-peripheral nodules = hematogenous metastases.

whyNot.A: Aerogenous spread is a feature of some mucinous lung adenocarcinomas and produces consolidation, not round nodules.
whyNot.B: Transdiaphragmatic extension produces pleural or basal masses adjacent to the diaphragm, not nodules throughout both lungs.
whyNot.D: Synchronous multiple primary cancers are uncommon; with a known prior cancer, metastases are far more likely.
whyNot.E: Lymphangitic spread thickens interlobular septa and bronchovascular bundles rather than forming discrete round nodules.

items.objective: Recognize the hematogenous pattern of pulmonary metastases.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has progressive shortness of breath for 6 weeks and a dry cough. The chest radiograph shows only subtle linear opacities at both bases. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. High-resolution CT shows smooth and beaded thickening of the interlobular septa and of the bronchovascular bundles, with small bilateral effusions. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her lung involvement?

options.label: A
options.html: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from tumor necrosis

options.label: C
options.html: Growth of tumor within pulmonary lymphatic channels

options.label: D
options.html: Radiation-induced fibrosis of the alveolar septa

items.explanationHtml:
Dyspnea out of proportion to the radiograph with septal and bronchovascular thickening is lymphangitic carcinomatosis: tumor grows in and distends the lymphatics that run in the interlobular septa and around bronchovascular bundles, impairing gas exchange and lymph drainage. Breast, stomach, lung and pancreas are common primaries. The prognosis is poor.

Takeaway: septal and peribronchovascular thickening plus severe dyspnea in a cancer patient = lymphangitic spread.

whyNot.A: Alveolar hemorrhage causes ground-glass or consolidative opacities and often hemoptysis.
whyNot.B: Eosinophilic pneumonia causes peripheral consolidation and blood or lavage eosinophilia.
whyNot.D: Radiation fibrosis follows the radiation field with sharp borders and volume loss, not diffuse beaded septal thickening.
whyNot.E: Tumor microemboli can cause pulmonary hypertension and dyspnea with a near-normal CT, but they do not thicken septa and bundles.

items.objective: Explain the lymphatic mechanism and CT pattern of lymphangitic carcinomatosis.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man had a left nephrectomy for a kidney tumor 5 years ago. He now has hemoptysis, and CT shows a 2-cm endobronchial mass in the right lower lobe bronchus and three lung nodules. Biopsy shows nests of tumor cells with abundant clear cytoplasm in a delicate, highly vascular network. Positive immunostaining for which of the following best supports a renal origin?
items.explanationHtml:
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma metastasizes to the lung (often as nodules, sometimes endobronchial) and stains for PAX8, a transcription factor of renal, Müllerian and thyroid epithelium. Combined with TTF-1 negativity, it distinguishes a renal metastasis from a primary lung tumor.

Takeaway: PAX8 = kidney (also ovary, thyroid); TTF-1 = lung (and thyroid).

whyNot.A: Calretinin marks mesothelial cells and mesothelioma.
whyNot.B: CDX2 marks intestinal adenocarcinoma such as colorectal cancer.
whyNot.C: GATA3 marks breast and urothelial carcinomas.
whyNot.E: TTF-1 marks lung adenocarcinoma and thyroid carcinoma, not renal cell carcinoma.

items.objective: Use immunohistochemistry to identify renal cell carcinoma metastatic to the lung.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man who worked for 25 years fitting insulation in ships has increasing breathlessness and dull right chest pain. CT shows a right pleural effusion and nodular pleural thickening that encases the right lung and extends into the fissures. A thoracoscopic biopsy shows a malignant epithelioid tumor. Which of the following immunostaining results best supports mesothelioma rather than metastatic adenocarcinoma?
items.explanationHtml:
Mesothelial cells express calretinin, WT1, D2-40 and CK5/6, while adenocarcinomas express epithelial markers such as CEA, claudin-4, MOC-31 and, for lung primaries, TTF-1 and napsin A. A panel of two positive mesothelial and two positive carcinoma markers is the standard approach.

Takeaway: calretinin/WT1 positive, CEA/TTF-1 negative = mesothelioma.

whyNot.B: CEA and claudin-4 are epithelial carcinoma markers and are typically negative in mesothelioma.
whyNot.C: Chromogranin and synaptophysin indicate a neuroendocrine tumor such as small cell carcinoma.
whyNot.D: S-100 and SOX10 indicate melanoma, which can mimic other tumors but is not mesothelial.
whyNot.E: TTF-1 and napsin A mark lung adenocarcinoma that has spread to the pleura, not mesothelioma.

items.objective: Distinguish mesothelioma from adenocarcinoma by immunohistochemistry.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old retired pipefitter has a chest radiograph before hernia surgery. He has no respiratory symptoms, and lung examination is normal. The radiograph shows several discrete, partly calcified opacities along the lateral chest walls and over both domes of the diaphragm; the lungs are clear. Which of the following is the best interpretation of these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Benign pleural plaques from past asbestos exposure

options.label: B
options.html: Calcified metastases from an occult primary

options.label: D
options.html: Healed primary tuberculosis of the pleura

items.explanationHtml:
Calcified plaques on the parietal and diaphragmatic pleura are pleural plaques, the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure. They are collagenous, benign and do not progress to mesothelioma; they indicate that the person was exposed, and that exposure (not the plaque) carries the cancer risk.

Takeaway: pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure; they are not premalignant.

whyNot.B: Metastases are within the lung or form pleural nodules with effusion; they rarely produce flat, calcified diaphragmatic plaques.
whyNot.C: Mesothelioma causes a unilateral effusion and progressive rind-like thickening with symptoms, not discrete bilateral calcified plaques in a well patient.
whyNot.D: Tuberculous pleuritis heals with unilateral pleural thickening and blunting, not bilateral diaphragmatic plaques.
whyNot.E: Eggshell calcification in silicosis affects hilar lymph nodes, not the pleura.

items.objective: Interpret pleural plaques as a benign marker of asbestos exposure.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with pleural mesothelioma. She has never worked in a trade with asbestos exposure and lived in a recently built house. Her mother died of uveal melanoma, a maternal uncle had renal cell carcinoma, and she has had two atypical melanocytic skin tumors removed. A germline loss-of-function variant in which of the following genes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome (autosomal dominant) causes mesothelioma, uveal and cutaneous melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and distinctive melanocytic skin tumors. BAP1 is a deubiquitinase and tumor suppressor; tumors arise after loss of the second allele.

Takeaway: mesothelioma without asbestos + family uveal melanoma/RCC = germline BAP1.

whyNot.B: BRCA1 predisposes to breast and ovarian cancer, not this cluster of mesothelioma and uveal melanoma.
whyNot.C: NF2 is often lost somatically in mesothelioma, but germline NF2 variants cause vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas.
whyNot.D: Germline RB1 variants cause retinoblastoma and later osteosarcoma.
whyNot.E: Li-Fraumeni (TP53) gives sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors and adrenocortical carcinoma at young ages.

items.objective: Identify BAP1 tumor predisposition as a cause of familial mesothelioma.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man who has smoked 2 packs a day for 40 years has 2 weeks of facial swelling and headache that worsen when he bends forward. His face is plethoric, his neck veins are distended and do not pulsate, and dilated veins run across the upper anterior chest. Serum sodium is 124 mEq/L. CT shows a large right paratracheal mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following tumor types is most likely?

options.label: C
options.html: Pancoast tumor of the lung apex

items.explanationHtml:
Facial swelling and plethora, nonpulsatile distended neck veins and chest-wall collaterals mean superior vena cava obstruction. A bulky central mediastinal mass in a heavy smoker with hyponatremia (SIADH) is classic for small cell lung carcinoma, the most common cause of malignant SVC syndrome, followed by non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Takeaway: SVC syndrome + central mass + SIADH in a smoker = small cell carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Carcinoid tumors are usually endobronchial and slow growing; they rarely cause bulky mediastinal disease or SIADH.
whyNot.B: Mesothelioma spreads along the pleura and rarely compresses the SVC; it does not cause SIADH.
whyNot.C: A Pancoast tumor at the apex causes Horner syndrome and shoulder or arm pain, not SVC obstruction with SIADH.
whyNot.D: Hamartomas are small peripheral benign nodules that do not compress mediastinal veins.

items.objective: Identify small cell carcinoma as the leading cause of SVC syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had cough and blood-streaked sputum for 3 weeks. Ten weeks ago she had suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole. Her serum hCG level has risen over the past 4 weeks. Chest CT shows many round nodules in both lungs, several surrounded by a ground-glass halo. Biopsy of a nodule would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Hydropic chorionic villi with circumferential trophoblast proliferation

options.label: B
options.html: Large polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm and lymphocytic stroma

options.label: C
options.html: Mature tissues from all three germ layers

options.label: D
options.html: Primitive embryonal cells forming Schiller-Duval bodies

options.label: E
options.html: Sheets of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast without chorionic villi

items.explanationHtml:
Rising hCG after a molar pregnancy with hemorrhagic lung nodules is gestational choriocarcinoma, which spreads early through the blood. It consists of malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with hemorrhage and necrosis but no villi. It is highly sensitive to chemotherapy.

Takeaway: choriocarcinoma = trophoblast without villi, very high hCG, hemorrhagic lung metastases.

whyNot.A: Hydropic villi with trophoblast proliferation describe the mole itself (or an invasive mole), not choriocarcinoma.
whyNot.B: Clear polygonal cells with lymphocytic stroma describe seminoma or dysgerminoma.
whyNot.C: Mature tissues from three germ layers describe a mature teratoma, which does not secrete hCG.
whyNot.D: Schiller-Duval bodies are typical of yolk sac tumor, which secretes AFP rather than hCG.

items.objective: Identify the histology of choriocarcinoma metastatic to the lung.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy has had 3 months of pain and swelling above the right knee. A radiograph shows a destructive lesion in the metaphysis of the distal femur with a sunburst periosteal reaction and a Codman triangle. CT of the chest shows four lung nodules, two of which contain calcification. Which of the following features of the primary tumor best explains the calcification in the lung nodules?

options.label: A
options.html: Dense fibrous stroma with dystrophic calcification

options.label: B
options.html: Multinucleated giant cells in a background of spindle cells

options.label: D
options.html: Small round blue cells with a t(11;22) translocation

options.label: E
options.html: Tumor cells laying down osteoid matrix

items.explanationHtml:
A metaphyseal distal-femur tumor in an adolescent with a sunburst reaction and Codman triangle is osteosarcoma, defined by malignant cells that make osteoid. The lung is its main site of metastasis, and the metastases can mineralize because they make bone matrix too.

Takeaway: calcified lung metastases in a teenager suggest osteosarcoma.

whyNot.A: Dystrophic calcification of fibrous tissue does not describe a primary tumor that makes matrix.
whyNot.B: Giant cell tumor arises in the epiphysis of young adults and is usually benign; it rarely gives lung metastases.
whyNot.C: Chondrosarcoma affects older adults and the axial skeleton and pelvis more often.
whyNot.D: Ewing sarcoma (t(11;22)) arises in the diaphysis with an onion-skin reaction and does not make osteoid.

items.objective: Explain why osteosarcoma lung metastases may calcify.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman with lung adenocarcinoma has a left pleural effusion. Pleural fluid analysis shows a pleural/serum protein ratio of 0.7, a pleural/serum LDH ratio of 1.2 and malignant cells on cytology. Which of the following best explains the accumulation of fluid?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia

options.label: C
options.html: Leakage of chyle from a torn thoracic duct

options.label: D
options.html: Leaky pleural capillaries and blocked lymphatics

options.label: E
options.html: Movement of ascitic fluid through diaphragmatic defects

items.explanationHtml:
The fluid is an exudate by Light criteria. Tumor implants and the inflammation they cause make pleural capillaries leak protein, and tumor obstructs the lymphatic stomata of the parietal pleura and the mediastinal nodes that normally clear pleural fluid.

Takeaway: malignant effusion = exudate from leaky capillaries plus blocked lymphatic outflow.

whyNot.A: Low oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis) also produces a transudate.
whyNot.B: Raised hydrostatic pressure (heart failure) produces a transudate with low protein and LDH ratios.
whyNot.C: Chylothorax is milky with high triglycerides; it is not the mechanism of a carcinomatous effusion.
whyNot.E: Hepatic hydrothorax from ascites crossing the diaphragm is a transudate in a patient with cirrhosis.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of a malignant pleural exudate.

items.stemHtml: A pleural tumor from a 69-year-old former shipyard worker is examined by electron microscopy to separate mesothelioma from metastatic adenocarcinoma. Which of the following ultrastructural findings most strongly supports mesothelioma?

options.label: B
options.html: Membrane-bound dense-core granules in the cytoplasm

options.label: C
options.html: Rod-shaped organelles with internal tubules in endothelial cells

options.label: D
options.html: Short, stubby microvilli covered by a prominent glycocalyx

items.explanationHtml:
Mesothelial cells and mesothelioma have long, slender, often branching microvilli with a high length-to-width ratio and little glycocalyx. Adenocarcinoma cells have short, straight microvilli with a glycocalyx and rootlets.

Takeaway: long, slender microvilli on electron microscopy = mesothelioma.

whyNot.B: Dense-core neurosecretory granules indicate a neuroendocrine tumor such as small cell carcinoma or carcinoid.
whyNot.C: Weibel-Palade bodies are found in endothelial cells and vascular tumors.
whyNot.D: Short microvilli with glycocalyx are the pattern of adenocarcinoma.
whyNot.E: Birbeck granules indicate Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

items.objective: Recognize the ultrastructural signature of mesothelioma.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has had 6 months of intermittent cough and wheezing, worse at night and after running in cold air. Between episodes she feels well. She does not smoke. Lung examination and pulse oximetry are normal today. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic study?

options.label: A
options.html: Chest x-ray, posteroanterior and lateral views

options.label: B
options.html: High-resolution CT of the chest without contrast

options.label: E
options.html: Spirometry before and after an inhaled bronchodilator

items.explanationHtml:
Variable symptoms with nocturnal and exercise triggers suggest asthma. The best initial test is spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility: an obstructive pattern that improves by at least 12% and 200 mL in FEV1 supports the diagnosis. If spirometry is normal, a methacholine challenge or peak-flow variability is the next step.

Takeaway: Confirm suspected asthma with pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry first.

whyNot.A: Imaging is not needed for a typical presentation without red flags and does not confirm asthma.
whyNot.B: CT is reserved for suspected bronchiectasis, interstitial disease or other alternative diagnoses.
whyNot.C: Bronchoprovocation is useful when spirometry is normal and suspicion remains; spirometry comes first.
whyNot.D: Allergen testing helps phenotype asthma once diagnosed but does not establish the diagnosis.

items.objective: Choose the initial diagnostic test for suspected asthma.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with asthma diagnosed by spirometry 1 year ago uses an albuterol inhaler about three times a month for wheeze. He has not woken at night with symptoms and has had no exacerbations. His inhaler technique is good. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a daily long-acting muscarinic antagonist

options.label: B
options.html: Add daily oral montelukast to albuterol

options.label: E
options.html: Prescribe a 5-day course of oral prednisone

items.explanationHtml:
For mild asthma in adults and adolescents, current strategy prefers as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol as the reliever. It reduces severe exacerbations compared with a SABA alone and avoids the poor adherence of daily controllers in people with few symptoms. Formoterol works within minutes, so it relieves symptoms while delivering corticosteroid with each use.

Takeaway: Mild asthma: as-needed ICS–formoterol, not SABA alone.

whyNot.A: A LAMA is an add-on for moderate–severe asthma already on ICS–LABA.
whyNot.B: Leukotriene antagonists are less effective than inhaled corticosteroids and carry neuropsychiatric warnings.
whyNot.D: Reliever-only short-acting β2-agonist treatment is associated with more severe exacerbations; an inhaled corticosteroid should be part of treatment.
whyNot.E: Systemic steroids are for exacerbations, not for mild stable symptoms.

items.objective: Select reliever therapy that includes an inhaled corticosteroid for mild asthma.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman with asthma comes to the emergency department with 2 days of worsening dyspnea. Despite three nebulized albuterol–ipratropium treatments, intravenous methylprednisolone and intravenous magnesium, she is now drowsy and can say only single words. Respirations are 10/min and shallow. Breath sounds are barely audible. Pulse oximetry on oxygen shows 89%. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.21, PaCO2 62 mm Hg and PaO2 58 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat nebulized albuterol every 20 minutes and reassess in 1 hour

items.explanationHtml:
She has life-threatening asthma: altered consciousness, a silent chest, a slowing respiratory rate and hypercapnic acidosis. In an attack, PaCO2 should be low from hyperventilation; a high PaCO2 means fatigue. The next step is endotracheal intubation. Ventilate with a low rate and long expiratory time to limit auto-PEEP.

Takeaway: Drowsiness and a rising PaCO2 in acute asthma mean intubation.

whyNot.B: Methylxanthines add toxicity with little benefit and do not address her failing ventilation.
whyNot.C: A drowsy patient who cannot protect her airway is not a candidate, and NIV has no clear role in asthma respiratory failure.
whyNot.D: She is drowsy and hypercapnic with acidosis; delaying definitive airway management is dangerous.
whyNot.E: More bronchodilator alone will not reverse established ventilatory failure with a depressed sensorium.

items.objective: Recognize impending respiratory failure in acute asthma and intubate.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has 2 years of exertional dyspnea and a morning cough. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58 and FEV1 of 61% of predicted. Which of the following interventions is most likely to slow the decline of his lung function?
items.explanationHtml:
Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms COPD. Smoking cessation is the only intervention proven to slow the accelerated decline in FEV1, and it reduces mortality. Offer counseling plus pharmacotherapy such as varenicline or nicotine replacement.

Takeaway: Stopping smoking is what slows COPD progression.

whyNot.A: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce exacerbations in selected patients but do not alter the long-term decline of FEV1.
whyNot.B: Bronchodilators improve symptoms and exacerbations but have not been shown to change the rate of FEV1 decline meaningfully.
whyNot.C: Oxygen improves survival only with severe resting hypoxemia, which he does not have.
whyNot.D: Rehabilitation improves exercise capacity and quality of life but does not slow lung function decline.

items.objective: Identify smoking cessation as the disease-modifying intervention in COPD.

items.stemHtml: The patient quits smoking and starts a once-daily long-acting muscarinic antagonist–long-acting β2-agonist inhaler, which he uses correctly. Over the next year he has two exacerbations treated with prednisone, one requiring hospitalization. His blood eosinophil count is 420/µL. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his maintenance therapy?

options.label: C
options.html: Add long-term azithromycin as first choice

options.label: E
options.html: Switch to a long-acting β2-agonist alone

items.explanationHtml:
Exacerbations despite LAMA–LABA with blood eosinophils ≥ 300/µL predict a good response to an inhaled corticosteroid, so triple therapy is preferred. When eosinophils are low, an ICS is unlikely to help and raises pneumonia risk; then roflumilast or azithromycin is considered.

Takeaway: In COPD, add an ICS for exacerbations when eosinophils are high.

whyNot.B: Maintenance oral steroids cause substantial harm without benefit in COPD.
whyNot.C: Azithromycin is an option, but with eosinophils this high an inhaled corticosteroid is the preferred addition.
whyNot.D: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and little benefit; it is not preferred.
whyNot.E: Removing the LAMA would step therapy down despite exacerbations.

items.objective: Escalate COPD maintenance therapy using exacerbation history and eosinophils.

items.stemHtml: Two years later, when clinically stable, his resting room-air arterial blood gas shows pH 7.38, PaCO2 47 mm Hg and PaO2 53 mm Hg; repeat testing 3 weeks later is similar. He has no peripheral edema. Which of the following interventions is most likely to prolong his survival?

options.label: B
options.html: Daily low-dose oral morphine for dyspnea

options.label: C
options.html: Nocturnal oxygen only, if desaturation occurs during sleep

options.label: E
options.html: Supplemental oxygen for at least 15 hours a day

items.explanationHtml:
Long-term oxygen therapy prolongs survival in stable COPD with severe resting hypoxemia: PaO2 ≤ 55 mm Hg or SaO2 ≤ 88% (or 56–59 mm Hg with cor pulmonale, edema or polycythemia). Benefit requires use for at least 15 hours a day; continuous use is better.

Takeaway: PaO2 ≤ 55 mm Hg at rest in stable COPD → long-term oxygen ≥ 15 h/day.

whyNot.A: Statins do not reduce COPD exacerbations or mortality from COPD itself.
whyNot.B: Opioids may ease refractory dyspnea in palliative care but do not prolong survival.
whyNot.C: Oxygen limited to nocturnal desaturation has not been shown to prolong survival.
whyNot.D: Pulmonary vasodilators are not indicated for pulmonary hypertension due to COPD and can worsen V/Q matching.

items.objective: Apply the criteria for survival-improving long-term oxygen in COPD.

items.stemHtml:
A 71-year-old woman with COPD comes to the emergency department with 3 days of increased dyspnea and green sputum. She is alert, answers questions in short sentences and is coughing up secretions effectively. Respirations are 28/min, with accessory muscle use. She has received nebulized albuterol–ipratropium, oral prednisone and oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 90%. Arterial blood gas results 1 hour later are shown.

TestResult
pH7.28
PaCO269 mm Hg
PaO261 mm Hg
HCO3-31 mEq/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Increase oxygen to keep SpO2 at 98–100%

items.explanationHtml:
She has an exacerbation with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35, PaCO2 high, bicarbonate partly compensated). In an alert patient who can protect the airway, bilevel noninvasive ventilation reduces work of breathing, lowers PaCO2 and reduces intubation and death. Antibiotics are also indicated because sputum is purulent with more dyspnea.

Takeaway: COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic acidosis in an alert patient → NIV.

whyNot.A: Intubation is for NIV failure or contraindications (coma, inability to protect the airway, instability); she is alert and clearing secretions.
whyNot.B: More oxygen would worsen hypercapnia through V/Q changes and the Haldane effect; the target is 88–92%.
whyNot.C: Respiratory stimulants are not recommended and do not replace ventilatory support.
whyNot.D: Bicarbonate does not treat respiratory acidosis and can worsen CO2 retention.

items.objective: Choose noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory acidosis in a COPD exacerbation.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man has 3 months of progressive dyspnea and noisy breathing on exertion. Eight months ago he was intubated for 3 weeks for severe pneumonia. He does not smoke. A flow–volume loop is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
The loop shows flattening of both the expiratory and inspiratory limbs, the signature of a fixed upper airway obstruction. After prolonged intubation, cuff-related ischemia can cause tracheal stenosis that presents weeks to months later with stridor and exertional dyspnea. Confirm with CT and bronchoscopy; treatment is dilation or resection.

Takeaway: Plateaus on both limbs of the flow–volume loop = fixed upper airway obstruction, e.g. post-intubation tracheal stenosis.

whyNot.A: Asthma gives a scooped expiratory limb, often reversible, and normal inspiratory flow.
whyNot.B: COPD gives a concave (scooped) expiratory limb with preserved inspiratory flow.
whyNot.C: Fibrosis gives a narrow loop shifted to low volumes with preserved flow shape.
whyNot.E: Variable extrathoracic obstruction flattens only the inspiratory limb.

items.objective: Interpret a flow–volume loop showing fixed upper airway obstruction.
