items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man has had a daily productive cough for years and three episodes of pneumonia. He also has chronic sinusitis and has had two episodes of acute pancreatitis. He and his wife have been unable to conceive; semen analysis shows a low ejaculate volume with no sperm. CT shows upper-lobe bronchiectasis. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to establish the diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, recurrent pancreatitis and obstructive azoospermia from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens point to cystic fibrosis, sometimes first diagnosed in adulthood with milder CFTR variants. Confirm with sweat chloride testing (with CFTR genetic testing).

Takeaway: Adult bronchiectasis plus pancreatitis or obstructive azoospermia → sweat chloride.

whyNot.A: Low nasal NO supports primary ciliary dyskinesia, which causes immotile sperm rather than absent sperm with low volume.
whyNot.B: Hypogammaglobulinemia causes recurrent infections but not pancreatitis or absent vas deferens.
whyNot.C: α1-antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema and liver disease, not this pattern.
whyNot.E: These test for ABPA, a complication rather than a unifying diagnosis here.

items.objective: Choose the diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis presenting in adulthood.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has 1 year of exertional dyspnea. She smoked half a pack a day for 10 years and quit 8 years ago. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55. Chest CT shows emphysema most prominent at the lung bases. In addition to starting inhaled bronchodilators, which of the following tests is most appropriate?
items.explanationHtml:
Early, basal-predominant emphysema in a light smoker suggests α1-antitrypsin deficiency. Measure the serum level, then phenotype or genotype if it is low. All patients with COPD should be tested once. A confirmed diagnosis matters for augmentation therapy, liver surveillance and family screening.

Takeaway: Test every COPD patient once for α1-antitrypsin deficiency, especially young patients with basal emphysema.

whyNot.A: ANCA testing is for vasculitis, not emphysema.
whyNot.B: Obstruction is already established; a challenge test adds nothing.
whyNot.C: ACE levels are nonspecific and relate to sarcoidosis, an interstitial disease.
whyNot.E: Cystic fibrosis presents with bronchiectasis and upper-lobe disease, not basal emphysema.

items.objective: Identify when to test for α1-antitrypsin deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man comes to the emergency department with wheezing after cleaning a dusty basement. He has had similar episodes since childhood. He coughs up thick sputum plugs. Microscopy of the sputum shows coiled mucus casts and many slender, needle-shaped crystals. These crystals are formed from a protein released by which of the following cells?
items.explanationHtml:
Needle-shaped Charcot-Leyden crystals are made of galectin-10, a protein abundant in eosinophils (and basophils). Their presence with coiled mucus casts of shed epithelium points to eosinophilic airway inflammation, typical of allergic asthma driven by IL-5.

Takeaway: Crystals in asthmatic sputum come from eosinophils; the coiled casts come from mucus and shed epithelium.

whyNot.A: Macrophages may contain hemosiderin or dust but are not the source of the crystals.
whyNot.B: Shed epithelium contributes to the coiled mucus casts (Curschmann spirals), not to the crystals.
whyNot.D: Goblet cells produce mucus, the matrix of plugs, not crystals.
whyNot.E: Neutrophils release elastase and form neutrophil extracellular traps; they do not form these crystals and dominate type 2-low or infected airways.

items.objective: Identify the eosinophil as the source of Charcot-Leyden crystals in asthmatic sputum.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman who has never smoked has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea. Chest CT shows emphysema that is most marked in both lower lobes. Serum aminotransferase activities are mildly increased. A liver biopsy shows round eosinophilic globules in periportal hepatocytes that stain with periodic acid–Schiff after diastase digestion. Which of the following best explains her liver disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of interlobular bile ducts

options.label: B
options.html: Copper accumulation from defective biliary excretion

options.label: C
options.html: Iron overload from increased intestinal absorption

options.label: D
options.html: Retention of misfolded, polymerized protein in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: E
options.html: Unopposed neutrophil elastase activity in the hepatic sinusoids

items.explanationHtml:
Severe α1-antitrypsin deficiency (usually PiZZ) produces a misfolded protein that polymerizes and is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes, seen as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules. The retained protein injures hepatocytes (a toxic gain of function) and causes cirrhosis, while the lack of circulating inhibitor (loss of function) leaves lung elastin exposed to neutrophil elastase, causing panacinar, lower-lobe emphysema.

Takeaway: α1-antitrypsin deficiency hurts the lung by loss of function and the liver by retention of misfolded protein.

whyNot.A: This describes primary biliary cholangitis, a cholestatic disease without emphysema.
whyNot.B: That is Wilson disease (ATP7B), which causes neuropsychiatric and liver disease, not emphysema.
whyNot.C: Hemochromatosis causes cirrhosis with iron (Prussian blue) staining, not PAS-positive globules or emphysema.
whyNot.E: Elastase imbalance explains the lung disease; the liver injury comes from the retained protein itself.

items.objective: Explain the different mechanisms of lung and liver injury in α1-antitrypsin deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has progressive dyspnea. He is thin, with an increased anteroposterior chest diameter, and breathes out through pursed lips. Which of the following sets of pulmonary function results is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: FEV1/FVC decreased; total lung capacity decreased; DLCO decreased

options.label: B
options.html: FEV1/FVC decreased; total lung capacity increased; DLCO decreased

options.label: C
options.html: FEV1/FVC decreased; total lung capacity increased; DLCO increased

options.label: D
options.html: FEV1/FVC increased; total lung capacity decreased; DLCO decreased

options.label: E
options.html: FEV1/FVC normal; total lung capacity normal; DLCO decreased

items.explanationHtml:
Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and elastic tissue. Loss of recoil and of radial traction causes expiratory airway collapse (low FEV1/FVC), air trapping and hyperinflation (high TLC and RV). Loss of alveolar–capillary surface area lowers the DLCO.

Takeaway: Emphysema: obstruction, hyperinflation and a low DLCO.

whyNot.A: A low TLC defines restriction; emphysema causes hyperinflation with a normal or high TLC.
whyNot.C: DLCO rises with alveolar hemorrhage, polycythemia or asthma, but falls when alveolar walls are destroyed.
whyNot.D: This is the interstitial fibrosis pattern.
whyNot.E: An isolated low DLCO suggests pulmonary vascular disease or anemia, not obstruction with hyperinflation.

items.objective: Predict the pulmonary function pattern of emphysema.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with COPD starts a once-daily inhaled maintenance drug. Two weeks later she reports a dry mouth and, separately, difficulty starting her urinary stream. The drug most likely improves her airflow by blocking which of the following receptors on airway smooth muscle?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-acting muscarinic antagonists such as tiotropium block M3 receptors, preventing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion. Their anticholinergic effects explain dry mouth and urinary retention; they can rarely precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Takeaway: LAMAs relax airway smooth muscle by blocking M3 receptors; watch for dry mouth and urinary retention.

whyNot.A: Adenosine antagonism is a theophylline action, an oral drug with toxicity mostly cardiac and neurologic.
whyNot.B: Leukotriene receptor antagonists are oral asthma drugs without anticholinergic adverse effects.
whyNot.C: Antihistamines are not maintenance bronchodilators for COPD.
whyNot.E: Blocking β1 receptors would not relax airways; β-blockade can worsen bronchospasm.

items.objective: Relate the mechanism and adverse effects of long-acting muscarinic antagonists.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman has severe asthma with frequent exacerbations despite adherence to high-dose inhaled corticosteroid–formoterol and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist. Her blood eosinophil count is 750/µL. She begins an injected monoclonal antibody that binds a receptor on eosinophils and depletes them through antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Which of the following is the target of this antibody?
items.explanationHtml:
Benralizumab binds IL-5 receptor α on eosinophils and basophils; its afucosylated Fc portion strongly engages NK-cell Fc receptors, so the cells are killed by antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, producing near-complete eosinophil depletion.

Takeaway: Anti-IL-5 drugs starve eosinophils; anti-IL-5Rα kills them by ADCC.

whyNot.A: Mepolizumab and reslizumab bind circulating IL-5, starving eosinophils of a survival signal, rather than binding a receptor and recruiting killer cells.
whyNot.B: That is omalizumab, which prevents IgE from binding FcεRI and does not deplete eosinophils directly.
whyNot.C: Dupilumab blocks IL-4Rα (inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 signaling); it does not deplete eosinophils and can transiently raise their count.
whyNot.E: Tezepelumab neutralizes this soluble alarmin; it does not bind a cell receptor to kill eosinophils.

items.objective: Distinguish the targets of asthma biologics.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years has coughed up mucoid sputum most days for several years, especially in winter. He dies in a motor vehicle collision. Which of the following findings in his bronchi is most characteristic of his chronic condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Enlarged airspaces with loss of alveolar walls

options.label: C
options.html: Hypertrophy of submucosal mucous glands relative to wall thickness

options.label: D
options.html: Permanent dilation of bronchi with destroyed muscular walls

options.label: E
options.html: Thickened subepithelial basement membrane with eosinophils

items.explanationHtml:
Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically by productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years. Its hallmark lesion is hypertrophy and hyperplasia of submucosal mucous glands, measured as an increased Reid index (gland thickness / wall thickness), with goblet-cell hyperplasia and small-airway inflammation.

Takeaway: Chronic bronchitis = mucous gland hypertrophy (high Reid index).

whyNot.A: This is emphysema, a disease of the acinus rather than the bronchi.
whyNot.B: Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis.
whyNot.D: This describes bronchiectasis, which causes copious purulent sputum.
whyNot.E: These are features of asthma.

items.objective: Recognize the histologic hallmark of chronic bronchitis.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent pneumonia, bulky foul-smelling stools and poor weight gain. A sweat test shows a chloride concentration of 92 mmol/L. Which of the following best explains the high chloride concentration in his sweat?

options.label: A
options.html: Excess aldosterone action on the sweat duct

options.label: B
options.html: Excess chloride secretion by the sweat gland secretory coil

options.label: C
options.html: Failure of chloride reabsorption from the lumen of the sweat duct

options.label: D
options.html: Increased activity of the epithelial sodium channel in the duct

options.label: E
options.html: Increased paracellular permeability of the duct epithelium

items.explanationHtml:
In the sweat duct, CFTR is the route by which chloride is reabsorbed from primary sweat, with sodium following through ENaC. When CFTR fails, chloride (and sodium) stay in the lumen, so sweat is salty. In airways, by contrast, CFTR secretes chloride; its loss dehydrates the surface liquid and thickens mucus.

Takeaway: Cystic fibrosis raises sweat chloride by failure of ductal reabsorption.

whyNot.A: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and lowers sweat salt.
whyNot.B: The secretory coil produces isotonic sweat normally; the defect is downstream.
whyNot.D: ENaC activity in the duct would remove sodium, and chloride follows only through CFTR; it would not raise sweat chloride.
whyNot.E: Duct tight junctions are tight to chloride; leakiness is not the mechanism in cystic fibrosis.

items.objective: Explain the basis of the sweat chloride test in cystic fibrosis.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He has had chronic sinusitis and a daily productive cough since childhood. Chest CT shows bronchiectasis in the middle and lower lobes, and his cardiac apex is on the right. Semen analysis shows a normal sperm count with no motile sperm. Which of the following structures is most likely defective?
items.explanationHtml:
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome when situs inversus is present) results from defects in axonemal dynein arms or other ciliary components. Immotile respiratory cilia cause chronic sinusitis, otitis and bronchiectasis; immotile sperm flagella cause male infertility; failure of nodal cilia during embryogenesis randomizes left–right orientation, so about half have situs inversus.

Takeaway: Bronchiectasis + sinusitis + immotile sperm ± situs inversus = dynein arm defect.

whyNot.B: CFTR disease causes infertility through absent vas deferens (no sperm in semen), not through immotile sperm, and does not cause situs inversus.
whyNot.C: Kinesin moves cargo toward microtubule plus ends in axons; it does not power ciliary beating.
whyNot.D: This is Chediak-Higashi syndrome: giant granules, albinism and infections, not situs inversus.
whyNot.E: IgA deficiency causes sinopulmonary infections but not immotile sperm or situs inversus.

items.objective: Identify the structural defect in primary ciliary dyskinesia.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman with long-standing asthma has had more frequent attacks and brownish mucus plugs for 6 months. Chest CT shows dilated central bronchi. Total serum IgE is 2,800 IU/mL (normal below 100), the blood eosinophil count is 1,100/µL, and serum IgE and IgG against Aspergillus fumigatus are increased. A biopsy shows no fungal invasion of tissue. Which of the following types of hypersensitivity mainly mediate her disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is an immune response to Aspergillus growing in airway mucus. IgE-mediated (type I) reactions cause bronchospasm and eosinophilia; IgG–antigen complexes (type III) contribute to bronchial wall inflammation and central bronchiectasis. Treatment is systemic corticosteroids, with itraconazole to reduce fungal burden.

Takeaway: ABPA is type I plus type III hypersensitivity to airway-colonizing Aspergillus.

whyNot.A: There is no tissue invasion; invasive aspergillosis occurs in neutropenic or immunosuppressed hosts.
whyNot.C: IgE-mediated reactions explain wheeze and eosinophilia, but the specific IgG and central bronchial wall damage point to immune complexes as well.
whyNot.D: Antibodies against fixed tissue antigens are not the mechanism.
whyNot.E: Delayed T-cell hypersensitivity with granulomas suggests hypersensitivity pneumonitis or tuberculosis, not this IgE/IgG picture.

items.objective: Classify the hypersensitivity mechanisms of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with severe emphysema performs a forced expiration. Despite increasing effort, his peak expiratory flow and the flow over the rest of the maneuver do not rise. Which of the following best explains why greater effort fails to increase expiratory flow?

options.label: A
options.html: Dynamic compression of airways that have lost elastic recoil and radial traction

options.label: B
options.html: Increased airway resistance from mucous gland hypertrophy in the large bronchi

options.label: C
options.html: Increased pulmonary capillary pressure compressing the small airways

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced surfactant production by type II pneumocytes

items.explanationHtml:
During forced expiration, pleural pressure becomes positive and compresses the airways. Flow is driven by the difference between alveolar pressure and pleural pressure, which equals elastic recoil pressure. In emphysema, recoil is low and the walls of small airways have lost the tethering of surrounding alveoli, so the point where intraluminal pressure equals surrounding pressure moves toward the alveoli, and the airways collapse earlier. Extra effort raises pleural and alveolar pressure equally, so flow does not rise.

Takeaway: Loss of recoil and tethering makes expiratory flow in emphysema effort-independent through dynamic airway compression.

whyNot.B: Large-airway mucus contributes in chronic bronchitis but does not explain effort-independent flow limitation.
whyNot.C: Interstitial edema is a feature of heart failure, not emphysema.
whyNot.D: Muscle weakness would reduce the effort itself, not make flow independent of effort.
whyNot.E: Surfactant deficiency lowers compliance and causes atelectasis, the opposite of emphysema.

items.objective: Explain effort-independent expiratory flow limitation in emphysema.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has 14 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. He is a retired accountant who smoked for 25 years and quit 15 years ago. He takes no medications. Pulse oximetry is 95% at rest and falls to 87% after walking 3 minutes. He has digital clubbing and fine, dry inspiratory crackles over both lower posterior chest. Chest radiograph shows low lung volumes with bilateral basal reticular opacities. Spirometry shows FVC 64% of predicted with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.84. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Crackles, clubbing, exertional desaturation and a restrictive pattern with basal reticulation point to fibrotic interstitial lung disease. High-resolution CT defines the pattern and distribution and is the single most useful test. A definite UIP pattern (basal, subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) in an older patient without exposures, drugs or connective tissue disease establishes IPF without biopsy.

Takeaway: Suspected ILD: HRCT is the key next test; biopsy only when HRCT is indeterminate.

whyNot.A: Small transbronchial samples rarely show the UIP pattern and are not the first test.
whyNot.C: ACE is neither sensitive nor specific and would not characterize the fibrosis.
whyNot.D: Biopsy is reserved for patients whose HRCT and clinical picture remain indeterminate; a typical HRCT can make it unnecessary.
whyNot.E: V/Q scanning looks for pulmonary embolism, which does not explain months of crackles, clubbing and restriction.

items.objective: Choose high-resolution CT as the initial imaging test for suspected interstitial lung disease.

items.stemHtml: High-resolution CT in the same patient shows bilateral subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycomb cysts and traction bronchiectasis, and no ground-glass opacity or nodules. Antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are negative. A multidisciplinary team diagnoses idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. In addition to pulmonary rehabilitation and oxygen with exertion, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib or pirfenidone slows the annual decline in forced vital capacity in IPF and is the standard drug treatment. Neither reverses established fibrosis. Patients should also be referred early for lung transplant evaluation if they are candidates, and receive vaccinations and supplemental oxygen as needed.

Takeaway: IPF is treated with an antifibrotic (nintedanib or pirfenidone), not immunosuppression.

whyNot.A: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for some severe autoimmune ILDs and vasculitis; it has no benefit in IPF.
whyNot.B: Mycophenolate is used for connective tissue disease–associated ILD, which has been excluded.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids do not slow IPF and add infection and metabolic risk.
whyNot.E: This triple regimen increased deaths and hospitalizations in IPF and is avoided.

items.objective: Select antifibrotic therapy for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has 1 week of fever, painful swelling of both ankles and tender red nodules on her shins. She has no cough or dyspnea. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F). Chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. Spirometry is normal. Interferon-γ release assay is negative. ECG is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Fever, erythema nodosum, ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar adenopathy form Löfgren syndrome, an acute presentation of sarcoidosis. It can be diagnosed clinically when the picture is typical and infection has been reasonably excluded, and more than 80% remit within 1–2 years. NSAIDs relieve the arthritis and erythema nodosum. Follow-up with imaging, PFTs and screening for eye, cardiac and calcium involvement continues.

Takeaway: Löfgren syndrome is treated symptomatically with NSAIDs; it usually resolves without steroids or biopsy.

whyNot.A: Nothing suggests tuberculosis: the IGRA is negative and the picture is classic for Löfgren syndrome.
whyNot.B: This combination is characteristic enough that tissue diagnosis is usually unnecessary; invasive biopsy adds risk without changing care.
whyNot.C: Steroid-sparing agents are for chronic, treatment-requiring sarcoidosis, not a self-limited presentation.
whyNot.E: Löfgren syndrome usually remits spontaneously; systemic glucocorticoids are reserved for organ-threatening disease.

items.objective: Manage Löfgren syndrome without biopsy or systemic glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has 5 months of dry cough and fatigue. Chest CT shows bilateral hilar and subcarinal lymphadenopathy, with nodes up to 2.5 cm, and a few small perilymphatic nodules in the upper lobes. She has no skin lesions and no palpable peripheral lymph nodes. Eye examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Empiric prednisone with repeat CT in 3 months

options.label: D
options.html: Surgical lung biopsy by video-assisted thoracoscopy

items.explanationHtml:
Sarcoidosis is diagnosed by a compatible clinical and radiographic picture, noncaseating granulomas in tissue and exclusion of other granulomatous diseases. When the most accessible abnormal tissue is mediastinal lymph nodes, EBUS-TBNA has a high diagnostic yield and is less invasive than mediastinoscopy. Samples also go for mycobacterial and fungal culture and flow cytometry if lymphoma is a concern.

Takeaway: Suspected sarcoidosis: biopsy the least invasive involved site; for mediastinal nodes, EBUS-TBNA.

whyNot.B: Treating without tissue risks missing lymphoma, tuberculosis or fungal infection.
whyNot.C: A raised ACE is supportive at best; it cannot confirm sarcoidosis or exclude lymphoma and infection.
whyNot.D: This is more invasive than needed when enlarged mediastinal nodes can be sampled bronchoscopically.
whyNot.E: PET shows activity but cannot distinguish sarcoidosis from lymphoma or infection without tissue.

items.objective: Choose EBUS-guided needle aspiration to confirm suspected sarcoidosis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman has 9 months of cough and dyspnea. She keeps six parakeets in her living room. Inspiratory squeaks are heard over both lungs. HRCT shows mosaic attenuation with air trapping on expiratory images and mid-zone centrilobular nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows 45% lymphocytes. Pulmonary function is mildly restrictive. Which of the following is the most important step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Remove the birds from her home

items.explanationHtml:
Bird exposure, centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation with air trapping and a lymphocytic BAL indicate hypersensitivity pneumonitis. The cornerstone of treatment is complete avoidance of the antigen, which includes removing the birds, cleaning or replacing contaminated furnishings, and avoiding feather bedding. Systemic glucocorticoids are added for severe or progressive disease.

Takeaway: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: antigen avoidance first; steroids only if severe or progressive.

whyNot.A: Transplant is for end-stage fibrosis; this mild, potentially reversible disease needs antigen removal.
whyNot.C: There is no infection to treat; antibiotics do not alter the immune reaction.
whyNot.D: Inhaled steroids do not treat the parenchymal inflammation of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
whyNot.E: An antifibrotic may be used later for progressive fibrosis, but removing the antigen comes first.

items.objective: Prioritize antigen avoidance in hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

items.stemHtml:
A 46-year-old man has exertional dyspnea that has slowly worsened over 2 years. He does not smoke. His lungs are clear on auscultation. Pulmonary function testing shows:

MeasureResult (% predicted)
FEV173%
FVC71%
FEV1/FVC0.82
Total lung capacity76%
Expiratory reserve volume22%
DLCO (corrected for alveolar volume)104%

Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
The pattern is mild restriction (low TLC with a normal FEV1/FVC) and a normal DLCO, meaning the alveolar membrane is healthy and the restriction is outside the lung. A markedly reduced expiratory reserve volume is characteristic of obesity, because abdominal and chest wall fat lowers the resting lung volume. Weight loss improves these values.

Takeaway: Restriction with normal DLCO and a very low ERV suggests obesity.

whyNot.A: Asthma produces obstruction and a normal or high DLCO, not a reduced total lung capacity.
whyNot.B: Emphysema is obstructive (low FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC) with a high TLC and low DLCO.
whyNot.C: Fibrosis restricts the lung but lowers DLCO, and crackles are usually heard.
whyNot.E: Pulmonary vascular disease lowers DLCO with near-normal volumes.

items.objective: Interpret pulmonary function tests showing extraparenchymal restriction from obesity.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old retired electrician who installed insulation in ships for 20 years in his youth has a chest CT for chronic cough. It shows bilateral calcified pleural plaques and no parenchymal fibrosis or masses. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. Spirometry is normal. Which of the following interventions would most reduce his risk of dying from an asbestos-related disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual chest CT to screen for mesothelioma

options.label: E
options.html: Surgical pleurectomy to remove the plaques

items.explanationHtml:
Asbestos and tobacco multiply each other's lung cancer risk, so quitting smoking is the single most effective step for a person with asbestos exposure. He also qualifies for annual low-dose CT screening for lung cancer if he meets current age and pack-year criteria. Pleural plaques themselves do not become malignant.

Takeaway: After asbestos exposure, smoking cessation gives the largest reduction in lung cancer risk.

whyNot.A: No screening test has been shown to reduce mesothelioma deaths.
whyNot.B: There is no evidence that steroids prevent asbestosis or cancer.
whyNot.C: He is not hypoxemic, and oxygen does not prevent asbestos-related disease.
whyNot.E: Plaques are benign markers of exposure; removing them has no benefit.

items.objective: Counsel smoking cessation as the key preventive measure after asbestos exposure.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man who fabricates engineered-stone kitchen countertops is diagnosed with silicosis after a chest CT shows multiple upper-lobe nodules and calcified hilar nodes. He feels well. He has no cough, fever or weight loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional test?

options.label: B
options.html: Bronchoscopy with lavage for acid-fast bacilli

items.explanationHtml:
Silicosis substantially raises the risk of progressing from latent to active tuberculosis. Every patient with silicosis should be tested for latent infection (IGRA or tuberculin skin test) and treated if positive once active disease has been excluded. Engineered-stone workers can develop accelerated silicosis within a few years of exposure, so removal from exposure is also essential.

Takeaway: Diagnose silicosis → test for latent tuberculosis and treat if positive.

whyNot.A: ANCA testing would be for suspected vasculitis, which nothing suggests.
whyNot.B: Sputum or lavage for active tuberculosis is for symptoms or suspicious imaging; screening for latent infection comes first.
whyNot.C: There is no clinical sign of pulmonary hypertension in this asymptomatic man.
whyNot.E: ACE has no role in the management of silicosis.

items.objective: Screen patients with silicosis for latent tuberculosis infection.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old woman with mild asthma has 2 months of cough, fevers, night sweats and a 5-kg weight loss. Her leukocyte count is 11,400/mm3 with 18% eosinophils. Chest radiograph shows bilateral, peripheral, pleural-based opacities sparing the central lung. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows 42% eosinophils; bacterial, fungal and mycobacterial cultures are negative. Strongyloides serology is negative. ANCA tests are negative and there is no neuropathy or rash. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Weeks of systemic symptoms, peripheral pleural-based infiltrates (the reverse of the pulmonary edema pattern), blood and BAL eosinophilia and an asthma history describe chronic eosinophilic pneumonia. Once infection and parasites are excluded, systemic glucocorticoids produce rapid improvement, often within days. Relapse during tapering is common.

Takeaway: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia responds dramatically to systemic glucocorticoids after infection is excluded.

whyNot.A: There is no parasite: travel history and serology are negative, and the illness is chronic and progressive.
whyNot.B: Imatinib treats the PDGFRA-rearranged hypereosinophilic syndrome, which has multiorgan involvement and sustained marked eosinophilia.
whyNot.C: Cultures are negative and the eosinophilic lavage argues against bacterial pneumonia.
whyNot.E: Fungal cultures are negative and the picture is not invasive aspergillosis.

items.objective: Treat chronic eosinophilic pneumonia with systemic glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man has had asthma for 3 years and chronic sinus congestion with nasal polyps. Over the past month he has developed numbness of the right foot and weakness of left wrist extension, and palpable purpura on both legs. The leukocyte count is 13,200/mm3 with 26% eosinophils. Chest radiograph shows patchy, shifting opacities. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein and no casts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Adult-onset asthma, sinus disease with polyps, marked eosinophilia, transient infiltrates and then a small-vessel vasculitis with mononeuritis multiplex and purpura define eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. ANCA (usually anti-MPO) is positive in only about 40%, so a negative test does not exclude it. Cardiac involvement is the main cause of death and should be sought.

Takeaway: Asthma + eosinophilia + mononeuritis multiplex = EGPA; ANCA is often negative.

whyNot.A: ABPA complicates asthma with eosinophilia and infiltrates but does not cause vasculitic neuropathy or purpura.
whyNot.C: GPA causes destructive sinus disease and nodules but not asthma or prominent eosinophilia.
whyNot.D: PAN causes mononeuritis multiplex but spares the lungs and does not cause asthma or eosinophilia.
whyNot.E: Loeffler syndrome causes transient migratory eosinophilic infiltrates (often from migrating larvae) without asthma history, vasculitis or kidney involvement.

items.objective: Diagnose eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with known pulmonary sarcoidosis has 2 weeks of polyuria, thirst and constipation. Serum calcium is 12.6 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), parathyroid hormone is low and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is high. She has started taking a vitamin D supplement. She receives intravenous normal saline and the supplement is stopped. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH and high calcitriol in sarcoidosis comes from 1α-hydroxylase in granuloma macrophages. Glucocorticoids suppress this macrophage enzyme and lower calcium within days; they are the treatment of choice for symptomatic or renal-impairing hypercalcemia. Hydration and stopping vitamin D supplements help, and sun exposure should be limited.

Takeaway: Sarcoid hypercalcemia (low PTH, high calcitriol) is treated with glucocorticoids.

whyNot.A: Cinacalcet lowers PTH secretion; PTH is already suppressed.
whyNot.B: Calcitriol is the problem; giving more would worsen hypercalcemia.
whyNot.C: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion and would worsen hypercalcemia.
whyNot.E: The parathyroid glands are not the cause; PTH is appropriately low.

items.objective: Treat symptomatic sarcoidosis-related hypercalcemia with glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. For 30 years he worked as a pipefitter in a naval shipyard. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. There are fine crackles at both lung bases. Chest CT shows subpleural reticulation in both lower lobes and calcified plaques on the diaphragmatic pleura. Bronchoalveolar lavage contains golden-brown, beaded rod-shaped bodies that stain blue with Prussian blue. Which of the following malignancies is this patient at greatest absolute risk of developing?
items.explanationHtml:
Pleural plaques, lower-lobe fibrosis and ferruginous bodies (asbestos fibers coated with iron and protein) establish asbestosis. Asbestos increases the risk of both lung carcinoma and mesothelioma, but bronchogenic carcinoma is by far the more common cancer, and asbestos and tobacco act synergistically (the combined risk is greater than the sum of the separate risks).

Takeaway: Asbestos is most specific for mesothelioma but most often causes lung carcinoma, especially in smokers.

whyNot.B: Asbestos and tobacco raise laryngeal cancer risk modestly, but the absolute risk is much lower than for lung carcinoma.
whyNot.C: Mesothelioma is strongly linked to asbestos and is the more specific association, but it is far less common than lung carcinoma, especially in someone who also smoked.
whyNot.D: Swallowed fibers have been linked to some gastrointestinal cancers, but small bowel cancer is rare and not a major asbestos outcome.
whyNot.E: Thymoma has no association with asbestos or tobacco.

items.objective: Identify bronchogenic carcinoma as the most common malignancy after asbestos exposure.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man who has worked for 20 years in a granite quarry has progressive dyspnea. Chest radiograph shows multiple small nodules in both upper lobes and calcification at the rim of enlarged hilar lymph nodes. Lung biopsy shows whorled, hyalinized collagen nodules containing weakly birefringent particles under polarized light. This patient is at markedly increased risk of which of the following infections?
items.explanationHtml:
Upper-lobe nodules, eggshell calcification of hilar nodes and silicotic nodules identify silicosis. Silica particles are toxic to alveolar macrophages and disrupt phagolysosome function, impairing the killing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Patients with silicosis have a several-fold higher risk of active tuberculosis and should be screened and treated for latent infection.

Takeaway: Silicosis means upper-lobe nodules, eggshell nodes and a high risk of tuberculosis.

whyNot.A: A fungus ball can colonize an old cavity, but the classic, well-established infectious risk of silicosis is mycobacterial.
whyNot.B: Legionella is acquired from contaminated water systems and is not linked to silica exposure.
whyNot.C: Pneumocystis infection requires profound T-cell immunosuppression (eg, HIV with a low CD4 count), which silica does not cause.
whyNot.D: Pseudomonas affects patients with cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, ventilators or neutropenia, not silicosis specifically.

items.objective: Relate silica-induced macrophage dysfunction to an increased risk of tuberculosis.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman who machines metal alloys for aerospace components has 8 months of cough, exertional dyspnea and fatigue. Chest CT shows hilar lymphadenopathy and small nodules along the bronchovascular bundles. Transbronchial biopsy shows well-formed noncaseating granulomas. Stains for mycobacteria and fungi are negative. Her peripheral blood lymphocytes proliferate when cultured with a metal salt from her workplace. Which of the following immune mechanisms best explains her lung disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Antigen-specific CD4+ T-helper-1 cells activating macrophages

options.label: B
options.html: Direct toxic injury to alveolar epithelium without sensitization

options.label: D
options.html: IgG antibodies against the alveolar basement membrane

options.label: E
options.html: Immune complexes depositing in alveolar capillary walls

items.explanationHtml:
This is chronic beryllium disease. Beryllium acts as a hapten presented on HLA class II molecules (an HLA-DPB1 variant confers susceptibility), sensitizing CD4+ Th1 cells. These release interferon-γ and TNF-α, which turn macrophages into epithelioid cells and build granulomas. The beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test detects that sensitization and distinguishes berylliosis from sarcoidosis, which looks identical histologically.

Takeaway: Berylliosis is a type IV (Th1) hypersensitivity that mimics sarcoidosis; the lymphocyte proliferation test separates them.

whyNot.B: Direct toxicity without sensitization is the mechanism of silica; the positive lymphocyte proliferation test here shows specific T-cell sensitization.
whyNot.C: IgE-mediated (type I) reactions cause immediate bronchospasm and urticaria, not granulomas.
whyNot.D: Antibodies against basement membrane (type II) cause anti-GBM disease with hemorrhage, not granulomas.
whyNot.E: Immune-complex (type III) injury causes vasculitis and complement-mediated inflammation, not tight granulomas that form after T-cell sensitization.

items.objective: Explain the cell-mediated mechanism of chronic beryllium disease.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis has increasing dyspnea when lying flat. Her lungs are clear. Which of the following sets of pulmonary function results is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC decreased, total lung capacity increased, DLCO decreased

options.label: B
options.html: FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC decreased, total lung capacity normal, DLCO normal

options.label: C
options.html: FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC normal, total lung capacity decreased, DLCO decreased

options.label: D
options.html: FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC normal, total lung capacity decreased, DLCO normal

options.label: E
options.html: FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC normal, total lung capacity normal, DLCO decreased

items.explanationHtml:
Respiratory muscle weakness restricts lung expansion, so TLC and vital capacity fall. Airway caliber is normal, so the FEV1/FVC ratio is normal. The alveolar–capillary membrane is healthy, so DLCO (corrected for alveolar volume) is normal. Orthopnea suggests diaphragm weakness.

Takeaway: Restriction with a normal DLCO points outside the lung parenchyma: muscles, chest wall or obesity.

whyNot.A: This is emphysema: obstruction, hyperinflation and loss of alveolar capillary surface.
whyNot.B: This is pure airway obstruction such as asthma or chronic bronchitis.
whyNot.C: Restriction with a low DLCO means parenchymal disease such as pulmonary fibrosis, not a weak respiratory pump.
whyNot.E: An isolated low DLCO suggests pulmonary vascular disease or anemia.

items.objective: Distinguish extraparenchymal from parenchymal restriction using DLCO.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has 4 months of dry cough, painful red eyes and fatigue. Chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL, phosphorus is 4.2 mg/dL and parathyroid hormone is low. Biopsy of a mediastinal lymph node shows noncaseating granulomas. Which of the following best explains her hypercalcemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Calcitriol production by macrophages in granulomas

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased renal calcium excretion caused by thiazide-like action of ACE

options.label: C
options.html: Increased renal 1α-hydroxylase activity driven by parathyroid hormone

options.label: D
options.html: Osteoclast activation by granulomas within bone

options.label: E
options.html: Parathyroid hormone–related peptide secreted by a tumor

items.explanationHtml:
Activated macrophages in sarcoid granulomas express 1α-hydroxylase and convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol without the normal PTH feedback. Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, raising serum calcium and urinary calcium; PTH falls appropriately. Sunlight exposure and vitamin D supplements can unmask it.

Takeaway: Granulomatous hypercalcemia is PTH-independent calcitriol made by macrophages.

whyNot.B: Angiotensin-converting enzyme raised in sarcoidosis has no effect on renal calcium handling.
whyNot.C: PTH is suppressed, so renal 1α-hydroxylase is not being stimulated.
whyNot.D: Bone granulomas are uncommon and are not the main cause; the effect is mainly increased gut absorption of calcium.
whyNot.E: PTHrP mediates humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy and does not raise 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D; no tumor is present.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man has 18 months of worsening exertional dyspnea and dry cough. He has digital clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. He has no occupational exposures, takes no medications and has no symptoms of connective tissue disease. Surgical lung biopsy is performed. Which of the following microscopic findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Alveoli filled with pigmented macrophages and little fibrosis

options.label: B
options.html: Hyaline membranes lining alveolar ducts throughout both lungs

options.label: C
options.html: Loose, poorly formed granulomas centered on bronchioles

options.label: D
options.html: Patchy subpleural fibrosis of differing ages with fibroblastic foci and honeycomb cysts

options.label: E
options.html: Uniform alveolar wall thickening by lymphocytes and fibrosis of the same age

items.explanationHtml:
An older man with insidious dyspnea, clubbing, basal crackles and no exposure or connective tissue disease has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Its histology is usual interstitial pneumonia: patchy, subpleural and basal fibrosis showing temporal heterogeneity, with dense old scar next to active fibroblastic foci and normal lung, plus honeycombing.

Takeaway: UIP = patchy, temporally heterogeneous subpleural fibrosis with fibroblastic foci and honeycombing.

whyNot.A: This is desquamative interstitial pneumonia, seen in current smokers.
whyNot.B: Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes is acute (ARDS or acute interstitial pneumonia), not an 18-month illness.
whyNot.C: Bronchiolocentric granulomatous inflammation suggests hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which needs an antigen exposure.
whyNot.E: Temporally uniform inflammation and fibrosis is the NSIP pattern, typical of connective tissue disease.

items.objective: Recognize usual interstitial pneumonia as the histologic pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis begins a twice-daily oral medication that slows the decline in her forced vital capacity. Two months later she has diarrhea and mildly elevated aminotransferases. The drug's main antifibrotic action is most likely mediated by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of glucocorticoid receptors in alveolar macrophages

options.label: B
options.html: Antagonism of the IL-5 receptor on eosinophils

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of calcineurin in T lymphocytes

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of growth factor receptor tyrosine kinases on fibroblasts

items.explanationHtml:
Nintedanib is an intracellular inhibitor of several receptor tyrosine kinases, including those for platelet-derived growth factor, fibroblast growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor. Blocking these signals reduces fibroblast proliferation, migration and transformation into myofibroblasts. Diarrhea and liver enzyme elevation are its main adverse effects. Pirfenidone, the other antifibrotic, works through less clearly defined anti-TGF-β and antioxidant effects and causes photosensitivity.

Takeaway: Nintedanib slows IPF by blocking PDGF, FGF and VEGF receptor tyrosine kinases; expect diarrhea.

whyNot.A: Glucocorticoids do not slow IPF and were harmful in combination regimens.
whyNot.B: Anti-IL-5 drugs treat eosinophilic asthma and EGPA, not fibrotic lung disease.
whyNot.C: Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) suppress T-cell activation and have no role in IPF.
whyNot.D: This is mycophenolate, used for connective tissue disease–associated ILD, not the IPF antifibrotic described.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism and main adverse effects of nintedanib.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of fever, chills, cough and breathlessness for 6 months. Each episode begins about 6 hours after he cleans the lofts where he keeps racing pigeons and resolves over 2 days. Between episodes he feels well. Chest CT during an episode shows diffuse centrilobular ground-glass nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows a marked lymphocytosis. Which of the following best describes the immune mechanism of his disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Complement-fixing antibodies against type II pneumocytes

options.label: B
options.html: Direct toxic injury from inhaled particles

options.label: D
options.html: Immune-complex formation together with T-cell–mediated inflammation

items.explanationHtml:
This is hypersensitivity pneumonitis from avian antigens (bird fancier's lung). Precipitating IgG antibodies form immune complexes with inhaled antigen (type III), and with continued exposure CD4+ and CD8+ T cells drive granulomatous inflammation (type IV). The hallmark is symptoms 4–8 hours after exposure, centrilobular nodules and a BAL lymphocytosis.

Takeaway: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis combines type III and type IV reactions to an inhaled organic antigen.

whyNot.A: No autoantibody against lung cells is involved; the antigen is inhaled bird protein.
whyNot.B: Toxic injury would not depend on sensitization or recur with each small exposure.
whyNot.C: Type I reactions start within minutes and cause wheeze with eosinophils; the 6-hour delay and lymphocytic lavage argue against it.
whyNot.E: Superantigens cause toxic shock physiology, not recurrent episodes tied to a specific antigen.

items.objective: Identify the hypersensitivity mechanisms of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl who recently arrived from a rural tropical region has 1 week of dry cough and low-grade fever. Chest radiographs taken 5 days apart show patchy infiltrates that have moved from the right lower zone to the left mid zone. The leukocyte count is 10,800/mm3 with 24% eosinophils. Which of the following organisms most likely causes these findings during its migration through the lungs?
items.explanationHtml:
Simple pulmonary eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome) produces transient, migratory infiltrates with blood eosinophilia. It occurs when helminth larvae pass from the bloodstream into the alveoli, ascend the airways and are swallowed. Ascaris is the classic cause; hookworm and Strongyloides also have a lung phase. The illness is usually mild and self-limited.

Takeaway: Migrating infiltrates plus eosinophilia = larval lung migration (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides).

whyNot.B: Pinworm infection stays in the gut and perianal area; its larvae do not migrate through the lungs.
whyNot.C: Giardia is a protozoan that does not invade tissue or cause eosinophilia.
whyNot.D: Beef tapeworm infection is intestinal and has no pulmonary migration phase.
whyNot.E: Whipworm develops entirely in the intestine and does not pass through the lungs.

items.objective: Identify helminths whose larvae migrate through the lungs and cause Loeffler syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old farmer develops cough, chest tightness and dyspnea 3 hours after climbing into a silo that was filled with fresh corn silage 4 days earlier. A chest radiograph shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates. He recovers with supportive care but returns 5 weeks later with progressive dyspnea and fixed airflow obstruction. Which of the following inhaled agents most likely caused his illness?
items.explanationHtml:
Fresh silage releases nitrogen dioxide, which is heavier than air and pools above the silage for days to weeks after filling. NO2 is poorly water-soluble, so it reaches the distal airways, where it forms nitric acid. Injury causes delayed pulmonary edema; a second phase weeks later is bronchiolitis obliterans with fixed obstruction.

Takeaway: Silo-filler's disease is NO2 injury: delayed pulmonary edema, then bronchiolitis obliterans.

whyNot.A: Carbon monoxide causes tissue hypoxia without direct lung injury or later bronchiolitis.
whyNot.B: Hydrogen sulfide accumulates in manure pits and sewers and causes sudden collapse by blocking cytochrome oxidase.
whyNot.C: Methane is an asphyxiant that displaces oxygen; it is not a direct irritant.
whyNot.E: Spores from moldy hay cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer's lung), not acute chemical edema days after silo filling.

items.objective: Recognize silo-filler's disease and its biphasic course.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old former coal miner with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has a chest radiograph showing several well-defined nodules, 1–3 cm across, in the periphery of both lungs. Some nodules have central cavitation. He is asymptomatic apart from his joint disease. Mycobacterial and fungal studies are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Rheumatoid pneumoconiosis (Caplan syndrome) is the development of multiple peripheral necrobiotic nodules in a person with rheumatoid arthritis who has been exposed to coal, silica or asbestos dust. The nodules resemble rheumatoid nodules with dust rings and may cavitate or calcify. Infection and cancer still have to be excluded.

Takeaway: Rheumatoid arthritis + mineral dust + multiple peripheral nodules = rheumatoid pneumoconiosis.

whyNot.B: Cavitating nodules occur, but GPA brings sinus disease, renal involvement and PR3-ANCA, and has no link to coal dust.
whyNot.C: Cavitating metastases are possible, but multiple stable peripheral nodules in a dust-exposed rheumatoid patient fit a benign immune process.
whyNot.D: Progressive massive fibrosis forms large, conglomerate upper-lobe masses in heavy coal or silica exposure, not multiple discrete peripheral nodules linked to rheumatoid disease.
whyNot.E: Septic emboli come with fever, bacteremia and a source such as tricuspid endocarditis.

items.objective: Recognize rheumatoid pneumoconiosis in a dust-exposed patient with rheumatoid arthritis.

items.stemHtml:
A 56-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia was intubated 6 hours ago for hypoxemic respiratory failure. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 112 kg (247 lb). Chest x-ray shows bilateral alveolar opacities; echocardiography shows normal ventricular function. Current ventilator settings and measurements:

ParameterValue
ModeVolume assist-control
Tidal volume700 mL
Respiratory rate16/min
PEEP8 cm H2O
FIO20.70
Plateau pressure34 cm H2O
PaO288 mm Hg
PaCO238 mm Hg

Which of the following is the most appropriate change to the ventilator settings?

options.label: B
options.html: Lower the tidal volume to about 420 mL with a faster rate

options.label: C
options.html: Raise the tidal volume to 900 mL to recruit alveoli

items.explanationHtml:
He has moderate ARDS (PaO2/FIO2 = 88/0.7 ≈ 126). Lung-protective ventilation uses about 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight, which depends on height and sex, not on actual weight: 50 + 0.91 × (175 − 152.4) ≈ 70.6 kg, so about 420 mL. His current 700 mL is about 10 mL/kg predicted and his plateau pressure exceeds 30 cm H2O. Raise the rate (up to about 35/min) to limit hypercapnia; some rise in PaCO2 is acceptable (permissive hypercapnia).

Takeaway: ARDS: tidal volume ~6 mL/kg predicted body weight and plateau pressure ≤ 30 cm H2O.

whyNot.A: Lowering PEEP would derecruit alveoli and worsen oxygenation; moderate ARDS usually needs the same or more PEEP.
whyNot.C: Larger tidal volumes overdistend the open lung (volutrauma) and raise mortality; his plateau pressure is already too high.
whyNot.D: Nothing suggests auto-PEEP, and cutting the rate while tidal volume is lowered would cause excessive hypercapnia.
whyNot.E: High-frequency oscillation did not improve, and may have worsened, survival in adult ARDS trials.

items.objective: Set lung-protective tidal volume from predicted body weight in ARDS.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with ARDS from aspiration pneumonia has been ventilated for 30 hours with a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, PEEP 14 cm H2O and FIO2 0.80. Plateau pressure is 28 cm H2O. Her PaO2 is 70 mm Hg. She is deeply sedated, has no ventilator dyssynchrony, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg on a low dose of norepinephrine. She has no spinal injury or open abdomen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Administer exogenous surfactant via the endotracheal tube

options.label: B
options.html: Increase the tidal volume to 8 mL/kg predicted body weight

options.label: D
options.html: Place the patient in the prone position for at least 16 hours a day

items.explanationHtml:
Her PaO2/FIO2 ratio is 70/0.8 ≈ 88: severe ARDS despite lung-protective settings. Prone positioning for long sessions (at least 12–16 hours a day) improves survival when the ratio is below about 150. It recruits dorsal lung, makes ventilation more uniform and reduces overdistension. Contraindications include unstable spine fractures, open abdomen and severe hemodynamic instability, none of which she has.

Takeaway: severe ARDS (P/F < 150) despite low tidal volume and PEEP → prone ventilation; ECMO is the next rescue.

whyNot.A: Surfactant replacement benefits premature neonates but has not improved outcomes in adult ARDS.
whyNot.B: Raising tidal volume would increase plateau pressure above 30 cm H<sub>2</sub>O and cause ventilator-induced lung injury.
whyNot.C: ECMO is a rescue therapy after proning has failed; when used for ARDS with preserved cardiac function it is venovenous, not venoarterial.
whyNot.E: Inhaled nitric oxide transiently improves oxygenation but does not improve survival and is not routine therapy.

items.objective: Choose prone positioning for severe ARDS that persists despite lung-protective ventilation.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with severe COPD comes to the emergency department with 3 days of increased dyspnea and purulent sputum. She is alert, answers questions in short phrases, and is using accessory muscles. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 106/min, respirations are 30/min, blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.29, PaCO2 66 mm Hg and PaO2 52 mm Hg. She is given nebulized bronchodilators, systemic glucocorticoids and antibiotics, and oxygen is titrated to a saturation of 88–92%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.html: Oxygen by nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min

items.explanationHtml:
An acute COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic acidosis (pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 45 mm Hg) in an alert, cooperative patient who protects her airway is the strongest indication for noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (bilevel). NIV unloads fatigued respiratory muscles, raises alveolar ventilation, and reduces the need for intubation, hospital stay and mortality. Recheck the gas after 1–2 hours; intubate if pH and PaCO2 fail to improve or mental status declines.

Takeaway: hypercapnic acidosis in COPD with an alert patient → bilevel NIV; intubate if it fails or contraindications appear.

whyNot.A: Intubation is for patients who cannot protect the airway, are drowsy or unstable, or fail NIV; she is alert and stable.
whyNot.B: Heliox lowers airway resistance in upper airway obstruction and some asthma cases but has no proven role in COPD exacerbations.
whyNot.C: Methylxanthines add toxicity (arrhythmias, seizures) with little benefit and are not recommended for exacerbations.
whyNot.E: High-concentration oxygen would worsen V/Q matching and hypercapnia in a CO<sub>2</sub> retainer.

items.objective: Select noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory failure in a COPD exacerbation.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 3 days after a 14-hour flight with sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. She takes an estrogen-containing hormone therapy. Pulse is 112/min, respirations are 24/min, blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. The left calf is swollen and tender. Chest x-ray is normal. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Because clinical suspicion is high and she has no bleeding risk factors, subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
items.explanationHtml:
Tachycardia, hypoxemia, unilateral calf swelling, recent long travel and estrogen use give her a high clinical probability of PE ("PE likely"). In that group, skip D-dimer and confirm with CT pulmonary angiography, which also shows alternative diagnoses and the RV/LV ratio. Starting anticoagulation before imaging is appropriate when suspicion is high and bleeding risk is low.

Takeaway: high pretest probability → CTPA (no D-dimer); low/intermediate → D-dimer first; contrast contraindicated → V/Q.

whyNot.B: Stress testing evaluates coronary ischemia and is unsafe and irrelevant when PE is suspected.
whyNot.C: D-dimer helps only to exclude PE when pretest probability is low or intermediate; with high probability a normal result would not be trusted and imaging is needed anyway.
whyNot.D: Echocardiography can show RV strain but cannot confirm or exclude PE in a stable patient.
whyNot.E: V/Q scanning is the alternative when contrast is contraindicated; her kidney function is normal and she has no contrast allergy.

items.objective: Choose CT pulmonary angiography for a stable patient with high clinical probability of PE.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) CT pulmonary angiography in the same woman shows emboli in segmental arteries of both lower lobes. The right-to-left ventricular diameter ratio is normal and serum troponin is within the reference range. Blood pressure remains 126/78 mm Hg. She has no history of bleeding, cancer or kidney disease, and her pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Warfarin started today, with heparin stopped once the first dose is given

items.explanationHtml:
She has low-risk PE (normotensive, no RV dysfunction, normal troponin). A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban (which needs no parenteral lead-in) is first-line therapy for most patients without cancer, pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome or severe renal failure, and suitable low-risk patients can complete treatment at home. Treat for at least 3 months. Her hormone therapy should be stopped.

Takeaway: stable PE without RV strain → DOAC; thrombolysis only for hypotension; filter only if anticoagulation is impossible.

whyNot.A: Aspirin is far less effective than anticoagulation for treating acute VTE.
whyNot.B: A filter is used only when anticoagulation is contraindicated; it does not treat the clot.
whyNot.D: Thrombolysis is reserved for PE with hypotension (high risk); she is normotensive without RV strain, so bleeding risk outweighs benefit.
whyNot.E: Warfarin must overlap with heparin for at least 5 days and until the INR is therapeutic; early it is transiently prothrombotic (protein C falls first).

items.objective: Select a DOAC as initial therapy for low-risk pulmonary embolism.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) Thirty hours after starting apixaban, the same woman becomes acutely more dyspneic and lightheaded while walking to the bathroom. Pulse is 132/min and blood pressure is 78/48 mm Hg, unchanged after a 500-mL fluid bolus. Jugular veins are distended. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening. She has not had recent surgery, stroke or bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat CT pulmonary angiography in 48 hours

items.explanationHtml:
Sustained hypotension with acute RV failure now makes this a high-risk (massive) PE. Without contraindications, give systemic thrombolysis (for example alteplase) and switch to unfractionated heparin, because it is short-acting and reversible. Use cautious vasopressor support (norepinephrine) and avoid large fluid boluses. Surgical or catheter-directed embolectomy is the alternative when thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails.

Takeaway: PE with sustained hypotension → systemic thrombolysis (embolectomy if contraindicated); RV failure tolerates fluid poorly.

whyNot.A: A dilated, failing RV is harmed by large fluid volumes, which worsen septal shift and LV underfilling; vasopressors support pressure while definitive therapy is given.
whyNot.B: A filter does not relieve the obstruction already in the lungs and is not indicated when anticoagulation can continue.
whyNot.C: Delaying definitive therapy in obstructive shock risks cardiac arrest; the diagnosis is already established.
whyNot.D: Warfarin is no more effective than apixaban and would not treat shock.

items.objective: Treat high-risk pulmonary embolism with obstructive shock using systemic thrombolysis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department with 2 days of mild dyspnea and a swollen, aching left leg. Pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. The left calf is 3 cm larger in circumference than the right and is tender along the deep veins. Lung examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic study?

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the chest without contrast

items.explanationHtml:
Pregnancy is hypercoagulable, and D-dimer rises normally across gestation. When a pregnant patient with suspected PE has leg symptoms, begin with compression ultrasonography. A proximal DVT confirms venous thromboembolism and justifies therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin without chest imaging. If ultrasound is negative and suspicion remains, proceed to chest x-ray and then V/Q scanning or CTPA; the fetal radiation dose of either is very low.

Takeaway: suspected PE in pregnancy with leg symptoms → leg compression ultrasound first; treat VTE in pregnancy with LMWH.

whyNot.A: Invasive angiography is rarely used and carries more procedural and radiation risk than noninvasive tests.
whyNot.B: CTPA is appropriate if leg imaging is negative and PE is still suspected, but starting with ultrasound may avoid chest radiation altogether.
whyNot.D: Chest MRI is not a validated first-line test for PE.
whyNot.E: A V/Q scan is a reasonable chest test later in the algorithm, but leg imaging comes first when there are DVT symptoms.

items.objective: Order compression ultrasonography first for suspected PE in a pregnant patient with DVT symptoms.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man is evaluated for progressive exertional dyspnea. Seven months ago he was treated for an acute pulmonary embolism and has taken anticoagulation since. Initially his breathing improved, but over the past 3 months he becomes short of breath after one flight of stairs. Pulmonary function tests are normal. Transthoracic echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function, a dilated right ventricle and an estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 62 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent or new dyspnea months after an acute PE with echo evidence of pulmonary hypertension suggests chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), where emboli organize into fibrotic obstructions. A V/Q scan is the screening test of choice: it is more sensitive than CT angiography, and a normal scan essentially excludes CTEPH. Mismatched perfusion defects lead to right heart catheterization and pulmonary angiography to plan pulmonary endarterectomy, which can be curative.

Takeaway: pulmonary hypertension after PE → V/Q scan for CTEPH; treat with lifelong anticoagulation and evaluate for endarterectomy.

whyNot.A: Cardiac MRI quantifies RV function but does not establish the cause of pulmonary hypertension.
whyNot.B: Waiting would delay diagnosis of a potentially curable cause of pulmonary hypertension.
whyNot.C: PAH-specific drugs are not started before the type of pulmonary hypertension is confirmed by testing and catheterization.
whyNot.D: Sildenafil is not started before classification; the likeliest diagnosis here may be curable surgically.

items.objective: Use V/Q scanning to screen for CTEPH in pulmonary hypertension after pulmonary embolism.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man with a recent left hemispheric stroke has dysphagia. A nurse places a small-bore nasogastric feeding tube at the bedside. She hears a gurgling sound over the epigastrium while injecting air through the tube and starts continuous enteral feeding. Two hours later he coughs, becomes tachypneic and has an oxygen saturation of 84%. Chest x-ray shows the tube coursing down the right main bronchus with its tip in the right lower lobe and new right basal opacities. Which of the following measures would most reliably have prevented this complication?

options.label: A
options.html: Checking the pH of fluid aspirated from the tube

options.label: B
options.html: Elevating the head of the bed to 30 degrees before feeding

options.label: C
options.html: Injecting a larger volume of air while auscultating

options.label: D
options.html: Radiographic confirmation of tip position before use

options.label: E
options.html: Using a larger-bore, stiffer feeding tube

items.explanationHtml:
Blindly placed feeding tubes enter the airway in a small but important fraction of insertions, more often in patients with impaired cough or gag (stroke, sedation, intubation). The auscultation ("whoosh") test is unreliable. Radiographic confirmation of the tube tip before the first feed is the accepted standard and should be repeated if displacement is suspected. Feeding into the lung causes pneumonitis, pneumothorax and acute respiratory failure.

Takeaway: confirm blind feeding-tube placement with a radiograph before feeding; auscultation is not reliable.

whyNot.A: Aspirate pH can support gastric placement but is unreliable alone (acid suppressants, small aspirates) and is not the confirmatory standard.
whyNot.B: Head elevation reduces aspiration of gastric contents but does not prevent feeding directly into the airway through a misplaced tube.
whyNot.C: Auscultation cannot distinguish bronchial from gastric placement; sound transmits through the chest.
whyNot.E: Tube size does not prevent airway placement; small-bore tubes are preferred for comfort.

items.objective: Apply radiographic confirmation of feeding tube position to prevent respiratory failure from misplaced enteral feeding.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man is admitted with septic shock from a perforated colon. On hospital day 2 he develops worsening hypoxemia and needs intubation. Chest x-ray shows new bilateral patchy opacities. Echocardiography shows normal left ventricular size and function. Despite treatment he dies on day 5. Microscopic examination of the lungs is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Alveoli filled with granular PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous material

options.label: B
options.html: Eosinophilic membranes of fibrin and cell debris lining alveolar ducts

options.label: C
options.html: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages within alveoli and thickened alveolar septa

options.label: D
options.html: Neutrophil-filled alveoli with uniform consolidation confined to one lobe

items.explanationHtml:
Sepsis is the commonest extrapulmonary cause of ARDS. Bilateral opacities with respiratory failure not explained by heart failure (normal echo) within a week of the insult define the syndrome. Its histologic correlate in the first week is diffuse alveolar damage: edema, necrosis of type I pneumocytes and hyaline membranes of fibrin and debris lining alveolar ducts and alveoli.

Takeaway: early ARDS = diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes; type II pneumocytes proliferate later as the epithelium repairs.

whyNot.A: PAS-positive surfactant-like material filling alveoli is pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (anti-GM-CSF antibodies), a slowly progressive disease.
whyNot.C: Hemosiderin-laden (heart failure) cells reflect chronic passive congestion from raised left atrial pressure; his heart function is normal and the course is acute.
whyNot.D: Lobar pneumonia gives consolidation limited to a lobe; his opacities are bilateral and diffuse, arising from an extrapulmonary trigger.
whyNot.E: Noncaseating granulomas along lymphatics suggest sarcoidosis, a chronic disease unrelated to sepsis.

items.objective: Identify hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage) as the histologic hallmark of early ARDS.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman with severe acute pancreatitis is intubated for worsening hypoxemia and bilateral alveolar opacities. On a fraction of inspired oxygen of 1.0 with low tidal volumes, her PaO2 is 61 mm Hg and PaCO2 is 40 mm Hg. Increasing the inspired oxygen from 0.6 to 1.0 raised the PaO2 only from 56 to 61 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains her hypoxemia?

options.label: B
options.html: Diffusion limitation across a thickened alveolar membrane

options.label: C
options.html: Low inspired partial pressure of oxygen

items.explanationHtml:
In ARDS, protein-rich fluid floods and collapses alveoli. Blood perfusing these unventilated units never meets alveolar gas, so it returns to the left heart with venous oxygen content: an intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0). Because the added oxygen cannot reach shunted blood, PaO2 barely rises with 100% oxygen, which distinguishes shunt from V/Q mismatch and diffusion limitation. PEEP helps by reopening collapsed units.

Takeaway: hypoxemia that hardly improves on 100% oxygen means shunt; ARDS hypoxemia is mainly shunt.

whyNot.A: Her PaCO<sub>2</sub> is normal, so ventilation is adequate; hypoventilation also corrects readily with oxygen.
whyNot.B: Diffusion limitation is overcome by raising the alveolar oxygen tension, so PaO<sub>2</sub> would rise substantially on 100% oxygen.
whyNot.C: She is breathing 100% oxygen; inspired oxygen is high, not low.
whyNot.E: High-V/Q units are dead space; they waste ventilation but do not by themselves cause hypoxemia. Low-V/Q units would respond well to oxygen.

items.objective: Explain why shunt causes hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen in ARDS.

items.stemHtml:
A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found difficult to rouse at home. Respirations are 6/min and shallow. Pupils are pinpoint. The lungs are clear. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air at sea level shows:

TestResult
pH7.22
PaCO270 mm Hg
PaO254 mm Hg
HCO3−27 mEq/L

Assume a respiratory quotient of 0.8 and an inspired oxygen partial pressure of 150 mm Hg. Which of the following best describes his alveolar–arterial (A–a) oxygen gradient and the cause of hypoxemia?

options.label: A
options.html: About 42 mm Hg; aspiration with intrapulmonary shunt

items.explanationHtml:
PAO2 = 150 − (70 / 0.8) = 150 − 87.5 = 62.5 mm Hg. A–a gradient = 62.5 − 54 ≈ 8 mm Hg, which is normal. Hypoxemia with a normal gradient and high PaCO2 is alveolar hypoventilation, here from opioid-induced depression of the medullary respiratory center (pinpoint pupils). The near-normal bicarbonate shows the acidosis is acute.

Takeaway: high PaCO2 + normal A–a gradient = pure hypoventilation (drugs, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall); a raised gradient means lung disease.

whyNot.A: A gradient of about 42 mm Hg would point to lung disease such as aspiration, but the calculated gradient is normal and the lungs are clear.
whyNot.B: Diffusion limitation raises the A–a gradient; his gradient is normal and nothing suggests interstitial disease.
whyNot.D: V/Q mismatch raises the A–a gradient; a normal gradient points away from intrinsic lung disease.
whyNot.E: 96 mm Hg is the inspired value minus PaO<sub>2</sub> with no CO<sub>2</sub> correction; it is not the A–a gradient.

items.objective: Calculate the A–a gradient and use it to identify hypoventilation as the cause of hypoxemia.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain 4 days after a total hip replacement. Pulse is 118/min and respirations are 28/min. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows pH 7.50, PaCO2 29 mm Hg and PaO2 63 mm Hg. CT angiography shows a thrombus in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery. Which of the following best explains her PaCO2?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased carbon dioxide production from reduced activity

options.label: B
options.html: Hyperventilation from chemoreceptor and juxtacapillary receptor stimulation

options.label: C
options.html: Increased alveolar dead space in the occluded segment

options.label: D
options.html: Renal compensation for a primary metabolic acidosis

options.label: E
options.html: Right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale

items.explanationHtml:
Pulmonary embolism typically produces acute respiratory alkalosis. Hypoxemia (from low-V/Q units as flow is diverted to the remaining vessels) stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors, and stretch and irritant (J) receptors in the lung add to the drive to breathe. The resulting rise in minute ventilation lowers PaCO2 despite the new dead space.

Takeaway: PE: tachypnea, hypoxemia, raised A–a gradient and low PaCO2 (respiratory alkalosis); hypercapnia appears only with massive PE or exhaustion.

whyNot.A: CO<sub>2</sub> production after surgery is normal or increased; reduced production would not explain an acute fall to 29 mm Hg.
whyNot.C: Dead space wastes ventilation and, at a fixed minute ventilation, would raise PaCO<sub>2</sub>, not lower it.
whyNot.D: Her pH is alkalemic, so a primary metabolic acidosis is not present; and the kidney does not lower PaCO<sub>2</sub>.
whyNot.E: A shunt would worsen oxygenation but does not explain a low PaCO<sub>2</sub>; there is no evidence of an intracardiac shunt.

items.objective: Explain the respiratory alkalosis that accompanies acute pulmonary embolism.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has 1 year of progressive exertional dyspnea and two episodes of near-syncope while climbing stairs. Her mother died of a similar illness at age 41. Examination shows a loud pulmonic component of S2 and a right ventricular heave. Right heart catheterization shows mean pulmonary arterial pressure 48 mm Hg and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 9 mm Hg. Testing for connective tissue disease, HIV and chronic thromboembolism is negative. A germline variant in the gene encoding which of the following is most likely?

options.label: E
options.html: Surfactant protein C (a type II pneumocyte product)

items.explanationHtml:
Precapillary pulmonary hypertension (mPAP > 20 mm Hg, PCWP ≤ 15 mm Hg) in a young woman with an affected parent and no secondary cause is heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension. Most familial cases carry loss-of-function variants in BMPR2, a TGF-β superfamily receptor whose signaling normally restrains vascular smooth muscle proliferation. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, so many carriers never develop disease.

Takeaway: familial PAH = BMPR2 (autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance) → medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation, plexiform lesions.

whyNot.A: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar emphysema and liver disease, not isolated precapillary pulmonary hypertension.
whyNot.C: CFTR variants cause cystic fibrosis with bronchiectasis and pancreatic insufficiency; pulmonary hypertension appears only late, from lung disease.
whyNot.D: Fibrillin-1 variants cause Marfan syndrome with aortic root dilation and lens dislocation.
whyNot.E: Surfactant protein C variants cause familial interstitial lung disease, which would give a restrictive picture rather than isolated vascular disease.

items.objective: Associate heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension with BMPR2 loss-of-function variants.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension starts an oral medication. Before each monthly refill she must have liver aminotransferase levels checked and a pregnancy test, and she agrees to use two reliable forms of contraception. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of prostacyclin (IP) receptors on vascular smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in arteriolar smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.html: Competitive antagonism at the endothelin-1 receptor

options.label: D
options.html: Direct stimulation of soluble guanylate cyclase

items.explanationHtml:
Bosentan is a dual endothelin receptor (ETA/ETB) antagonist. Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor and smooth muscle mitogen that is overexpressed in PAH. Class adverse effects are teratogenicity (so pregnancy testing and contraception are mandatory), edema and anemia; bosentan specifically causes dose-related hepatotoxicity, so aminotransferases are monitored.

Takeaway: endothelin receptor antagonists (-sentans): teratogenic; bosentan is hepatotoxic.

whyNot.A: Prostacyclin-pathway drugs (epoprostenol, treprostinil, selexipag) cause flushing and jaw pain; they do not require monthly liver tests.
whyNot.B: Calcium channel blockers are used only in vasoreactive PAH; they are not teratogenic and need no liver monitoring.
