whyNot.D: Riociguat is teratogenic but does not carry the hepatotoxicity monitoring described here.
whyNot.E: PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) are not teratogenic or hepatotoxic; their key interaction is hypotension with nitrates.

items.objective: Identify endothelin receptor antagonism from the monitoring requirements of bosentan.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is admitted after a motorcycle crash with a closed fracture of the left femoral shaft, which is placed in traction. Thirty-six hours later he becomes agitated and confused and is short of breath. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 30/min, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. There are nonblanching petechiae over the axillae, upper chest and conjunctivae. The platelet count is 140,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Pulmonary embolism from deep venous thrombosis

items.explanationHtml:
Fat embolism syndrome occurs 24–72 hours after fractures of long bones or the pelvis (or orthopedic surgery). Marrow fat globules enter torn venules, lodge in the pulmonary and systemic microcirculation, and are hydrolyzed into free fatty acids that injure endothelium. The classic triad is hypoxemia, neurologic change and petechiae in nondependent areas (axillae, upper trunk, conjunctivae). Early fixation of fractures lowers the risk; treatment is supportive.

Takeaway: long-bone fracture + 1–3 days + hypoxemia + confusion + axillary/conjunctival petechiae = fat embolism.

whyNot.B: Meningococcemia causes fever and petechiae, but the timing after a long-bone fracture and the axillary and conjunctival distribution fit fat embolism; purpura in meningococcemia is usually widespread with shock.
whyNot.C: Thromboembolic PE causes hypoxemia but not petechiae or this degree of confusion; it usually occurs later than 36 hours after injury.
whyNot.D: TTP needs severe thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolysis; his platelet count is near normal.
whyNot.E: Air embolism follows a vascular access event and is abrupt, not a delayed syndrome after a fracture.

items.objective: Recognize fat embolism syndrome after a long-bone fracture.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man has a central venous catheter removed from the right internal jugular vein while he sits upright in a chair. As the catheter comes out he takes a deep breath and gasps. Within a minute he becomes dyspneic and hypotensive, and a loud churning sound is heard over the precordium. Which of the following most directly allowed this complication to occur?

options.label: A
options.html: Central venous pressure falling below atmospheric pressure during inspiration

options.label: B
options.html: High right atrial pressure forcing blood out of the venotomy

options.label: C
options.html: Positive intrathoracic pressure generated by a Valsalva maneuver

options.label: D
options.html: Release of a catheter-tip thrombus into the pulmonary artery

options.label: E
options.html: Trendelenburg positioning that raised jugular venous pressure

items.explanationHtml:
Air enters a vein whenever the pressure inside it is lower than atmospheric pressure. In an upright patient, jugular and central venous pressures are low, and deep inspiration makes intrathoracic (and central venous) pressure negative, so air is sucked through the open tract. A large bolus forms an air lock in the right ventricular outflow tract (the churning “mill-wheel” murmur), causing obstructive shock. Lines are therefore removed with the patient supine or head-down while exhaling or performing a Valsalva maneuver, and the site is covered with an occlusive dressing.

Takeaway: venous air embolism needs an open vein + venous pressure below atmospheric (upright, inspiring); prevent with head-down position and exhalation/Valsalva.

whyNot.B: High right atrial pressure would push blood out of the vein and keep air out, not draw it in.
whyNot.C: A Valsalva maneuver raises intrathoracic and venous pressure and is used to prevent air entry during line removal.
whyNot.D: Catheter thrombus embolism would cause PE without the churning precordial sound, which reflects air in the right ventricle.
whyNot.E: Head-down positioning raises neck venous pressure above atmospheric and is protective; he was upright.

items.objective: Explain the pressure conditions that allow venous air embolism during central line removal.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman is evaluated after drainage of a brain abscess. She has had nosebleeds several times a month since childhood. Examination shows small red macules that blanch with pressure on her lips, tongue and fingertips. Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air when standing and 94% lying down. Contrast echocardiography shows bubbles appearing in the left atrium after several cardiac cycles. Her father has had similar nosebleeds and iron-deficiency anemia. Which of the following best describes the inheritance of her condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, a first-degree relative and visceral arteriovenous malformations define hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), an autosomal dominant disorder of TGF-β pathway genes (ENG, ACVRL1). Delayed bubbles in the left heart on contrast echocardiography indicate an intrapulmonary shunt through a pulmonary AVM. The shunt bypasses the lung's capillary filter, so paradoxical emboli cause stroke and brain abscess; lower-lobe AVMs cause desaturation when upright (orthodeoxia). Treatment of significant AVMs is transcatheter embolization.

Takeaway: HHT is autosomal dominant; pulmonary AVMs → hypoxemia, orthodeoxia, paradoxical stroke and brain abscess.

whyNot.B: Autosomal recessive disorders usually affect siblings of unaffected carrier parents; here an affected parent passes the trait to his daughter.
whyNot.C: Mitochondrial disorders are transmitted only by mothers; this trait came from her father.
whyNot.D: An X-linked dominant trait from an affected father would affect all his daughters; it is possible but HHT is autosomal, and male-to-female transmission alone does not establish X linkage.
whyNot.E: X-linked recessive disorders mainly affect males and are not passed from father to daughter as a disease.

items.objective: Recognize hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with pulmonary AVMs and its autosomal dominant inheritance.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man has loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. His wife has seen him stop breathing during sleep. He has hypertension that is uncontrolled despite three drugs, and he had a myocardial infarction last year with an ejection fraction now of 35%. BMI is 36 kg/m2; neck circumference is 46 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study?

options.label: A
options.html: Arterial blood gas on room air

items.explanationHtml:
He has a high probability of obstructive sleep apnea. Because he also has significant heart failure (a risk for central apnea and Cheyne–Stokes breathing), the appropriate study is in-laboratory polysomnography, which records airflow, effort, oximetry and EEG and separates obstructive from central events. Home sleep testing is reserved for patients without major cardiopulmonary comorbidity.

Takeaway: Suspected sleep apnea with heart failure or other major comorbidity → in-lab polysomnography.

whyNot.A: A blood gas screens for hypoventilation but does not diagnose sleep apnea.
whyNot.C: This test is for narcolepsy and hypersomnolence, after sleep apnea has been excluded.
whyNot.D: Oximetry alone cannot distinguish obstructive from central events or measure the apnea–hypopnea index reliably.
whyNot.E: Spirometry does not evaluate sleep-disordered breathing.

items.objective: Choose the diagnostic study for suspected sleep apnea with cardiopulmonary comorbidity.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman has daytime sleepiness that caused her to drift out of her lane twice while driving. Polysomnography shows an apnea–hypopnea index of 38 events per hour, almost all obstructive, with nadir oxygen saturation of 79%. BMI is 33 kg/m2. In addition to weight-loss counseling and advice to avoid driving while drowsy, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Zolpidem at bedtime for sleep quality

items.explanationHtml:
She has severe, symptomatic obstructive sleep apnea (AHI 30 or more). CPAP splints the upper airway open, abolishing most events and improving sleepiness, driving risk and blood pressure. Oral appliances or hypoglossal nerve stimulation are options if she cannot tolerate CPAP.

Takeaway: Moderate–severe symptomatic OSA → CPAP.

whyNot.A: Wakefulness agents may help residual sleepiness after effective airway treatment, but they do not treat the airway obstruction.
whyNot.C: Oxygen alone does not prevent apneas, arousals or the cardiovascular effects.
whyNot.D: Surgery is not first-line and is less effective than positive airway pressure.
whyNot.E: Sedative-hypnotics can worsen airway collapse and are avoided.

items.objective: Select first-line therapy for severe obstructive sleep apnea.

items.stemHtml: In January, a 36-year-old woman and her two children come to the emergency department with headache, nausea and dizziness that began this morning. The symptoms improve outdoors. Their home has an old gas furnace. The woman briefly lost consciousness in the bathroom. Pulse is 108/min and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air is 99%. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Noncontrast CT scan of the head

options.label: E
options.html: Serum methemoglobin by standard pulse oximetry

items.explanationHtml:
A household cluster of headache and nausea in winter that improves away from home, with a faulty gas appliance, suggests carbon monoxide poisoning. Pulse oximetry is falsely normal because carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light like oxyhemoglobin. Confirm with a co-oximetry carboxyhemoglobin level on a blood sample; start 100% oxygen while waiting.

Takeaway: Suspected CO poisoning → co-oximetry; ignore a normal pulse oximeter.

whyNot.A: PaO2 is normal in this poisoning and therefore unhelpful.
whyNot.C: CT may be needed for persistent deficits but does not confirm the cause of a household cluster of symptoms.
whyNot.D: Lactate is a marker of severity and possible cyanide co-exposure, not a diagnostic test for this poisoning.
whyNot.E: Standard pulse oximetry cannot measure dyshemoglobins.

items.objective: Confirm carbon monoxide poisoning with co-oximetry.

items.stemHtml: Her carboxyhemoglobin level is 29%. She is receiving 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask. A pregnancy test is negative. Neurologic examination now is normal; her ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management for her?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge home once the carboxyhemoglobin level is below 5%

items.explanationHtml:
Normobaric 100% oxygen continues for everyone. Hyperbaric oxygen is commonly recommended for CO poisoning with loss of consciousness or syncope, neurologic signs, carboxyhemoglobin above about 25% (lower in pregnancy), myocardial ischemia or severe acidosis, because it eliminates CO faster and may reduce delayed neurologic sequelae. She meets two criteria. The children also need levels and treatment, and the home must be inspected before anyone returns.

Takeaway: CO poisoning with syncope or a level above about 25% → consider hyperbaric oxygen.

whyNot.A: Her loss of consciousness and high level warrant consideration of hyperbaric therapy; home also must be made safe first.
whyNot.B: Exchange transfusion is not a treatment for CO poisoning.
whyNot.D: Cyanide antidote is for smoke inhalation with severe lactic acidosis or shock; this is a furnace exposure without those features.
whyNot.E: Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, not CO poisoning.

items.objective: Identify indications for hyperbaric oxygen in carbon monoxide poisoning.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has a transesophageal echocardiogram after topical benzocaine spray to the pharynx. Thirty minutes later he is dyspneic and cyanotic. Pulse oximetry reads 84% and does not improve with 6 L/min of oxygen. Arterial blood is dark brown; PaO2 is 190 mm Hg. Co-oximetry shows a methemoglobin level of 34%. He has no history of G6PD deficiency. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Increase oxygen to 15 L/min and observe

items.explanationHtml:
Topical benzocaine is a classic cause of methemoglobinemia: cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, oximetry near 85%, normal PaO2 and chocolate-brown blood. Symptomatic patients or those with high levels need intravenous methylene blue, which uses NADPH to reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+. Avoid it in G6PD deficiency and be cautious with serotonergic drugs (it inhibits MAO).

Takeaway: Symptomatic methemoglobinemia → IV methylene blue.

whyNot.A: Hyperbaric oxygen is a rescue option if methylene blue fails or is contraindicated.
whyNot.B: Oxygen cannot bind ferric heme; with a level of 34% and symptoms, an antidote is needed.
whyNot.C: Hydroxocobalamin is a cyanide antidote.
whyNot.E: N-acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen toxicity.

items.objective: Treat drug-induced methemoglobinemia with methylene blue.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman plans a trek in Nepal with a planned rapid ascent from 1,400 m to 3,800 m over 2 days. On a previous trip she had a severe headache, nausea and poor sleep on reaching 3,500 m. She has no history of sulfonamide allergy or kidney stones. Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis to recommend in addition to advice about gradual ascent?

options.label: A
options.html: Acetazolamide starting the day before ascent

options.label: B
options.html: Furosemide starting on the day of ascent

options.label: C
options.html: Nifedipine starting on the day of ascent

options.label: D
options.html: Propranolol starting on the day of ascent

options.label: E
options.html: Sildenafil starting on the day of ascent

items.explanationHtml:
Her history and a fast ascent put her at high risk of acute mountain sickness. Acetazolamide, started the day before ascent, speeds acclimatization by inducing a mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation. Dexamethasone is an alternative when acetazolamide is not tolerated. Gradual ascent remains the main preventive measure.

Takeaway: Prevent AMS with gradual ascent and acetazolamide for higher-risk travelers.

whyNot.B: Diuretics like furosemide do not prevent AMS and can cause dehydration.
whyNot.C: Nifedipine prevents HAPE in susceptible people but does not prevent acute mountain sickness.
whyNot.D: β-blockers have no role in altitude illness prophylaxis.
whyNot.E: PDE5 inhibitors are used to prevent HAPE, not AMS.

items.objective: Recommend prophylaxis for acute mountain sickness.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man on day 3 of a climb camps at 4,600 m. Over the last day he has developed dyspnea at rest, a cough productive of pink frothy sputum and marked fatigue. He is alert and has a normal neurologic examination. Pulse is 124/min, respirations are 30/min and SpO2 is 68% on room air. There are crackles in both lung fields. A helicopter evacuation and bottled oxygen are available. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: D
options.html: Oral acetazolamide and rest at the current altitude

options.label: E
options.html: Oral dexamethasone and rest at the current altitude

items.explanationHtml:
He has high-altitude pulmonary edema: a noncardiogenic edema from exaggerated, uneven hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Definitive treatment is descent and supplemental oxygen. Nifedipine is added when descent or oxygen is not possible; a portable hyperbaric bag can buy time.

Takeaway: HAPE → descend and give oxygen.

whyNot.A: The setting, rapid onset and altitude point to HAPE; antibiotics do not treat it.
whyNot.C: HAPE is not volume overload; diuretics can cause hypotension.
whyNot.D: Acetazolamide prevents and treats AMS; it is not adequate treatment for HAPE.
whyNot.E: Dexamethasone is the drug for high-altitude cerebral edema, which he does not have.

items.objective: Manage high-altitude pulmonary edema.

items.stemHtml:
A 52-year-old woman has progressive dyspnea, leg swelling and daytime sleepiness. She snores loudly. She does not smoke and takes no sedatives. BMI is 46 kg/m2. There is pitting edema to the knees. Spirometry shows a proportionate mild reduction in FEV1 and FVC with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.81. Chest x-ray shows clear lungs. Thyroid function is normal. Results on room air while awake are shown.

TestResult
pH7.37
PaCO254 mm Hg
PaO262 mm Hg
HCO3-31 mEq/L
Hematocrit53%

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Central sleep apnea from heart failure

items.explanationHtml:
Obesity (BMI ≥ 30), awake hypercapnia (PaCO2 ≥ 45 mm Hg) with a compensatory rise in bicarbonate, and no other cause of hypoventilation define obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Edema and polycythemia suggest pulmonary hypertension and chronic hypoxemia. Treatment is positive airway pressure during sleep (CPAP if severe OSA coexists, otherwise noninvasive ventilation) and substantial weight loss.

Takeaway: Obesity + awake hypercapnia + no other cause = obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

whyNot.A: Central apnea in heart failure is usually associated with low or normal PaCO2, not chronic hypercapnia.
whyNot.B: Her FEV1/FVC ratio is normal and she has no smoking history.
whyNot.C: There are no neuromuscular symptoms, and her obesity is the obvious cause.
whyNot.E: OSA alone does not cause awake hypercapnia.

items.objective: Diagnose obesity hypoventilation syndrome from an awake blood gas.

items.stemHtml:
A 74-year-old woman is on the surgical ward 12 hours after a hip replacement. She has a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump and also took her usual bedtime lorazepam. The nurse finds her difficult to rouse. Respirations are 7/min and shallow, and pupils are small. SpO2 is 93% on 4 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Results of arterial blood gas analysis are shown.

TestResult
pH7.23
PaCO266 mm Hg
PaO279 mm Hg
HCO3-27 mEq/L

After stopping the analgesia pump and supporting her airway, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Arterial blood gas repeated in 2 hours

options.label: B
options.html: Increase oxygen to 10 L/min by face mask

items.explanationHtml:
She has acute hypoventilation (acute respiratory acidosis with little bicarbonate rise) from opioid and benzodiazepine sedation. Supplemental oxygen has kept her SpO2 acceptable while PaCO2 rose, a common pitfall. Give naloxone in small titrated doses to restore adequate breathing, and support ventilation with a bag-valve mask if needed.

Takeaway: Normal SpO2 on oxygen does not exclude opioid hypoventilation; give naloxone.

whyNot.A: Delay risks respiratory arrest.
whyNot.B: More oxygen hides the problem and does nothing for ventilation.
whyNot.C: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in patients who take benzodiazepines chronically; the opioid is the main and reversible cause.
whyNot.E: Small pupils, slow breathing and a recent opioid infusion explain her state; reversal comes first.

items.objective: Recognize and reverse opioid-induced hypoventilation masked by supplemental oxygen.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 25% has fatigue and unrefreshing sleep. He takes furosemide and lisinopril only. Polysomnography shows an apnea–hypopnea index of 34 events per hour, mostly central apneas with a waxing–waning pattern of breathing between them. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
He has central sleep apnea with Cheyne–Stokes breathing due to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and he is on incomplete therapy. First optimize heart failure treatment (ARNI or ACE inhibitor, evidence-based β-blocker, mineralocorticoid antagonist, SGLT2 inhibitor), which often reduces the central events. CPAP or nocturnal oxygen may be added if symptoms persist. Adaptive servo-ventilation is contraindicated with an ejection fraction of 45% or less.

Takeaway: Central sleep apnea in HFrEF: treat the heart failure first; avoid adaptive servo-ventilation.

whyNot.A: Adaptive servo-ventilation increased cardiovascular mortality in patients with an ejection fraction of 45% or less and should not be used.
whyNot.B: Theophylline is arrhythmogenic and is not used in heart failure.
whyNot.D: Sedatives do not treat central apnea and are risky.
whyNot.E: Airway surgery does not treat central apnea.

items.objective: Manage central sleep apnea in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

items.stemHtml:
A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive at home at sea level. Respirations are 6/min and shallow, and his pupils are pinpoint. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows:

TestResult
pH7.19
PaCO270 mm Hg
PaO258 mm Hg
HCO3-26 mEq/L

Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his hypoxemia?
items.explanationHtml:
PAO2 = 150 − 70/0.8 = 150 − 87.5 ≈ 62.5 mm Hg. A–a gradient = 62.5 − 58 ≈ 4.5 mm Hg, which is normal. Hypoxemia with a high PaCO2 and a normal gradient is pure hypoventilation, here from opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, slow breathing). The acute respiratory acidosis has barely raised bicarbonate.

Takeaway: High PaCO2 + normal A–a gradient = hypoventilation.

whyNot.A: Diffusion limitation widens the A–a gradient and does not raise PaCO2.
whyNot.C: Inspired oxygen is normal at sea level indoors, and this alone would not raise PaCO2.
whyNot.D: A shunt would widen the A–a gradient; the gradient here is only about 5 mm Hg.
whyNot.E: V/Q mismatch would widen the A–a gradient, which here is normal.

items.objective: Calculate the A–a gradient to identify hypoventilation as the cause of hypoxemia.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman becomes hypoxemic on the second day after abdominal surgery. Chest x-ray shows complete opacification of the left lower lobe with volume loss and the mediastinum shifted toward the left. While she breathes 100% oxygen through a tight-fitting mask, her PaO2 is 74 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains the failure of 100% oxygen to correct her hypoxemia?
items.explanationHtml:
The collapsed lobe from a mucus plug (atelectasis) is perfused but not ventilated (V/Q = 0). Blood through it never meets alveolar gas, so it remains at mixed venous PO2 regardless of FiO2. Blood from ventilated units is already nearly saturated and cannot make up the deficit. Failure of 100% oxygen to correct hypoxemia is the hallmark of shunt. Treatment targets the shunt: airway clearance, incentive spirometry and bronchoscopy if needed.

Takeaway: Hypoxemia that 100% oxygen cannot fix means shunt.

whyNot.A: Diffusion limitation corrects with a higher alveolar PO2.
whyNot.B: Hypoventilation corrects readily with supplemental oxygen.
whyNot.C: She is breathing 100% oxygen, so inspired PO2 is high.
whyNot.E: Low V/Q units eventually reach a high PO2 on 100% oxygen; poor correction suggests units with no ventilation at all.

items.objective: Distinguish shunt from V/Q mismatch by the response to supplemental oxygen.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man is found confused in his garage, where a gasoline-powered generator had been running. Pulse oximetry shows 99%, and arterial PaO2 is 98 mm Hg. Which of the following changes best describes his arterial oxygen content and his oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve?

options.label: A
options.html: Oxygen content decreased; curve shifted to the left

options.label: B
options.html: Oxygen content decreased; curve shifted to the right

options.label: D
options.html: Oxygen content normal; curve shifted to the left

options.label: E
options.html: Oxygen content normal; curve shifted to the right

items.explanationHtml:
Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with far greater affinity than oxygen, so it occupies sites and lowers oxygen content. It also increases the affinity of the remaining hemes for oxygen, shifting the curve to the left and impairing tissue unloading. PaO2 measures dissolved oxygen and stays normal, and standard pulse oximetry misreads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin.

Takeaway: CO: low oxygen content, left shift, normal PaO2 and a falsely normal oximeter.

whyNot.B: CO shifts the curve to the left, impairing release of oxygen to tissues.
whyNot.C: Oxygen content cannot rise when binding sites are lost.
whyNot.D: CO occupies heme sites, so oxygen content falls even though PaO2 is normal.
whyNot.E: Neither change is correct; this pattern resembles acidosis or fever.

items.objective: Describe the effects of carbon monoxide on oxygen content and the dissociation curve.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman develops cyanosis and headache an hour after a dental procedure using a benzocaine spray. Pulse oximetry reads 85% and does not change with oxygen; arterial PaO2 is 210 mm Hg on supplemental oxygen. Her blood is dark brown. She is treated with intravenous methylene blue, which works as an electron carrier for a red-cell reductase. The cofactor this reductase requires is generated mainly by which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Methylene blue is reduced to leucomethylene blue by NADPH–methemoglobin reductase; leucomethylene blue then reduces ferric (Fe3+) methemoglobin back to ferrous hemoglobin. In red cells, NADPH comes from the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD). This is why methylene blue may fail, and can trigger hemolysis, in G6PD deficiency.

Takeaway: Methylene blue needs NADPH from G6PD to reduce methemoglobin.

whyNot.A: This enzyme consumes reduced glutathione to detoxify peroxides; it does not generate the cofactor.
whyNot.B: This step makes NADH, which cytochrome b5 reductase uses for the physiologic pathway, not the methylene blue pathway.
whyNot.D: This side branch of glycolysis makes 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, not a reducing cofactor.
whyNot.E: Mature red cells have no mitochondria.

items.objective: Link methylene blue's action to NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 30-year-old woman flies to a city at 3,600 m (about 11,800 ft). Within hours of arrival her minute ventilation has increased. Which of the following receptors mainly initiates this response?

options.label: A
options.html: Aortic arch baroreceptors responding to low blood pressure

options.label: B
options.html: Carotid body chemoreceptors responding to low arterial PO2

options.label: C
options.html: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors responding to interstitial fluid

options.label: D
options.html: Medullary central chemoreceptors responding to low arterial PO2

options.label: E
options.html: Pulmonary stretch receptors responding to lung inflation

items.explanationHtml:
At altitude, inspired and arterial PO2 fall. The carotid bodies are the main sensors of arterial hypoxemia and signal through the glossopharyngeal nerve to raise ventilation. The resulting respiratory alkalosis at first restrains the central drive; over several days, renal bicarbonate excretion corrects pH and ventilation rises further.

Takeaway: Hypoxemia is sensed by the carotid bodies; PaCO2 by the central chemoreceptors.

whyNot.A: Baroreceptors regulate blood pressure, not ventilation at altitude.
whyNot.C: J receptors respond to pulmonary congestion or edema, not to altitude itself.
whyNot.D: Central chemoreceptors respond to CSF pH (driven by PaCO2), not to hypoxemia.
whyNot.E: Stretch receptors terminate inspiration (Hering–Breuer); they do not sense hypoxemia.

items.objective: Identify the peripheral chemoreceptors as the sensors of hypoxemia at altitude.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man planning to trek to 4,500 m had headache, nausea and insomnia on a previous trip at a similar altitude. He is given a drug to start the day before ascent. The drug speeds acclimatization mainly by which of the following effects?

options.label: A
options.html: Blocking L-type calcium channels in pulmonary arteriolar smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibiting phosphodiesterase-5 in the pulmonary vasculature

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibiting renal carbonic anhydrase to cause a metabolic acidosis

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulating renal erythropoietin release and red-cell production

items.explanationHtml:
Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, causing bicarbonate diuresis and a mild metabolic acidosis. The acidosis counteracts the respiratory alkalosis that limits ventilation at altitude, so ventilation and oxygenation improve faster. Adverse effects: paresthesias, polyuria, altered taste of carbonated drinks and, with chronic use, calcium phosphate stones.

Takeaway: Acetazolamide prevents mountain sickness by producing a metabolic acidosis that drives ventilation.

whyNot.A: Nifedipine prevents high-altitude pulmonary edema in susceptible people but does not speed acclimatization or prevent AMS.
whyNot.B: 2,3-BPG rises naturally at altitude; no drug used for AMS works this way.
whyNot.C: PDE5 inhibitors can prevent HAPE but do not prevent acute mountain sickness.
whyNot.E: Erythropoiesis takes weeks and is not the mechanism of prophylaxis.

items.objective: Explain how acetazolamide prevents acute mountain sickness.

items.stemHtml: In a healthy person standing upright, which of the following best describes the alveoli at the lung apex compared with those at the base?

options.label: A
options.html: Greater blood flow per alveolus and higher alveolar PO2

options.label: B
options.html: Greater ventilation per alveolus and lower alveolar PO2

options.label: C
options.html: Higher ventilation–perfusion ratio and higher alveolar PO2

options.label: D
options.html: Higher ventilation–perfusion ratio and lower alveolar PO2

options.label: E
options.html: Lower ventilation–perfusion ratio and higher alveolar PCO2

items.explanationHtml:
Gravity increases both ventilation and blood flow toward the base, but blood flow rises more steeply. The apex therefore has the highest V/Q (about 3), the highest PAO2 and the lowest PACO2. The oxygen-rich apex favors Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an obligate aerobe, in reactivation disease.

Takeaway: Upright lung: apex has the highest V/Q and PAO2; base has the most ventilation and perfusion.

whyNot.A: Blood flow is lowest at the apex because of gravity.
whyNot.B: Ventilation per alveolus is lower at the apex, and PAO2 is higher there.
whyNot.D: A higher V/Q gives a higher, not lower, alveolar PO2.
whyNot.E: This describes the base.

items.objective: Describe regional V/Q differences in the upright lung.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has an SpO2 of 94% at rest. During a 6-minute walk it falls to 82%. His cardiac output rises normally with exercise. Which of the following best explains the exercise-induced desaturation?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased dead space from obliteration of pulmonary capillaries

options.label: C
options.html: Left shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced capillary transit time across a thickened alveolar membrane

options.label: E
options.html: Right-to-left intracardiac shunting through a patent foramen ovale

items.explanationHtml:
Normally, capillary blood reaches alveolar PO2 within the first third of its transit. Interstitial fibrosis thickens the membrane and reduces surface area, so equilibration takes longer. With exercise, higher cardiac output shortens transit time, and blood leaves the capillary before equilibrating: diffusion limitation, which shows up first on exertion. The DLCO is low.

Takeaway: Fibrosis + exercise = diffusion-limited oxygen transfer and desaturation.

whyNot.A: Patients with fibrosis hyperventilate during exercise; PaCO2 is usually low.
whyNot.B: Dead space raises PaCO2 and wasted ventilation but is not the main reason for desaturation on exertion here.
whyNot.C: Exercise shifts the curve to the right, aiding unloading.
whyNot.E: A shunt is possible but would not be the expected mechanism in fibrosis.

items.objective: Explain exercise desaturation in interstitial lung disease by diffusion limitation.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD and chronic hypercapnia arrives by ambulance after receiving oxygen at 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask for 40 minutes. His PaCO2 has risen from a baseline of 52 mm Hg to 74 mm Hg, although his respiratory rate and tidal volume are unchanged. Which of the following best explains most of the rise in PaCO2?

options.label: A
options.html: A left shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve

options.label: B
options.html: Absorption atelectasis creating a large right-to-left shunt

options.label: C
options.html: Increased CO2 production from the work of breathing

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of the hypoxic drive to breathe, causing a fall in minute ventilation

options.label: E
options.html: Release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and the Haldane effect

items.explanationHtml:
High-concentration oxygen relieves hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated units, sending more blood to areas that cannot clear CO2 and increasing dead-space-like inefficiency (worse V/Q matching). Oxygen also displaces CO2 from hemoglobin (Haldane effect), raising dissolved CO2. With fixed ventilation, PaCO2 rises. Hence controlled oxygen with a target SpO2 of 88–92%.

Takeaway: Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD is mainly V/Q worsening plus the Haldane effect, not loss of drive.

whyNot.A: The dissociation curve concerns oxygen binding; it does not cause CO2 retention.
whyNot.B: Shunt mainly impairs oxygenation; it changes PaCO2 little.
whyNot.C: CO2 production does not change enough to raise PaCO2 by over 20 mm Hg.
whyNot.D: His minute ventilation is unchanged, so a fall in drive does not explain the rise; this is a common misconception.

items.objective: Explain the mechanisms of oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD.

items.stemHtml:
A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted with left lower lobe pneumonia and started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin. After 72 hours he still has fevers to 38.9°C (102°F) and left pleuritic pain. Chest x-ray shows a moderate left pleural effusion that layers freely on decubitus views. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis results:

Pleural fluidResult
AppearanceTurbid, not purulent
pH7.08
Glucose34 mg/dL
LDH1,450 U/L
Leukocytes28,000/mm3, 90% neutrophils
Gram stainNo organisms seen

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add vancomycin and repeat the chest x-ray in 48 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Place a chest tube for drainage

items.explanationHtml:
The effusion is a complicated parapneumonic effusion: pH < 7.2 and glucose < 60 mg/dL, even though the Gram stain is negative. It needs chest tube drainage in addition to antibiotics. If drainage is incomplete because of loculations, give intrapleural tPA with DNase; failure leads to VATS debridement or decortication. Anaerobic coverage should be ensured.

Takeaway: parapneumonic effusion with pH < 7.2, glucose < 60 mg/dL, loculation, pus or positive Gram stain → chest tube + antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Broadening antibiotics alone does not clear an infected pleural collection; the fluid chemistry shows it needs drainage.
whyNot.B: This is an exudate from infection, not a transudate from volume overload.
whyNot.C: Pleurodesis fuses the pleura to prevent recurrent malignant effusions; it is contraindicated in active infection.
whyNot.E: Waiting allows loculation and an organized fibrous peel to form.

items.objective: Choose chest tube drainage for a complicated parapneumonic effusion on the basis of pleural fluid pH and glucose.

items.stemHtml:
A 79-year-old woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction was admitted 5 days ago with volume overload and has received intravenous furosemide, losing 6 kg. Her dyspnea has improved, but a moderate right pleural effusion persists, and a diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. She has no fever or weight loss.

TestSerumPleural fluid
Total protein6.8 g/dL3.7 g/dL
Albumin3.6 g/dL1.9 g/dL
LDH210 U/L (upper limit of normal 220)118 U/L

Pleural fluid cell count shows 900 cells/mm3, mostly lymphocytes and mesothelial cells. Cytology is pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
The protein ratio (3.7/6.8 ≈ 0.54) just meets Light's criteria for an exudate, but the LDH values do not. Diuresis concentrates pleural protein, so Light's criteria misclassify many heart-failure transudates as exudates after diuretic therapy. A serum-minus-pleural albumin gradient > 1.2 g/dL (here 3.6 − 1.9 = 1.7 g/dL) indicates a transudate. In this setting, continue treating the heart failure; investigate further only if the effusion does not resolve or cytology is abnormal.

Takeaway: diuresed heart-failure effusion that barely meets Light's criteria: albumin gradient > 1.2 g/dL → still a transudate.

whyNot.A: A chest tube is used for infected, bloody or rapidly recurring effusions; none is present.
whyNot.B: Biopsy is for undiagnosed exudates; this fluid is best explained by heart failure.
whyNot.C: Tuberculous effusions are lymphocytic exudates with high adenosine deaminase in an appropriate setting; nothing here suggests tuberculosis.
whyNot.E: Pleurodesis is palliation for recurrent malignant effusions, not for a heart-failure transudate.

items.objective: Use the serum-pleural albumin gradient to recognize a pseudoexudate after diuresis.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after a stab wound to the right chest. He is anxious and gasping. Pulse is 136/min, blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 82% on a nonrebreather mask. Breath sounds are absent on the right, the right chest is hyperresonant, the trachea is shifted to the left, and the neck veins are distended. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma

items.explanationHtml:
Hypotension, distended neck veins, an absent, hyperresonant hemithorax and tracheal deviation away from the injury define tension pneumothorax. Treat at once with needle decompression (4th–5th intercostal space, midaxillary line, or 2nd space, midclavicular line) or finger thoracostomy, followed by a chest tube. Imaging comes after decompression.

Takeaway: tension pneumothorax: decompress first, chest tube second, x-ray last.

whyNot.A: Resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating trauma with arrest or near-arrest that does not respond to simpler measures.
whyNot.B: FAST can help but delays decompression when the clinical picture is already diagnostic.
whyNot.D: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; waiting for an x-ray in a hypotensive patient risks cardiac arrest.
whyNot.E: Tamponade also causes hypotension and distended neck veins, but not absent breath sounds, hyperresonance or tracheal shift.

items.objective: Treat tension pneumothorax with immediate decompression before imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has had mild right-sided chest pain for 5 hours since it started while he was sitting at his desk. He has no medical history and smokes. Pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. He speaks in full sentences. Chest x-ray shows a small right apical pneumothorax with a 1.5-cm rim between the lung and the chest wall at the apex. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space

options.label: D
options.html: Observation with supplemental O<sub>2</sub> and a follow-up radiograph

items.explanationHtml:
A small, minimally symptomatic first primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a stable patient is managed conservatively: observation with supplemental oxygen (which speeds reabsorption of pleural air by raising the nitrogen gradient) and a repeat radiograph to confirm it is not enlarging. Advise smoking cessation, give return precautions and advise against flying until resolution. Larger or symptomatic collections are treated with needle aspiration or a small-bore drain.

Takeaway: small, stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax → observe with oxygen and repeat x-ray; drain if large, symptomatic or secondary.

whyNot.A: He is breathing comfortably with normal oxygenation; positive pressure could enlarge the pneumothorax.
whyNot.B: A chest drain is for large or symptomatic collections, failed aspiration or secondary pneumothorax; a large-bore tube is rarely needed for spontaneous pneumothorax.
whyNot.C: Needle decompression is for tension physiology, which he does not have.
whyNot.E: Surgery is for recurrence or persistent air leak, not a first small episode.

items.objective: Manage a small, stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax with observation.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman who works as a commercial airline pilot has a second right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax 8 months after the first, which was treated with needle aspiration. This episode required a small-bore chest drain, and the lung has now fully re-expanded with no air leak. She does not smoke. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to prevent recurrence?

options.label: C
options.html: No intervention because recurrences are self-limited

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat needle aspiration if symptoms recur

items.explanationHtml:
Indications for definitive prevention include a second ipsilateral pneumothorax, a first contralateral episode, bilateral pneumothoraces, a persistent air leak, and high-risk occupations such as pilots and divers. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection of apical blebs and pleurodesis (mechanical abrasion or partial pleurectomy) cuts the recurrence rate to a few percent.

Takeaway: recurrent (second ipsilateral) or occupational-risk pneumothorax → VATS bleb resection + pleurodesis.

whyNot.A: Bronchodilators do not prevent bleb rupture; she has no airway disease.
whyNot.B: Supplemental oxygen does not prevent recurrence; pressure changes in flight are the hazard.
whyNot.C: After a second episode the recurrence risk is high, and recurrence in flight could be dangerous.
whyNot.D: Aspiration treats an episode but does nothing to prevent the next one.

items.objective: Recommend VATS with pleurodesis to prevent recurrent primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man with alcohol use disorder comes to the emergency department 6 hours after an episode of forceful vomiting followed by severe retrosternal and upper abdominal pain. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Crepitus is palpable at the base of the neck. Chest x-ray shows pneumomediastinum and a small left pleural effusion. ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Forceful vomiting followed by severe chest pain, fever, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum and a left effusion indicates a transmural esophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome), usually of the left posterolateral distal esophagus. Confirm with water-soluble contrast esophagography (or CT with oral contrast). Management: nothing by mouth, broad-spectrum antibiotics with antifungal coverage, and urgent surgical consultation for repair and drainage.

Takeaway: vomiting → chest pain + pneumomediastinum (+ left effusion) = Boerhaave; confirm with water-soluble contrast study, not barium or endoscopy first.

whyNot.A: Barium that leaks into the mediastinum causes severe inflammation; it is used only if the water-soluble study is negative and suspicion remains.
whyNot.C: Bronchoscopy evaluates airway injury, which is not suggested by vomiting followed by mediastinal air and a left effusion.
whyNot.D: Endoscopy insufflates air and can extend a perforation; it is not the first diagnostic test.
whyNot.E: Myocardial infarction does not cause pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema.

items.objective: Choose water-soluble contrast esophagography to diagnose spontaneous esophageal rupture.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with obesity and diabetes had coronary artery bypass grafting through a median sternotomy 11 days ago. He now has fever to 38.9°C (102°F), pain around the incision and purulent drainage from its lower third. The sternum moves and clicks when he coughs. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm3. CT shows a retrosternal fluid collection with gas. Blood cultures are drawn. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat CT in 1 week to assess progression

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, purulent wound drainage, an unstable sternum and a retrosternal gas-containing collection after sternotomy indicate deep sternal wound infection with mediastinitis. Diabetes and obesity are major risk factors; staphylococci (S aureus and coagulase-negative species) predominate. Treatment is surgical debridement (often with negative-pressure wound therapy and later reconstruction) plus IV antibiotics covering MRSA until cultures return.

Takeaway: post-sternotomy fever + drainage + sternal click = mediastinitis → debridement + IV antibiotics.

whyNot.A: NSAIDs and colchicine treat post-pericardiotomy syndrome, which causes pleuritic pain and fever without purulent drainage or sternal instability.
whyNot.B: Oral therapy alone is inadequate for a deep sternal infection with a collection.
whyNot.C: Delay risks sepsis, osteomyelitis and graft infection.
whyNot.E: Echocardiography may be needed to look for endocarditis if blood cultures are positive, but it does not treat a mediastinal abscess.

items.objective: Manage post-sternotomy mediastinitis with surgical debridement and intravenous antibiotics.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man is brought in after a fall from a ladder onto his left side. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg after 1 L of crystalloid and 2 units of blood. Breath sounds are decreased on the left, and the left chest is dull to percussion. Chest x-ray shows opacification of the lower half of the left hemithorax. A 28-French chest tube is placed and immediately drains 1,650 mL of blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Monitor chest tube output hourly for 4 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Perform video-assisted thoracoscopic evacuation in 3 days

items.explanationHtml:
A massive hemothorax, with immediate chest tube output of about 1,500 mL or more (or continuing output of about 200 mL per hour for 2–4 hours) or persistent instability despite transfusion, is an indication for urgent thoracotomy to find and control the bleeding source (intercostal or internal thoracic arteries, lung parenchyma, great vessels). Continue balanced blood product resuscitation.

Takeaway: hemothorax: chest tube first; thoracotomy if ≥ 1,500 mL immediately, ~200 mL/h for 2–4 h, or ongoing instability.

whyNot.A: A second tube does not stop bleeding; the problem is ongoing hemorrhage, not inadequate drainage.
whyNot.B: Fibrinolytics are for loculated infected effusions or retained clot, and would worsen bleeding.
whyNot.C: Hourly monitoring guides the decision when initial output is below threshold; his initial drainage already exceeds it and he is unstable.
whyNot.D: Delayed VATS evacuates a retained hemothorax in a stable patient; it does not control active hemorrhage.

items.objective: Recognize the chest-tube output thresholds for thoracotomy in traumatic hemothorax.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has 2 weeks of worsening dyspnea, orthopnea and leg swelling. Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and bilateral pleural effusions, larger on the right. Thoracentesis shows clear, straw-colored fluid. Pleural/serum protein ratio is 0.3 and pleural/serum LDH ratio is 0.4. Serum albumin is 4.0 g/dL. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of fluid accumulation?

options.label: D
options.html: Obstruction of parietal pleural lymphatics by tumor

items.explanationHtml:
The fluid is a transudate (protein ratio ≤ 0.5, LDH ratio ≤ 0.6). In heart failure, raised venous and capillary hydrostatic pressures (pulmonary venous pressure drains much of the visceral pleura, systemic venous pressure the parietal pleura) push fluid across intact membranes faster than pleural lymphatics can remove it. Heart failure is the single commonest cause of pleural effusion; effusions are usually bilateral and often larger on the right.

Takeaway: transudate = pressure problem (heart failure, low albumin); exudate = leaky or blocked pleura (infection, cancer, inflammation).

whyNot.A: Low oncotic pressure causes transudates in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis, but his albumin is normal.
whyNot.B: Thoracic duct disruption produces a milky chylothorax rich in triglycerides, not a clear transudate.
whyNot.D: Lymphatic obstruction by tumor produces an exudate, usually with malignant cells.
whyNot.E: Inflammation increases permeability and produces an exudate; his ratios meet none of Light's criteria.

items.objective: Relate a transudative pleural effusion in heart failure to raised capillary hydrostatic pressure.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man undergoes transthoracic esophagectomy for adenocarcinoma. When oral feeding with a standard diet resumes on postoperative day 5, the output of his right chest drain rises to 1,200 mL/day and the fluid turns milky white. Pleural fluid triglyceride concentration is 420 mg/dL. Injury to which of the following structures is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Milky fluid with triglycerides > 110 mg/dL that rises when dietary fat is resumed is a chylothorax. Chylomicrons from the intestine reach the blood through the thoracic duct, which ascends in the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and the azygos vein, right next to the esophagus, and crosses to the left at about T4–T5. Esophagectomy is a classic cause of injury; a tear below the crossing produces a right-sided chylothorax.

Takeaway: chylothorax (TG > 110 mg/dL) = thoracic duct injury (surgery, trauma) or obstruction (lymphoma).

whyNot.A: Azygos injury would cause bleeding (hemothorax), not a triglyceride-rich effusion.
whyNot.B: Phrenic nerve injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis, not a pleural fluid leak.
whyNot.C: The right lymphatic duct drains only the right upper body and is not the main conduit for intestinal chylomicrons.
whyNot.D: A bronchial injury would cause an air leak and pneumothorax, not chylous fluid.

items.objective: Identify the thoracic duct as the source of a postoperative chylothorax.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old man has sudden, sharp right-sided chest pain and mild shortness of breath that began while he was watching television. He is 191 cm (6 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (146 lb), and smokes cigarettes. Over the right upper chest there are decreased breath sounds, decreased tactile fremitus and hyperresonance to percussion. The trachea is midline. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Destruction of alveolar walls from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

options.label: C
options.html: Obstruction of a bronchus by a carcinoid tumor

options.label: D
options.html: Rupture of an apical subpleural bleb

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnea at rest with a hyperresonant, quiet hemithorax in a tall, thin young male smoker is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. It results from rupture of small air-filled apical subpleural blebs; the apex is where pleural pressure is most negative and alveolar distending forces are greatest. Smoking increases the risk many-fold. A midline trachea and normal vital signs argue against tension.

Takeaway: tall, thin young smoker + sudden pleuritic pain + hyperresonance = primary spontaneous pneumothorax from apical blebs.

whyNot.A: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes basal panacinar emphysema in older adults and would make this a secondary pneumothorax.
whyNot.B: Pneumocystis can cause pneumothorax in people with advanced HIV infection, but he has no immunosuppression or preceding illness.
whyNot.C: Bronchial obstruction causes atelectasis with dullness and tracheal shift toward the lesion, not hyperresonance.
whyNot.E: He has no trauma; the pain began at rest.

items.objective: Recognize primary spontaneous pneumothorax and its cause in a tall, thin young smoker.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is intubated after a motor vehicle collision with multiple left rib fractures. Ten minutes after positive pressure ventilation starts, peak airway pressures rise sharply, oxygen saturation falls to 78%, and blood pressure drops to 70/40 mm Hg. Breath sounds are absent on the left, the trachea is deviated to the right, and the neck veins are distended. Which of the following best explains his hypotension?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased venous return to the right heart

options.label: B
options.html: Hemorrhage into the left pleural space

options.label: C
options.html: Hypoxemic depression of left ventricular contractility

options.label: E
options.html: Systemic vasodilation from a cytokine response

items.explanationHtml:
Rib fractures plus positive pressure ventilation have created a tension pneumothorax. Air enters the pleural space with each breath but cannot leave, so intrapleural pressure becomes strongly positive. The mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, the vena cavae are compressed and kinked, and high intrathoracic pressure opposes venous inflow: venous return and preload fall, causing obstructive shock with distended neck veins. Immediate decompression restores venous return.

Takeaway: tension pneumothorax = obstructive shock from reduced venous return; decompress before imaging.

whyNot.B: Hemorrhage would cause hypovolemia with flat neck veins; his veins are distended and the hemithorax is not described as dull.
whyNot.C: Hypoxemia contributes to deterioration but does not explain distended neck veins and mediastinal shift.
whyNot.D: Nothing suggests bradycardia; tension physiology usually causes tachycardia.
whyNot.E: Vasodilatory (distributive) shock does not produce tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds or raised venous pressure.

items.objective: Explain the hemodynamic mechanism of shock in tension pneumothorax.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has 3 weeks of progressive dyspnea. Examination of the left posterior chest from the scapular tip downward shows dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus and absent breath sounds. The trachea is displaced to the right. Which of the following is the most likely finding on imaging?

options.label: A
options.html: Hyperlucent left hemithorax with a visible visceral pleural line

options.label: C
options.html: Left lower lobe collapse from an endobronchial mass

options.label: D
options.html: Left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms

options.label: E
options.html: Overinflated left lung with flattened diaphragm

items.explanationHtml:
Dullness, decreased fremitus, absent breath sounds and the trachea pushed away together indicate a large pleural effusion, here most likely malignant. Fluid separates the lung from the chest wall, damping transmitted vibration and sound; a large volume displaces the mediastinum to the opposite side.

Takeaway: dull + decreased fremitus + trachea away = large effusion; dull + decreased fremitus + trachea toward = collapse.

whyNot.A: Pneumothorax would be hyperresonant, not dull.
whyNot.C: Lobar collapse is dull with reduced fremitus but pulls the trachea toward the affected side.
whyNot.D: Consolidation is dull but increases tactile fremitus and gives bronchial breath sounds.
whyNot.E: Hyperinflation is hyperresonant and does not deviate the trachea.

items.objective: Distinguish a large pleural effusion from consolidation, collapse and pneumothorax by examination.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has 4 months of drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen toward evening, and difficulty chewing at the end of meals. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive. Chest CT shows a 5-cm well-circumscribed mass in the anterior mediastinum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of the mass?
items.explanationHtml:
Fatigable ptosis, diplopia and bulbar weakness with acetylcholine receptor antibodies is myasthenia gravis. An anterior mediastinal mass in this setting is a thymoma; about 10–15% of patients with myasthenia have one, and many patients with thymoma develop myasthenia. Other paraneoplastic associations include pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia. Thymectomy is indicated for thymoma.

Takeaway: anterior mediastinal mass + myasthenia gravis = thymoma (others in the anterior compartment: teratoma/germ cell, lymphoma, thyroid).

whyNot.A: Bronchogenic cysts usually lie in the middle mediastinum near the carina and are not linked to myasthenia.
whyNot.B: Esophageal tumors are in the middle (visceral) compartment and cause dysphagia, not neuromuscular junction disease.
whyNot.C: Schwannomas arise from nerve sheaths in the posterior (paravertebral) mediastinum.
whyNot.D: Small cell carcinoma is associated with Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels), which improves with repeated effort; it usually arises centrally from the bronchi.

items.objective: Associate an anterior mediastinal mass in myasthenia gravis with thymoma.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy has 3 weeks of irritability and rapid, chaotic eye movements with jerking of the limbs. Chest x-ray shows a paraspinal mass in the right posterior mediastinum. Urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid levels are elevated. The tumor cells are most likely derived from which of the following embryonic tissues?

options.label: A
options.html: Endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch

items.explanationHtml:
A posterior mediastinal mass in a toddler with opsoclonus-myoclonus and raised urinary catecholamine metabolites is a neuroblastoma, a tumor of sympathetic neuroblasts. These derive from the neural crest, which also forms the adrenal medulla, dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, and melanocytes. The posterior mediastinum holds the sympathetic chain, which is why neurogenic tumors dominate there.

Takeaway: posterior mediastinum = neurogenic tumors; in children, neuroblastoma (neural crest).

whyNot.A: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus (anterior mediastinum) and inferior parathyroids.
whyNot.B: Foregut endoderm gives rise to bronchogenic and esophageal duplication cysts, not catecholamine-secreting tumors.
whyNot.C: Lateral plate mesoderm forms connective tissue, muscle and the serous membranes, not sympathetic neurons.
whyNot.E: Surface ectoderm forms epidermis, lens and the anterior pituitary.

items.objective: Relate posterior mediastinal neuroblastoma to its neural crest origin.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is admitted with right lower lobe pneumonia. After 3 days of antibiotics he remains febrile, and a right pleural effusion has enlarged. Thoracentesis yields turbid fluid with pH 7.05, glucose 28 mg/dL (serum glucose 132 mg/dL) and LDH 1,900 U/L. Which of the following best explains the low pleural glucose concentration?

options.label: A
options.html: Consumption of glucose by neutrophils and bacteria in the pleural space

options.label: B
options.html: Dilution of pleural fluid by a transudate from heart failure

options.label: D
options.html: Impaired glucose transport across a pleura thickened by rheumatoid nodules

options.label: E
options.html: Insulin-like peptide secreted by a pleural tumor

items.explanationHtml:
In a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, the pleural space fills with metabolically active neutrophils and bacteria. They consume glucose by anaerobic glycolysis and produce lactic acid and CO2, so pleural glucose and pH fall (glucose < 60 mg/dL, pH < 7.2), and cell lysis raises LDH. These values identify an infected effusion that needs drainage, not antibiotics alone.

Takeaway: low pleural pH and glucose in pneumonia = infected (complicated) effusion → drain it.

whyNot.B: Transudates have glucose similar to serum; dilution cannot drop glucose to 28 mg/dL while serum is 132 mg/dL.
whyNot.C: His serum glucose is normal, so systemic hypoglycemia is not the cause.
whyNot.D: Rheumatoid effusions can have very low glucose, but he has no arthritis and the setting is a pneumonia that is not responding.
whyNot.E: Paraneoplastic hypoglycemia lowers serum glucose too; there is no evidence of a tumor.

items.objective: Explain the low pH and glucose of a complicated parapneumonic effusion.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has 1 week of sharp left anterior chest pain that worsens with deep breathing, twisting and lifting her toddler. She has no fever, cough or dyspnea. Vital signs are normal. Pressing on the left third and fourth costosternal junctions reproduces the pain exactly; there is no swelling, redness or rash. Lung and heart examination and an ECG are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Pain reproduced exactly by palpation of several costosternal junctions, with no swelling and a normal examination and ECG, is costochondritis, a common benign cause of chest pain in young adults. It is a diagnosis of exclusion; reproducible tenderness alone does not exclude cardiac disease in older patients with risk factors. Treatment is reassurance, NSAIDs or acetaminophen, and activity modification.

Takeaway: costochondritis: reproducible tenderness of several costosternal joints without swelling; Tietze adds swelling.

whyNot.A: Pericarditis typically improves leaning forward and shows diffuse ST elevation or a friction rub; her ECG is normal.
whyNot.C: Zoster pain precedes a dermatomal rash and is burning or tingling; it is not reproduced by pressure on the joints.
whyNot.D: Lupus pleuritis comes with other systemic features and often a friction rub or effusion; she is otherwise well.
whyNot.E: Tietze syndrome involves visible, tender swelling of the cartilage, usually a single upper joint.

items.objective: Differentiate costochondritis from Tietze syndrome and other causes of pleuritic chest pain.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of cough that began suddenly while she was playing with her older brother's building toys 6 hours ago. She is alert and in no distress. Respirations are 30/min and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. There is a wheeze over the left chest with reduced air entry on the left. Chest x-rays taken during inspiration and expiration show that the left lung stays inflated on expiration and the mediastinum shifts to the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Nebulized albuterol and discharge with follow-up

items.explanationHtml:
A sudden choking or coughing episode, unilateral wheeze, and air trapping on the affected side (the lung does not deflate on expiration) indicate an aspirated foreign body acting as a one-way valve.

Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic. A normal chest x-ray does not exclude a foreign body, because most objects are not radiopaque.

Takeaway: suspected airway foreign body in a child is removed by rigid bronchoscopy.

whyNot.A: She is not completely obstructed; thrusts are for a conscious child who cannot speak or cough, and could move the object.
whyNot.B: CT adds delay and radiation; with a typical history and air trapping, bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.
whyNot.C: Bronchodilators do not treat a mechanical obstruction, and discharging a child with a likely retained foreign body is unsafe.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids do not remove the object; delay raises the risk of pneumonia and bronchiectasis.

items.objective: Manage suspected foreign body aspiration in a toddler with rigid bronchoscopy.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man suddenly stands up from a restaurant table clutching his throat. He cannot speak or cough, and his face is becoming dusky. A bystander confirms he was eating steak. He is conscious. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Blind finger sweep of the mouth

options.label: C
options.html: Five back blows followed by five chest thrusts

items.explanationHtml:
Inability to speak or cough with a dusky face means severe foreign-body airway obstruction. In a conscious adult or a child older than 1 year, give repeated abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unresponsive, then start CPR (check the mouth before breaths).

Chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts in late pregnancy and marked obesity.

Takeaway: severe choking in a conscious adult: abdominal thrusts; if unresponsive: CPR.

whyNot.A: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper; only remove an object you can see.
whyNot.B: He has a severe obstruction with no effective cough or voice, so encouragement alone is not enough.
whyNot.C: Back blows and chest thrusts in cycles are the technique for infants younger than 1 year.
whyNot.E: Chest compressions start when the person becomes unresponsive; he is still conscious.

items.objective: Choose abdominal thrusts for severe foreign-body airway obstruction in a conscious adult.

items.stemHtml: A 7-month-old boy suddenly stops making noise while eating small pieces of grape, starts to turn blue and is unable to cry. He is awake and moving his arms. His mother calls for help. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.label: B
options.html: Back blows alternating with chest thrusts

options.label: C
options.html: Blind finger sweep of the pharynx

options.label: D
options.html: Placing him upright on his mother's lap

items.explanationHtml:
A conscious infant younger than 1 year with severe obstruction (cannot cry or cough, cyanosis) gets cycles of 5 back blows (head lower than the chest, supported on the forearm) and then 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive. If he becomes unresponsive, start CPR.

Takeaway: for a choking infant, use back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts.

whyNot.A: Abdominal thrusts are avoided in infants because they can injure the liver.
whyNot.C: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only an object you can see.
whyNot.D: Positioning alone does not relieve a complete obstruction.
whyNot.E: Breaths will not move air past a complete obstruction in a conscious infant.

items.objective: Choose the correct choking maneuver for an infant younger than 1 year.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a house fire in which he was trapped in a closed room for about 15 minutes. He has partial-thickness burns of the face. His nasal hairs are singed, there is soot in his mouth and he coughs up black sputum. His voice has become progressively hoarse over the last 30 minutes. Pulse is 112/min, respirations are 24/min and oxygen saturation is 99% on a non-rebreather mask. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: High-flow humidified oxygen and repeat assessment in 2 hours

items.explanationHtml:
Enclosed-space fire, facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot and carbonaceous sputum indicate inhalation injury, and progressive hoarseness signals swelling of the supraglottis. Edema worsens over the first day, especially as fluids are given, so the airway should be secured early, before intubation becomes difficult or impossible.

His normal pulse oximetry is not reassuring: carboxyhemoglobin reads as oxyhemoglobin.

Takeaway: smoke inhalation with hoarseness or stridor needs early intubation.

whyNot.A: Imaging delays airway control and does not change the need to intubate.
whyNot.C: Supraglottic swelling progresses quickly, especially with fluid resuscitation; waiting can make intubation impossible.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids do not prevent burn-related airway swelling and do not replace a secure airway.
whyNot.E: Racemic epinephrine can briefly reduce swelling in croup but does not secure an airway that is closing from burn edema.

items.objective: Decide on early intubation for inhalation injury with signs of airway involvement.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) The patient from the house fire is intubated. Co-oximetry shows carboxyhemoglobin 24% (normal, <3% in nonsmokers) and a serum lactate of 2.0 mmol/L. He is hemodynamically stable, and on arrival he had no loss of consciousness or focal deficits. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment of his gas exposure?

options.label: E
options.html: Ventilation with 40% oxygen titrated to an oxygen saturation of 94%

items.explanationHtml:
Carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with 100% oxygen, which shortens the half-life of carboxyhemoglobin from several hours on room air to roughly an hour. Hyperbaric oxygen is considered for severe poisoning, such as loss of consciousness, neurologic deficits, cardiac ischemia or pregnancy with a high level.

Cyanide is suspected when there is severe lactic acidosis or shock after smoke inhalation; it is treated with hydroxocobalamin.

Takeaway: carbon monoxide poisoning: 100% oxygen; consider hyperbaric oxygen when severe.

whyNot.A: Hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide poisoning, suggested by severe lactic acidosis; his lactate is near normal.
whyNot.B: Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, not carbon monoxide poisoning.
whyNot.C: Bicarbonate does not remove carbon monoxide and would shift the curve further left.
whyNot.E: Titrating to pulse oximetry is unreliable here, and lower oxygen slows removal of carbon monoxide.

items.objective: Treat carbon monoxide poisoning after smoke inhalation with 100% oxygen.

items.stemHtml:
A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with swelling of her throat and lips that began 4 hours after a dental extraction. She has a muffled voice but no stridor. She has had swelling of her hands and episodes of severe crampy abdominal pain since adolescence. She has no hives. Her mother had similar episodes. She received intramuscular epinephrine, intravenous diphenhydramine and methylprednisolone 1 hour ago without improvement. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference
C44 mg/dL14–40 mg/dL
C1 esterase inhibitor, antigen6 mg/dL21–39 mg/dL
C1qNormal—
Serum tryptaseNormal—

While the anesthesiology team prepares for a possible difficult airway, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.label: A
options.html: A second dose of intramuscular epinephrine

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent nonpruritic swelling and abdominal attacks from adolescence, a family history, a dental trigger, low C4, low C1 inhibitor antigen and normal C1q indicate type I hereditary angioedema. (Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency usually starts later in life and has a low C1q.)

Laryngeal attacks are treated with a targeted drug: C1 inhibitor concentrate, the bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist icatibant, or a kallikrein inhibitor. Fresh frozen plasma is a fallback when these are not available. Prepare for a surgical airway in case the swelling progresses.

Takeaway: acute hereditary angioedema of the airway: C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, not epinephrine or antihistamines.

whyNot.A: Bradykinin-mediated swelling responds poorly to epinephrine, which has already failed.
whyNot.B: H2 and H1 antihistamines treat histamine-mediated angioedema; hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated and does not respond to them.
whyNot.D: Attenuated androgens are long-term prophylaxis and act too slowly for an acute laryngeal attack.
whyNot.E: Tranexamic acid has been used for prophylaxis but is not an effective treatment for an acute attack.

items.objective: Select targeted therapy for a laryngeal attack of hereditary angioedema.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy 5 hours ago. She now has neck pain, difficulty swallowing and noisy breathing. Respirations are 28/min and oxygen saturation is 90% on 4 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. The neck is tense and swollen beneath the incision, and there is inspiratory stridor. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.html: Ultrasound of the neck to size the collection

items.explanationHtml:
A tense swelling under a fresh thyroidectomy wound with stridor is an expanding hematoma compressing the airway and blocking venous drainage of the larynx. The incision (skin and deep layers) should be opened immediately at the bedside to release the clot, which usually relieves the obstruction, followed by return to the operating room for hemostasis.

Takeaway: airway compromise from a post-thyroidectomy hematoma: open the wound at the bedside first.

whyNot.B: Hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy causes tingling and tetany; it does not cause a tense, swollen neck.
whyNot.C: This does not relieve external compression by a hematoma.
whyNot.D: Intubation through a compressed, displaced and congested larynx may fail; decompression comes first.
whyNot.E: Imaging delays treatment of a compressive hematoma that is already obstructing the airway.

items.objective: Manage airway obstruction from a neck hematoma after thyroidectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man who had a tracheostomy 3 weeks ago after a stroke has sudden profuse bright red bleeding from the tracheostomy and around the tube. Pulse is 128/min and blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg. A surgical team is on the way. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrange urgent CT angiography of the chest

options.label: B
options.html: Give intravenous tranexamic acid and observe

options.label: C
options.html: Hyperinflate the cuff and compress toward the sternum

options.label: D
options.html: Perform flexible bronchoscopy at the bedside

options.label: E
options.html: Remove the tracheostomy tube and pack the stoma with gauze

items.explanationHtml:
Massive bleeding weeks after a tracheostomy is a tracheoinnominate fistula until proven otherwise. Overinflating the cuff can tamponade the bleeding point and protect the lower airway. If that fails, a finger is passed through the stoma to press the artery forward against the back of the sternum. The patient then goes straight to the operating room for repair.

Takeaway: massive tracheostomy bleeding: overinflate the cuff, compress the innominate artery, then surgery.

whyNot.A: Imaging delays treatment of a life-threatening bleed; the patient should go to the operating room.
whyNot.B: Antifibrinolytics will not control bleeding from an eroded artery.
whyNot.D: Bronchoscopy is used for a small sentinel bleed in a stable patient, not for active massive hemorrhage.
whyNot.E: Removing the tube loses the airway and its cuff; packing alone will not control arterial bleeding.

items.objective: Give emergency management for a tracheoinnominate fistula.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man has had bleeding from the right nostril for 30 minutes. He is upright and has held firm pressure on the soft part of his nose for 15 minutes without effect. Pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Anterior rhinoscopy shows oozing from a prominent vessel on the anterior septum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Most nosebleeds are anterior, from the Kiesselbach plexus. When pressure fails, apply a topical vasoconstrictor (such as oxymetazoline) and anesthetic, then cauterize a visible bleeding point, for example with silver nitrate (one side of the septum at a time). Anterior packing follows if bleeding continues.

Takeaway: anterior epistaxis: pressure, then vasoconstrictor and cautery, then anterior packing.

whyNot.A: Treatment should not wait for tests in a healthy young man with a visible bleeding point.
whyNot.B: His blood pressure is normal; lowering it is not the treatment for a visible anterior bleeding point.
whyNot.C: Posterior packing is for bleeding from the back of the nose that anterior measures do not control.
whyNot.D: Embolization is reserved for refractory, usually posterior, bleeding.

items.objective: Manage anterior epistaxis that persists after direct pressure.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being punched in the face. His nose is swollen and tender, and there is dried blood in both nostrils. Speculum examination shows a smooth, bluish swelling of the septum on both sides that does not shrink after a topical vasoconstrictor. He is breathing comfortably. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Closed reduction of the nasal bones in 5–7 days

options.label: C
options.html: Ice packs and oral analgesics only

options.label: D
options.html: Incision and drainage of the septal collection

options.label: E
options.html: Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and review in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
A boggy, bluish septal swelling after trauma that does not shrink with a vasoconstrictor is a septal hematoma. It separates the cartilage from the perichondrium that nourishes it, so it needs prompt incision and drainage followed by packing (many protocols also give antibiotics) to prevent necrosis, abscess and septal collapse.

Takeaway: always look for a septal hematoma after nasal trauma and drain it promptly.

whyNot.A: Reduction of a deformed nose can wait for the swelling to settle, but a septal hematoma cannot wait.
whyNot.B: CT is not needed to treat a septal hematoma and only delays drainage.
whyNot.C: Conservative care alone risks cartilage necrosis and a saddle-nose deformity.
whyNot.E: Antibiotics alone leave the blood in place, and the cartilage can die and become infected.

items.objective: Treat a nasal septal hematoma with incision and drainage.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after her neck struck the handlebars in a motorcycle crash. She has a hoarse voice, pain on swallowing and small-volume hemoptysis. There is crepitus over the anterior neck, and the laryngeal prominence cannot be felt. Over 20 minutes she develops inspiratory stridor and her oxygen saturation falls to 89% on a non-rebreather mask. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to secure her airway?

options.label: A
options.html: Bag-valve-mask ventilation until CT of the neck is done

options.label: D
options.html: Rapid sequence orotracheal intubation without visualization aids

items.explanationHtml:
Hoarseness, subcutaneous emphysema and loss of the laryngeal prominence after a blow to the neck indicate a laryngeal fracture. With a threatened airway, the safest option is a tracheostomy under local anesthesia, which places the airway below the injury. Orotracheal intubation risks a false passage, and a cricothyrotomy sits at the level of the damaged larynx.

When the airway is stable, CT of the larynx and flexible laryngoscopy guide repair.
