Takeaway: laryngeal fracture with airway compromise is managed by tracheostomy, not cricothyrotomy.

whyNot.A: Positive-pressure mask ventilation can worsen subcutaneous emphysema, and imaging should not delay a threatened airway.
whyNot.B: A cricothyrotomy enters at or next to the injured larynx and can worsen the injury or fail.
whyNot.C: Positive pressure through a disrupted larynx worsens air leak and does not bypass the obstruction.
whyNot.D: A blind tube can create a false passage or complete a partial laryngotracheal disruption.

items.objective: Choose the safest airway in a patient with laryngeal fracture and stridor.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a coughing fit while eating peanuts 2 hours ago. He now has a persistent cough. Breath sounds are reduced over one lung field and there is an expiratory wheeze on the same side. Into which of the following airways did the aspirated material most likely enter first?
items.explanationHtml:
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, continuing almost in line with the trachea. Aspirated objects in older children and adults therefore usually enter it.

A partially obstructing object can act as a one-way valve, giving unilateral wheeze and air trapping on the affected side.

Takeaway: aspirated foreign bodies favor the right main bronchus because of its width and steep angle.

whyNot.A: An object that lodges in the trachea causes bilateral findings and often severe distress, not one-sided wheeze.
whyNot.B: The left main bronchus leaves the trachea at a sharper angle and is narrower and longer, so objects enter it less often.
whyNot.C: The left upper lobe bronchus branches from the left main bronchus, which is the less likely path.
whyNot.D: The lingula is supplied from the left upper lobe bronchus, which is not the favored path.

items.objective: Identify the right main bronchus as the usual site of an aspirated foreign body and explain why.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman has a total thyroidectomy for a large multinodular goiter. In the recovery room, minutes after extubation, she develops inspiratory stridor and increasing respiratory distress. Her voice is weak but not hoarse. Laryngoscopy shows both vocal folds fixed close to the midline. Loss of function of which of the following muscles best explains her airway obstruction?
items.explanationHtml:
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds. It is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which runs in the tracheoesophageal groove and is at risk during thyroidectomy.

When both recurrent laryngeal nerves are injured, both folds rest near the midline. The voice may be nearly normal, but the glottic opening is narrow, giving inspiratory stridor and distress soon after extubation.

Takeaway: the posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal folds; bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury closes the glottis.

whyNot.A: The cricothyroid tenses the vocal folds to raise pitch; it is supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve and does not open the airway.
whyNot.B: The lateral cricoarytenoid adducts the folds; losing it would tend to leave the glottis open, not closed.
whyNot.D: The thyroarytenoid relaxes and shortens the folds; its loss changes voice quality but does not close the airway.
whyNot.E: The transverse arytenoid closes the back of the glottis; losing it would not narrow the airway.

items.objective: Relate bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury to loss of the posterior cricoarytenoid and airway obstruction.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old professional choir singer has a thyroid lobectomy. Afterwards her speaking voice is normal and laryngoscopy shows both vocal folds moving fully. However, she can no longer reach her higher notes and her voice tires quickly. During the operation, which of the following structures was most likely injured close to the vessels it accompanies?

options.label: A
options.html: Ansa cervicalis near the internal jugular vein

options.label: B
options.html: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve near the superior thyroid artery

options.label: C
options.html: Hypoglossal nerve near the lingual artery

options.label: D
options.html: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve near the superior laryngeal artery

options.label: E
options.html: Recurrent laryngeal nerve near the inferior thyroid artery

items.explanationHtml:
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid, which tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to stretch and tense the vocal folds for high notes. It runs with the superior thyroid artery and vein to the upper pole of the gland, where it can be injured when those vessels are tied.

Fold movement is preserved because abduction and adduction depend on the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Takeaway: loss of high pitch with normal fold movement after thyroid surgery points to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

whyNot.A: The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles; injury does not change vocal pitch.
whyNot.C: The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue; injury causes tongue deviation, not a change in pitch.
whyNot.D: The internal branch is sensory to the supraglottis; injury causes aspiration and loss of the cough reflex, not loss of pitch.
whyNot.E: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralyzes vocal fold movement; her folds move fully.

items.objective: Identify external superior laryngeal nerve injury from loss of vocal pitch after thyroid surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl has had several episodes of nonitchy swelling of the hands, face and once the throat since age 12, each lasting 2–3 days. Some episodes follow minor trauma, and one began after she started an estrogen-containing contraceptive. She never has hives. Her father has similar episodes. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely between attacks?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent nonpruritic swelling without urticaria, triggered by trauma and estrogen, with an affected parent, is hereditary angioedema, an autosomal dominant deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor.

Without the inhibitor, the C1 complex keeps cleaving C4, so C4 is low even between attacks. Kallikrein is also unrestrained and generates bradykinin, which causes the swelling.

Takeaway: hereditary angioedema is screened with a low C4; the swelling is caused by bradykinin.

whyNot.A: Elevated IgE suggests atopy; hereditary angioedema is not IgE mediated.
whyNot.B: Low C3 with normal C4 suggests alternative-pathway consumption, not uncontrolled C1 activity.
whyNot.D: Eosinophilia occurs with allergic disease, parasites and some drug reactions, not with hereditary angioedema.
whyNot.E: Tryptase rises transiently in mast-cell activation such as anaphylaxis, not in bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

items.objective: Recognize hereditary angioedema and predict a low C4 level.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with swelling of his lips and tongue that began 3 hours ago. He has no rash or itching. He has taken lisinopril for hypertension for 4 years. Accumulation of which of the following mediators is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
ACE is the same enzyme as kininase II, which breaks down bradykinin. ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, increasing vascular permeability; the same mechanism causes the dry cough.

Angioedema can begin years into therapy, as here, so a long history of uneventful use does not exclude the drug.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitor angioedema is caused by bradykinin, so it lacks hives and responds poorly to antihistamines.

whyNot.A: ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II levels.
whyNot.C: Histamine causes urticarial, itchy swelling after mast-cell activation; ACE inhibitors do not release it.
whyNot.D: Leukotrienes mediate bronchoconstriction and are raised by aspirin in susceptible people, not by ACE inhibition.
whyNot.E: Prostaglandin E2 is not the mediator of ACE inhibitor angioedema.

items.objective: Explain how ACE inhibitors cause angioedema through bradykinin.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman develops hives, throat tightness, a hoarse voice and wheezing within minutes of eating a cake containing tree nuts. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. Intramuscular epinephrine is given and her throat tightness improves. Stimulation of which of the following receptors most directly reduces her laryngeal mucosal swelling?

options.label: A
options.html: Muscarinic M3 receptors on airway glands

options.label: B
options.html: α<sub>1</sub>-adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.html: α<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors on sympathetic nerve terminals

options.label: E
options.html: β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle

items.explanationHtml:
Epinephrine's α1 effect constricts mucosal and skin vessels, reducing capillary leak and swelling and raising blood pressure. Its β2 effect relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and reduces mediator release from mast cells; its β1 effect supports cardiac output.

Takeaway: in anaphylaxis, epinephrine relieves upper airway edema through α1 vasoconstriction.

whyNot.A: Epinephrine does not act on muscarinic receptors.
whyNot.C: α<sub>2</sub> stimulation reduces norepinephrine release; it does not shrink swollen mucosa.
whyNot.D: β<sub>1</sub> effects raise heart rate and contractility; they help blood pressure but not mucosal edema.
whyNot.E: β<sub>2</sub> stimulation relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and helps the wheeze, but does not directly reduce laryngeal edema.

items.objective: Match epinephrine's receptor effects to its actions in anaphylaxis.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with hypertension has brisk bleeding from both nostrils and down the back of his throat. Bleeding continues despite well-placed bilateral anterior nasal packs. Endoscopy shows bleeding high in the posterior nasal cavity. The bleeding vessel is most likely a branch of which of the following arteries?
items.explanationHtml:
Posterior epistaxis comes mostly from the sphenopalatine artery, the terminal branch of the maxillary artery (from the external carotid). It is heavier than anterior bleeding, often runs down the throat, and is not controlled by anterior packing.

Anterior bleeding comes from the Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum.

Takeaway: posterior nosebleeds arise from the sphenopalatine branch of the maxillary artery.

whyNot.A: The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the pharynx and does not supply the posterior nasal cavity in a meaningful way.
whyNot.B: The facial artery supplies the anterior septum through the superior labial artery, a source of anterior bleeding.
whyNot.C: The lingual artery supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth, not the nasal cavity.
whyNot.E: The ophthalmic artery gives the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries, which supply the upper nasal cavity, not the main posterior source.

items.objective: Identify the arterial source of posterior epistaxis.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man with massive facial injuries cannot be intubated or ventilated with a bag and mask. A surgical airway is made through the membrane palpated in the midline between the laryngeal prominence above and a firm complete cartilaginous ring below. Which of the following structures is pierced?
items.explanationHtml:
The membrane between the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid cartilage (the only complete ring) is the cricothyroid membrane. It is superficial and lies below the vocal folds, with no major midline vessels, which makes it the target for an emergency cricothyrotomy.

Takeaway: cricothyrotomy goes through the cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

whyNot.B: The cricotracheal ligament lies below the cricoid cartilage, between it and the first tracheal ring.
whyNot.C: The hyoepiglottic ligament is deep, above the glottis, and is not used for a surgical airway.
whyNot.D: The thyrohyoid membrane lies above the thyroid cartilage, between it and the hyoid bone.
whyNot.E: The thyroid isthmus usually lies over the second to fourth tracheal rings, below the cricoid.

items.objective: Locate the cricothyroid membrane from surface landmarks.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old firefighter is brought out of a burning building. He has a headache and confusion. Pulse oximetry reads 98% on a non-rebreather mask. Arterial blood gas analysis with co-oximetry shows PaO2 380 mm Hg and carboxyhemoglobin 28%. Which of the following best describes the effect of the gas responsible on his blood oxygen transport?

options.label: A
options.html: Normal oxygen content with blocked mitochondrial oxygen use

options.label: B
options.html: Reduced dissolved oxygen with a right shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin curve

options.label: C
options.html: Reduced oxygen content from oxidation of heme iron to the ferric state

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced oxygen content with a left shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin curve

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced oxygen content with a right shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin curve

items.explanationHtml:
Carbon monoxide binds heme far more avidly than oxygen, so less hemoglobin carries oxygen and oxygen content falls, while PaO2 (dissolved oxygen) is unchanged. It also increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining sites (left shift), so tissues receive even less.

Pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin and reads falsely normal; co-oximetry is needed.

Takeaway: carbon monoxide lowers oxygen content and shifts the curve left while PaO2 and pulse oximetry stay normal.

whyNot.A: Blocked mitochondrial oxygen use describes cyanide; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen content.
whyNot.B: His PaO<sub>2</sub>, the dissolved oxygen, is high; carbon monoxide shifts the curve to the left.
whyNot.C: Oxidized (ferric) iron describes methemoglobinemia, not carbon monoxide.
whyNot.E: Carbon monoxide shifts the curve to the left, holding oxygen more tightly.

items.objective: Describe how carbon monoxide impairs oxygen transport.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy is hit in the nose during a soccer game. Two weeks later he has fever, nasal obstruction and severe nasal pain. Examination shows a fluctuant red swelling on both sides of the nasal septum. Untreated, this condition can cause collapse of the nasal bridge mainly because of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Pressure on the nasolacrimal duct blocks drainage

options.label: B
options.html: The nasal bones are replaced by fibrous tissue after fracture

options.label: C
options.html: The septal cartilage depends on the perichondrium for its blood supply

options.label: D
options.html: The sphenopalatine artery is compressed against the vomer

options.label: E
options.html: The upper lateral cartilages are resorbed by osteoclasts

items.explanationHtml:
A septal hematoma collects between the septal cartilage and its perichondrium. Cartilage has no blood vessels of its own and depends on diffusion from the perichondrium, so separating the two starves the cartilage. It can die within days, become infected (septal abscess, as here) and collapse, giving a saddle-nose deformity.

Takeaway: septal cartilage is avascular, so a septal hematoma must be drained before the cartilage dies.

whyNot.A: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus; its obstruction causes tearing, not septal collapse.
whyNot.B: Fractured nasal bones heal with bone; the saddle deformity is from septal cartilage loss.
whyNot.D: Arterial compression is not the mechanism; the cartilage is avascular and fed from the perichondrium.
whyNot.E: Cartilage is not resorbed by osteoclasts, and the problem is in the septal cartilage.

items.objective: Explain why a nasal septal hematoma threatens the septal cartilage.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman had a tracheostomy 12 days ago after prolonged ventilation. A small amount of bright red blood was suctioned from the tube yesterday. Today, sudden massive bleeding pours from the tracheostomy. Erosion of the anterior tracheal wall into which of the following vessels is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
The brachiocephalic artery crosses in front of the lower cervical trachea. Pressure from a low-placed tube, its tip or an overinflated cuff can erode through the tracheal wall into the artery, usually days to weeks after the procedure. A small sentinel bleed often comes before a massive one.

Takeaway: massive bleeding weeks after a tracheostomy suggests a tracheoinnominate fistula.

whyNot.B: The inferior thyroid artery lies lateral to the trachea and is not the vessel classically eroded by a tracheostomy tube.
whyNot.C: The internal jugular vein lies lateral in the carotid sheath and does not cause bright red arterial bleeding into the trachea.
whyNot.D: The left common carotid arises from the arch to the left of the trachea and is rarely eroded.
whyNot.E: A thyroid ima artery, when present, is small and inconstant; massive bleeding weeks later points to the innominate artery.

items.objective: Identify the brachiocephalic artery as the vessel involved in tracheoinnominate fistula.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after his car hit a tree. He is anxious and gasping. Pulse is 140/min, blood pressure is 72/40 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 82% on a non-rebreather mask. The left chest is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and the neck veins are distended. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Rapid sequence intubation before any chest procedure

items.explanationHtml:
Shock, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and distended neck veins after chest trauma are a tension pneumothorax. Decompress at once without waiting for imaging: a needle (4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line, or the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line) or finger thoracostomy, followed by a chest tube.

Takeaway: tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis treated by immediate decompression.

whyNot.B: Tamponade also causes distended neck veins, but breath sounds would be equal; absent breath sounds and hyperresonance point to the pleura.
whyNot.C: Imaging delays treatment of a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax in a patient in shock.
whyNot.D: Positive-pressure ventilation worsens a tension pneumothorax and can cause arrest.
whyNot.E: Fluids do not relieve the obstruction to venous return.

items.objective: Treat a tension pneumothorax with immediate decompression before imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has a 4-cm gunshot wound of the right anterior chest wall that makes a sucking noise and bubbles with each breath. He is breathing rapidly. Pulse is 110/min and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Breath sounds are reduced on the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of the wound?

options.label: B
options.html: Occlusive dressing taped on all four sides

options.label: C
options.html: Occlusive dressing taped on three sides

options.label: D
options.html: Placement of a chest tube through the wound

options.label: E
options.html: Primary suture closure of the wound in the emergency department

items.explanationHtml:
A chest wall defect that sucks and bubbles is an open pneumothorax. The first step is a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides (or a vented chest seal), which lets air escape on expiration but not enter on inspiration. A chest tube is then placed through a separate site, and the wound is closed surgically later.

Takeaway: open pneumothorax: three-sided occlusive dressing, then a chest tube away from the wound.

whyNot.A: He is maintaining his airway; sealing the wound and draining the pleura come first.
whyNot.B: A fully sealed dressing can trap air and create a tension pneumothorax if no chest tube is in place.
whyNot.D: A tube through the wound risks infection and malposition; it goes through a separate incision.
whyNot.E: Closing the wound without a chest tube risks tension pneumothorax and leaves contaminated tissue.

items.objective: Give initial treatment for an open pneumothorax.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after a stab wound to the left lateral chest. He is pale and anxious. Pulse is 124/min, blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 93% on a non-rebreather mask. The left chest is dull to percussion with markedly reduced breath sounds. The neck veins are flat. The trachea is midline. FAST shows no pericardial fluid. Two large-bore intravenous lines are running and blood is being given. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the chest with contrast

options.label: B
options.html: Diagnostic thoracentesis with a small catheter

options.label: D
options.html: Needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space

items.explanationHtml:
Dullness, reduced breath sounds, flat neck veins and shock after a stab wound indicate a hemothorax with hemorrhage. A large-bore chest tube drains the blood, lets the lung re-expand, and measures the rate of bleeding, which decides whether a thoracotomy is needed.

Takeaway: hemothorax with shock: resuscitate and place a chest tube to drain and measure the bleeding.

whyNot.A: An unstable patient should not leave the trauma bay for CT.
whyNot.B: A small catheter cannot evacuate a large hemothorax or measure ongoing bleeding.
whyNot.D: Dullness with flat neck veins indicates blood, not air under tension; a needle cannot drain blood.
whyNot.E: FAST shows no pericardial fluid, and the findings point to the pleural space.

items.objective: Treat a traumatic hemothorax with tube thoracostomy.

items.stemHtml: (Continuation.) In the same patient, the chest tube immediately drains 1,700 mL of blood. Despite 4 units of blood, pulse is 130/min and blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Observation with hourly measurement of chest tube output

options.label: D
options.html: Placement of a second chest tube

items.explanationHtml:
An immediate chest tube output of about 1,500 mL or more, continued drainage of roughly 200 mL/h for 2–4 hours, or persistent instability despite transfusion are indications for operative thoracotomy to control the bleeding source. He meets two of them.

Takeaway: massive hemothorax (≥1,500 mL initially or ongoing brisk bleeding with instability) needs thoracotomy.

whyNot.A: The patient remains unstable and needs control of bleeding, not imaging.
whyNot.B: Observation is for smaller volumes in a stable patient; a large initial output with ongoing shock needs surgery.
whyNot.D: A second tube does not stop the bleeding source.
whyNot.E: VATS is used for retained clot in stable patients, not for active massive bleeding.

items.objective: Identify the indications for thoracotomy in traumatic hemothorax.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman falls down 4 stairs. She has fractures of the right 5th to 8th ribs without pneumothorax or hemothorax. She has atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban and chronic kidney disease (creatinine 1.9 mg/dL). Despite scheduled acetaminophen and intravenous opioid doses, she has severe pain, takes shallow breaths and cannot cough effectively; incentive spirometry volumes are poor. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce her risk of pulmonary complications?

options.label: E
options.html: Strapping the chest wall with adhesive tape

items.explanationHtml:
Older adults with multiple rib fractures are at high risk of pneumonia and respiratory failure because pain stops them breathing deeply and coughing. When oral and intravenous analgesia are not enough, regional techniques improve pain and breathing. A thoracic epidural is effective but must be timed around anticoagulation, so a fascial plane block such as a serratus anterior or erector spinae block is the practical choice here.

Pair analgesia with incentive spirometry, early mobilization and monitoring.

Takeaway: rib fractures in older adults: escalate to regional analgesia to protect breathing and cough.

whyNot.A: Intubation is for respiratory failure; it adds risk and is not used to prevent pneumonia.
whyNot.B: Antibiotics do not prevent pneumonia due to poor cough and atelectasis, and they cause harm.
whyNot.D: NSAIDs are poorly suited to an older adult with chronic kidney disease taking an anticoagulant.
whyNot.E: Strapping limits chest expansion and worsens atelectasis.

items.objective: Choose regional analgesia for an older adult with multiple rib fractures and poor pain control.

items.stemHtml: A 37-year-old man has a right flail chest with an underlying pulmonary contusion after a motor vehicle crash. He has no other injuries. He is alert, with pulse 98/min, blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg, respirations 22/min and oxygen saturation 94% on 6 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Urine output is adequate. A thoracic epidural catheter provides good pain relief. Which of the following additional measures is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Avoiding excess intravenous fluids while maintaining adequate perfusion

options.label: B
options.html: External splinting with sandbags over the flail segment

options.label: C
options.html: Immediate intubation to stabilize the chest wall internally

options.label: E
options.html: Liberal crystalloid infusion to maintain high urine output

items.explanationHtml:
Contused lung leaks fluid readily, so excess crystalloid worsens edema and hypoxemia. Fluids are given to keep perfusion adequate but not in excess. With good analgesia, pulmonary hygiene and oxygen, many patients avoid intubation; mechanical ventilation is used if gas exchange or work of breathing fails. Surgical rib fixation is an option in selected patients.

Takeaway: pulmonary contusion: avoid fluid overload; ventilate for respiratory failure, not for the flail itself.

whyNot.B: Sandbags restrict ventilation and are no longer used.
whyNot.C: Ventilation is for respiratory failure, not routinely for the flail segment; he is oxygenating and ventilating.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids do not improve contusion outcomes and raise infection risk.
whyNot.E: Contused lung is prone to edema; excess fluid worsens gas exchange.

items.objective: Manage flail chest with pulmonary contusion using analgesia and judicious fluids.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed car crash. She is hemodynamically stable. A chest x-ray shows an obscured left hemidiaphragm, and the tip of her nasogastric tube is coiled above the expected level of the diaphragm in the left chest. CT confirms herniation of the stomach through a defect in the left hemidiaphragm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Nasogastric decompression and elective repair in 6 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
A nasogastric tube coiling in the left chest after blunt trauma is a classic sign of left diaphragmatic rupture. Acute injuries are repaired surgically, usually through a laparotomy, which also allows inspection and treatment of the abdominal injuries that often accompany it. Unrepaired defects enlarge and can cause later bowel obstruction or strangulation.

Takeaway: acute traumatic diaphragmatic rupture is repaired surgically, usually through the abdomen.

whyNot.A: Endoscopy does not repair the defect.
whyNot.B: A tube placed into a herniated stomach can perforate it.
whyNot.C: Decompression helps temporarily, but acute traumatic rupture is repaired during the same admission.
whyNot.D: The defect will not heal and herniated stomach can become strangulated.

items.objective: Manage an acute traumatic diaphragmatic rupture.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has a right pneumothorax after being crushed between two vehicles. A chest tube is placed. There is a large, continuous air leak, the right lung does not re-expand on a repeat x-ray, and subcutaneous emphysema is spreading over the neck and face. He is hemodynamically stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Increase suction on the chest tube and repeat the x-ray in 12 hours

items.explanationHtml:
A persistent large air leak, a lung that will not re-expand despite a chest tube, and spreading subcutaneous emphysema suggest a tracheobronchial injury. Bronchoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice and guides operative repair; airway management may need the tube placed beyond or away from the tear.

Takeaway: suspected tracheobronchial injury is confirmed with bronchoscopy.

whyNot.A: The findings indicate an airway injury, not a vascular one.
whyNot.B: An esophageal injury is possible after crushing, but a large air leak with a non-expanding lung points to the airway.
whyNot.D: More suction will not close a major airway tear and may worsen the leak.
whyNot.E: A V/Q scan evaluates pulmonary embolism, not airway disruption.

items.objective: Choose bronchoscopy to diagnose a tracheobronchial injury after blunt chest trauma.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is pulled from a backyard pool after an unknown time under water. He coughed and began crying immediately after his father gave two rescue breaths. In the emergency department 1 hour later he is alert and playful. Respirations are 24/min and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The lungs are clear. A chest x-ray is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Admission to the intensive care unit

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge home now with return precautions

items.explanationHtml:
After a submersion, symptoms from surfactant loss and alveolar edema can appear over the first several hours. A child who is alert with normal oxygen saturation, clear lungs and normal mental status is observed in the emergency department (commonly 4–8 hours from the event) and can then be discharged if still well. Hypoxemia, abnormal lung findings or altered mental status mean admission.

Takeaway: asymptomatic drowning victims are observed for several hours before discharge.

whyNot.A: He is well, with normal oxygenation and examination; intensive care is not needed.
whyNot.B: Respiratory deterioration can develop over hours after submersion; a short observation period comes first.
whyNot.C: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended after drowning.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoids do not prevent lung injury after drowning.

items.objective: Plan observation after a submersion injury in a well-appearing child.

items.stemHtml:
A 63-year-old man is receiving volume-control ventilation in the intensive care unit for pneumonia. Ten minutes ago a central venous catheter was placed in the right subclavian vein. The ventilator now alarms. Blood pressure falls from 128/76 to 84/52 mm Hg. Recent readings:

TimePeak airway pressure (cm H2O)Plateau pressure (cm H2O)SpO2
08:00282095%
08:40443686%

Breath sounds are absent on the right. The endotracheal tube is at the correct depth and a suction catheter passes easily. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Right chest decompression, then a chest tube

options.label: E
options.html: Withdrawing the endotracheal tube by 2 cm

items.explanationHtml:
A rise in both peak and plateau pressure means compliance has fallen, not that resistance has increased. Together with hypotension, a silent right chest and a recent right subclavian line, this is a tension pneumothorax. Decompress immediately (needle or finger thoracostomy) and place a chest tube.

High peak with normal plateau pressure points instead to the airway or tube (mucus plug, kinking, bronchospasm).

Takeaway: in a ventilated patient, raised peak and plateau pressures with hypotension and a silent side mean tension pneumothorax.

whyNot.A: Higher PEEP worsens a tension pneumothorax.
whyNot.B: Bronchospasm raises peak pressure with a normal plateau and does not explain one silent hemithorax.
whyNot.D: Suctioning treats a mucus plug, which raises peak but not plateau pressure, and a catheter already passes freely.
whyNot.E: The tube is at the correct depth; mainstem intubation would also silence the left, not the right, side.

items.objective: Interpret ventilator pressures to recognize tension pneumothorax in a ventilated patient.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is stabbed in the right chest. Ten minutes later he is agitated, with pulse 136/min and blood pressure 76/48 mm Hg. Breath sounds are absent on the right, the right chest is hyperresonant, and the neck veins are distended. Which of the following is the main reason for his hypotension?

options.label: A
options.html: Compression of the left ventricle by the right ventricle

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of blood into the right pleural space

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced venous return to the heart

items.explanationHtml:
Hyperresonance with absent breath sounds, hypotension and distended neck veins after a chest wound indicate a tension pneumothorax. Air that enters the pleural space and cannot leave raises intrathoracic pressure, displaces the mediastinum and compresses and kinks the vena cavae, so venous return and cardiac output fall: obstructive shock.

Takeaway: tension pneumothorax causes shock by obstructing venous return.

whyNot.A: Septal shift is not the main mechanism; the rising intrathoracic pressure impairs filling of the whole heart.
whyNot.B: Hypoxemia contributes little at this stage; the dominant problem is mechanical obstruction to venous return.
whyNot.C: A hemothorax causes dullness and flat neck veins; this chest is hyperresonant with distended neck veins.
whyNot.E: Vasovagal physiology causes bradycardia; he is tachycardic with signs of obstruction.

items.objective: Explain the hemodynamic mechanism of tension pneumothorax.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman needs a chest tube after a traumatic pneumothorax. The physician inserts it in the 5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line, passing the instrument directly over the upper border of the 6th rib. This technique is intended to avoid injury to which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior

options.label: C
options.html: Neurovascular bundle in the costal groove

items.explanationHtml:
The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above down. Passing a needle or tube just over the upper border of the rib below the space keeps it away from that bundle.

Takeaway: chest drains and needles go over the upper border of the rib to avoid the intercostal bundle.

whyNot.A: The internal thoracic artery runs beside the sternum, far from the midaxillary line.
whyNot.B: The long thoracic nerve runs on the outer surface of the serratus anterior, not along the rib margins.
whyNot.D: The phrenic nerve runs over the pericardium in the mediastinum, not in the chest wall.
whyNot.E: The thoracodorsal artery supplies the latissimus dorsi on the posterior axillary wall.

items.objective: Describe the position of the intercostal neurovascular bundle relative to the ribs.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is crushed between a forklift and a wall. On inspiration, a 10-cm area of the right lateral chest wall moves inward while the rest of the chest expands. Which of the following best explains the inward movement of this segment during inspiration?

options.label: A
options.html: Air leaking into the pleural space from a torn lung

options.label: B
options.html: Contraction of the intercostal muscles attached to it

options.label: C
options.html: Elastic recoil of the chest wall exceeding lung recoil

options.label: D
options.html: Negative pleural pressure acting on a detached segment

options.label: E
options.html: Paralysis of the hemidiaphragm on that side

items.explanationHtml:
When adjacent ribs are each broken in two or more places, the segment between the breaks is no longer held by the rigid cage. During inspiration pleural pressure becomes more negative and sucks the free segment inward; during expiration it moves out. This is paradoxical movement, the sign of a flail chest.

Takeaway: a flail segment moves inward on inspiration because it is pulled by falling pleural pressure.

whyNot.A: A pneumothorax collapses the lung but does not make an isolated wall segment move inward.
whyNot.B: Muscle contraction normally lifts the ribs outward; the segment moves passively, not by muscle action.
whyNot.C: The intact chest wall tends to spring outward, not inward.
whyNot.E: Diaphragmatic paralysis makes the abdomen move paradoxically, not a segment of rib cage.

items.objective: Explain paradoxical chest wall movement in flail chest.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man is brought to the hospital after a high-speed car crash. He has fractures of the left 4th to 7th ribs. On the second day his oxygen saturation is 88% on room air and improves only to 92% on high-flow oxygen. Arterial PaCO2 is 34 mm Hg. A CT scan shows patchy consolidation in the left lung beneath the fractures. Which of the following best describes the physiology causing his hypoxemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Diffusion limitation across a thickened alveolar membrane

options.label: C
options.html: Increased dead space from occluded pulmonary arteries

options.label: E
options.html: Shunt and low V/Q units, widened A–a gradient

items.explanationHtml:
A pulmonary contusion fills alveoli with blood and edema. Alveoli that remain perfused but are not ventilated act as a right-to-left shunt, and partially filled areas have low V/Q. Both widen the A–a gradient. Supplemental oxygen corrects the low-V/Q component but not true shunt, so his saturation improves only partly.

Contusions commonly worsen over the first 24–72 hours.

Takeaway: pulmonary contusion causes shunt-type hypoxemia that responds only partly to oxygen.

whyNot.A: Diffusion limitation matters in interstitial fibrosis or exercise; it is a small factor in contusion.
whyNot.B: His PaCO<sub>2</sub> is low, so he is not hypoventilating, and the gradient would be widened.
whyNot.C: Dead space raises PaCO<sub>2</sub> and wastes ventilation; it is the pattern of pulmonary embolism.
whyNot.D: He is breathing supplemental oxygen at sea level.

items.objective: Identify shunt physiology as the cause of hypoxemia in pulmonary contusion.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman is hit by a car. A chest x-ray shows a gastric air bubble and loops of bowel in the left hemithorax with the mediastinum shifted to the right. Injury on the left side is much more common than on the right in this condition mainly because of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: The esophageal hiatus weakens the left hemidiaphragm

options.label: B
options.html: The heart pulls the left hemidiaphragm upward

options.label: C
options.html: The left hemidiaphragm is thinner because it lacks a central tendon

options.label: D
options.html: The left phrenic nerve is longer and more easily injured

options.label: E
options.html: The liver protects the right hemidiaphragm

items.explanationHtml:
Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture is diagnosed far more often on the left because the liver absorbs and spreads the force on the right side. The higher intra-abdominal pressure then pushes the stomach, colon or spleen up into the chest.

Takeaway: blunt diaphragmatic rupture is usually left sided because the liver protects the right.

whyNot.A: The esophageal hiatus is near the midline and is not why blunt rupture favors the left.
whyNot.B: The heart rests on the central tendon; it does not cause left-sided rupture.
whyNot.C: Both hemidiaphragms insert into a shared central tendon.
whyNot.D: Nerve length does not explain mechanical rupture.

items.objective: Explain why traumatic diaphragmatic rupture usually involves the left hemidiaphragm.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man has a laceration of his left hemidiaphragm repaired after a stab wound. Afterward he describes pain at the tip of his left shoulder. Which of the following spinal cord segments carry the sensory fibers that explain this referred pain?
items.explanationHtml:
The central diaphragm and its pleura and peritoneum are supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). The supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4) supply the skin over the shoulder, so irritation of the diaphragm is felt at the shoulder tip. The edge of the diaphragm is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves.

Takeaway: diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

whyNot.A: C1–C2 supply the upper neck and the back of the scalp.
whyNot.C: C6–C8 supply the forearm and hand.
whyNot.D: T1–T2 supply the medial arm and upper chest wall.
whyNot.E: T7–T11 supply the lower chest wall, the edge of the diaphragm and the abdominal wall, not the shoulder.

items.objective: Relate referred shoulder pain to phrenic nerve innervation of the diaphragm.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy is pulled from a lake after being under water for about 2 minutes. After rescue breathing he is awake, but over the next 4 hours he becomes increasingly tachypneic and his oxygen saturation falls to 86% on room air. Chest x-ray shows bilateral patchy opacities. Which of the following is the main mechanism of his hypoxemia?

options.label: D
options.html: Reflex vasodilation of the pulmonary arteries

items.explanationHtml:
Aspirated water, fresh or salt, washes out and inactivates surfactant and causes alveolar edema. Alveoli collapse, shunt rises and compliance falls; the picture can progress to ARDS over hours. This is why patients who seem well after a submersion are observed before discharge.

Takeaway: drowning causes hypoxemia mainly through surfactant loss, alveolar collapse and shunt.

whyNot.A: The volume usually aspirated is too small to cause meaningful hemolysis or electrolyte change.
whyNot.B: He is tachypneic, not hypoventilating.
whyNot.C: Laryngospasm is brief and resolved when he began breathing.
whyNot.D: Vasodilation is not the mechanism; his problem is fluid-filled and collapsed alveoli.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of hypoxemia after a submersion injury.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old recreational diver runs out of air at a depth of 20 meters and ascends rapidly while holding her breath. Within 2 minutes of surfacing she becomes confused and develops weakness of the right arm and leg. Which of the following physical principles best explains how this injury occurred?

options.label: A
options.html: Boyle's law: trapped alveolar air overexpanded and ruptured

options.label: B
options.html: Charles's law: gas cooled and contracted in cold water

options.label: C
options.html: Dalton's law: the partial pressure of oxygen fell during ascent

options.label: D
options.html: Henry's law: nitrogen came out of solution in her tissues as pressure fell

options.label: E
options.html: Poiseuille's law: airway resistance rose as her airways narrowed

items.explanationHtml:
At a fixed temperature pressure and volume are inversely related (Boyle's law). Ascending from 20 m roughly reduces the surrounding pressure from 3 atmospheres to 1, so gas held in the lungs tries to expand to several times its volume. Alveoli rupture, and air enters the pulmonary veins and travels to the brain: arterial gas embolism, which causes neurologic signs within minutes of surfacing.

Takeaway: breath-holding during ascent causes alveolar rupture and arterial gas embolism by Boyle's law.

whyNot.B: Temperature-related changes in gas volume are small here and do not explain the injury.
whyNot.C: A fall in oxygen partial pressure does not cause focal neurologic deficits within minutes of surfacing.
whyNot.D: Bubble formation from dissolved nitrogen causes decompression sickness, which usually develops over hours, not minutes after a breath-hold ascent.
whyNot.E: Airway resistance does not explain a stroke-like deficit.

items.objective: Apply Boyle's law to pulmonary barotrauma and arterial gas embolism in divers.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old construction worker is pinned beneath a collapsed concrete slab across his chest for several minutes before rescue. His face, neck and upper chest are deep purple with innumerable petechiae, and both eyes show subconjunctival hemorrhage. Below a sharp line across the upper chest, the skin is normal. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: D
options.html: Retrograde venous pressure surge from thoracic compression

options.label: E
options.html: Superior vena cava obstruction by a mediastinal mass

items.explanationHtml:
Traumatic asphyxia follows sudden compression of the chest, often against a closed glottis. The pressure drives blood backward from the right atrium into the veins of the head and neck, which lack valves, rupturing venules and capillaries. The skin above the level of compression becomes congested and petechial, with subconjunctival hemorrhage.

Takeaway: traumatic asphyxia produces craniofacial congestion and petechiae from retrograde venous pressure.

whyNot.A: DIC causes widespread bleeding and petechiae that are not confined above a line of compression.
whyNot.B: Fat embolism causes petechiae over the chest and axillae 1–3 days after fractures, with hypoxemia and confusion, not immediate facial congestion.
whyNot.C: Thrombocytopenia causes petechiae everywhere, not a sharp upper-body distribution after a crush.
whyNot.E: SVC syndrome develops over weeks with a mass; this followed acute crushing.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of traumatic asphyxia.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old soldier is 6 meters from an explosion. He has no penetrating wounds, burns or fractures. He reports reduced hearing in both ears and develops cough with blood-tinged sputum and hypoxemia over the next hour. Chest x-ray shows bilateral perihilar opacities. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of his lung injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Primary blast injury from the pressure wave at air–tissue interfaces

options.label: B
options.html: Quaternary blast injury from inhaled toxic gases

options.label: C
options.html: Secondary blast injury from fragments propelled by the explosion

options.label: D
options.html: Tertiary blast injury from being thrown against a structure

options.label: E
options.html: Thermal injury of the lower airway

items.explanationHtml:
Primary blast injury is caused by the overpressure wave itself, which damages organs that contain air: the tympanic membranes (most often), the lungs and the bowel. Blast lung is alveolar hemorrhage and edema causing hypoxemia, hemoptysis and bilateral, often perihilar, opacities. A ruptured eardrum signals exposure to a significant pressure wave.

Takeaway: primary blast injury affects air-filled organs: ears, lungs and bowel.

whyNot.B: Quaternary injury includes burns and toxic inhalation; nothing suggests these.
whyNot.C: Secondary injury causes penetrating wounds; he has none.
whyNot.D: Tertiary injury causes blunt trauma and fractures from the body's displacement.
whyNot.E: Hot gases rarely injure the airway below the vocal folds, and he has no burns.

items.objective: Classify blast injuries and identify blast lung as a primary blast injury.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman has a right pneumothorax after a motorcycle crash. A chest tube is placed and connected to suction. There is a large continuous air leak in the drainage system during both inspiration and expiration, and subcutaneous emphysema spreads over the neck. A repeat chest x-ray shows the collapsed right lung lying against the lateral chest wall and diaphragm, away from the hilum. Where is the injury most likely located?

options.label: A
options.html: Cervical trachea at the level of the thyroid isthmus

options.label: C
options.html: Parietal pleura at the tube insertion site

options.label: D
options.html: Right main bronchus near the carina

options.label: E
options.html: Visceral pleura over the right upper lobe

items.explanationHtml:
A large continuous air leak that persists with suction, a lung that will not re-expand, and spreading subcutaneous emphysema indicate a major airway disruption. Blunt tracheobronchial injuries usually occur within a few centimeters of the carina. A complete tear of a main bronchus lets the lung drop away from the hilum toward the dependent chest (the fallen lung sign).

Bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis.

Takeaway: a persistent large air leak with a lung that will not re-expand means a bronchial tear near the carina.

whyNot.A: A cervical tracheal tear causes subcutaneous emphysema but not a pneumothorax that fails to re-expand with the lung fallen away from the hilum.
whyNot.B: Esophageal rupture causes pneumomediastinum and often a left effusion, not a massive air leak through a chest tube.
whyNot.C: A leak at the insertion site is intermittent and external; it does not stop the lung from re-expanding.
whyNot.E: A small peripheral lung tear usually seals and the lung re-expands with a chest tube.

items.objective: Recognize the signs of a main bronchus rupture after blunt trauma.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at 39 weeks by vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy; prenatal ultrasound was not done. Within minutes he is cyanotic with severe respiratory distress. Pulse is 170/min and oxygen saturation 70%. His abdomen is flat and sunken. Breath sounds are absent on the left, and heart sounds are best heard to the right of the sternum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Severe distress from birth, a scaphoid abdomen, absent left breath sounds and a right-shifted heart are the picture of a left posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia. A chest x-ray shows bowel loops in the chest.

Takeaway: scaphoid abdomen + shifted heart sounds in a distressed newborn = diaphragmatic hernia.

whyNot.B: There is no history of meconium-stained fluid, and the scaphoid abdomen points elsewhere.
whyNot.C: RDS affects preterm infants and gives symmetric findings.
whyNot.D: Pneumothorax shifts the heart but the abdomen is not scaphoid; the abdominal contents are in place.
whyNot.E: TTN is mild tachypnea in the first hours with symmetric breath sounds and no mediastinal shift.

items.objective: Recognize congenital diaphragmatic hernia in a newborn.

items.stemHtml: The newborn with a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia continues to have severe respiratory distress and oxygen saturation of 68%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Emergency surgical repair of the diaphragm

options.label: C
options.html: Endotracheal intubation and orogastric tube decompression

options.label: E
options.html: Needle decompression of the left chest

items.explanationHtml:
Avoid bag-mask ventilation. Intubate immediately, place an orogastric tube on suction to decompress the herniated bowel, and ventilate gently to limit barotrauma to hypoplastic lungs. Surgical repair is delayed until the infant's physiology is stable.

Takeaway: diaphragmatic hernia: intubate and decompress the stomach; no bag-mask; delayed repair.

whyNot.A: Bag-mask ventilation fills the herniated stomach and bowel with gas, further compressing the lungs.
whyNot.B: Repair is done after the infant is stabilized; early surgery does not improve outcome.
whyNot.D: CPAP pushes air into the gut and does not secure the airway in this severity.
whyNot.E: Needle decompression risks perforating herniated bowel; this is not a pneumothorax.

items.objective: Manage the initial airway in congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

items.stemHtml: The infant is intubated and transferred to a tertiary neonatal unit, where the hernia is repaired on day 5. The parents ask what will most determine whether their son survives. Which of the following is the best answer?

options.label: A
options.html: The degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension

options.label: B
options.html: The size of the abdominal incision

options.label: C
options.html: The timing of surgery within the first 24 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Whether he receives antenatal corticosteroids in a future pregnancy

options.label: E
options.html: Whether the hernia contained the spleen

items.explanationHtml:
Survival in congenital diaphragmatic hernia depends mainly on the severity of pulmonary hypoplasia and the associated persistent pulmonary hypertension; associated anomalies (cardiac, chromosomal) and liver herniation also worsen the outlook. Some infants need extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.

Takeaway: CDH prognosis = lung hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension, not the repair itself.

whyNot.B: Incision size does not affect survival.
whyNot.C: Early surgery does not improve survival; stabilization comes first.
whyNot.D: This is irrelevant to his own outcome.
whyNot.E: Organ content matters little except the liver; spleen herniation does not determine survival.

items.objective: State the main prognostic determinants in congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

items.stemHtml: A girl is born at 38 weeks by scheduled cesarean delivery without labor. At 2 hours of age she has a respiratory rate of 82/min with mild retractions and needs 25% oxygen. She is feeding poorly but is afebrile and well perfused. Her mother's group B streptococcal culture was negative. A chest x-ray shows streaky perihilar opacities and fluid in the horizontal fissure, with normal lung volumes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A term infant born by cesarean delivery without labor, with tachypnea, a mild oxygen need and perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissure, has transient tachypnea of the newborn from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. Care is supportive and it settles within 1–3 days.

Takeaway: term + cesarean without labor + fluid in the fissures = transient tachypnea of the newborn.

whyNot.A: There is no bowel in the chest or mediastinal shift.
whyNot.B: Pneumonia is possible but less likely in a well-perfused afebrile infant with a GBS-negative mother and this classic film; observe closely.
whyNot.C: There was no meconium-stained fluid, and the film lacks patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation.
whyNot.D: RDS is a disease of preterm infants and shows low volumes with ground-glass opacity.

items.objective: Distinguish transient tachypnea of the newborn from other causes of neonatal distress.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 28 weeks' gestation is placed on nasal CPAP in the delivery room. At 3 hours of age he has worsening grunting and retractions, and his oxygen requirement has risen from 30% to 50% to keep saturation at 90%. A chest x-ray shows low lung volumes with diffuse ground-glass opacity and air bronchograms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Increase the inspired oxygen to 100% and continue CPAP

options.label: E
options.html: Start ampicillin and gentamicin and observe

items.explanationHtml:
A preterm infant with RDS whose oxygen need is rising on CPAP should receive exogenous surfactant into the trachea (by brief intubation or a thin catheter), which improves oxygenation and lowers mortality and air leak.

Takeaway: RDS failing CPAP (rising oxygen need) → give surfactant.

whyNot.B: Nitric oxide is for persistent pulmonary hypertension in term and near-term infants, not routine preterm RDS.
whyNot.C: Postnatal steroids are not the treatment for acute RDS.
whyNot.D: Escalating oxygen alone raises the risk of oxygen toxicity without treating the cause.
whyNot.E: Antibiotics may be given while sepsis is excluded, but they do not treat surfactant deficiency.

items.objective: Treat neonatal respiratory distress syndrome that is failing CPAP.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 30 weeks' gestation comes to labor and delivery with regular contractions. Her cervix is 4 cm dilated and 80% effaced. Membranes are intact, and the fetal heart tracing is reassuring. She has no signs of infection. In addition to magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, which of the following is most appropriate to improve the neonate's respiratory outcome?

options.label: A
options.html: Amniocentesis for the lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio before deciding

options.label: E
options.html: Oral nifedipine as the sole intervention

items.explanationHtml:
For a pregnant patient at risk of delivery within 7 days between about 24 and 34 weeks, a course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) lowers neonatal RDS, intraventricular hemorrhage and death. Short-term tocolysis may be used to allow the course to finish.

Takeaway: preterm labor before 34 weeks → antenatal corticosteroids.

whyNot.A: Testing lung maturity is not needed before giving steroids at 30 weeks.
whyNot.B: There is no indication for delivery, and delivery now would remove the benefit of steroids.
whyNot.D: Antenatal TRH does not improve neonatal outcomes and is not used.
whyNot.E: A tocolytic can buy time for steroids, but by itself it does not mature the lungs.

items.objective: Use antenatal corticosteroids to prevent neonatal RDS in preterm labor.

items.stemHtml: A 7-week-old girl has noisy breathing that began at 2 weeks of age. The noise is high-pitched, occurs on inspiration, and is louder when she is lying on her back, crying or feeding. She feeds well without choking, has no cyanosis or apneas, and has gained weight along the 50th percentile. Flexible laryngoscopy in the office shows inward collapse of the supraglottic structures during inspiration. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Mild laryngomalacia (inspiratory stridor, worse supine and with feeding, normal growth, no apneas or cyanosis) is managed with reassurance and monitoring; most cases resolve by 12–24 months. Reflux is treated if present. Supraglottoplasty is for severe cases.

Takeaway: laryngomalacia with good growth and no red flags → reassure and follow.

whyNot.A: Steroids treat croup, not laryngomalacia.
whyNot.B: A vascular ring causes biphasic stridor with feeding difficulty; laryngoscopy already shows laryngomalacia.
whyNot.C: Tracheostomy is a last resort for severe obstruction.
whyNot.E: Surgery is reserved for severe disease with failure to thrive, apneas or cyanosis.

items.objective: Manage mild laryngomalacia in an infant.

items.stemHtml: A term newborn is cyanotic and has retractions while resting quietly and during attempts to breastfeed; when he cries vigorously, his color improves to pink. Oxygen saturation is 78% at rest and 94% while crying. A soft suction catheter cannot be passed through either nostril into the pharynx. He also has a coloboma of the left iris. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Newborns breathe mainly through the nose, so bilateral choanal atresia causes cyanosis at rest and with feeding that improves with crying (mouth breathing). The first step is to secure an oral airway (or intubate), then confirm with CT and repair surgically. A coloboma suggests CHARGE syndrome, which also needs cardiac and other evaluation.

Takeaway: cyanosis relieved by crying + a catheter that will not pass the nose → oral airway.

whyNot.A: Cardiac evaluation is needed for CHARGE, but the airway comes first.
whyNot.B: Sepsis does not explain cyanosis relieved by crying and an obstructed nose.
whyNot.C: Nasal CPAP cannot work through blocked choanae.
whyNot.D: Untreated bilateral choanal atresia causes hypoxemia and can be fatal.

items.objective: Give immediate airway management for bilateral choanal atresia.

items.stemHtml: A 5-month-old boy has had noisy breathing in both inspiration and expiration since about 1 month of age, worse when he is agitated. He takes a long time to finish bottles, coughs during feeds and has had two hospitalizations for wheezing illnesses. Growth is at the 10th percentile. Lungs are clear between episodes. A barium esophagram shows a posterior indentation of the esophagus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Biphasic stridor, recurrent wheezing illnesses and feeding difficulty with a posterior esophageal indentation indicate a vascular ring (most often a double aortic arch). Define the anatomy with CT or MR angiography; surgical division relieves the compression.

Takeaway: biphasic stridor + feeding difficulty + posterior esophageal indentation = vascular ring.

whyNot.A: Symptoms since 1 month of age and an esophageal indentation are not explained by a foreign body.
whyNot.B: Reflux does not cause a fixed posterior esophageal indentation.
whyNot.C: An H-type fistula causes coughing with feeds and aspiration pneumonia, but not biphasic stridor or a posterior indentation.
whyNot.D: Laryngomalacia gives inspiratory stridor, normal esophagram and no feeding-related dysphagia pattern like this.

items.objective: Diagnose a vascular ring in an infant with stridor and feeding difficulty.

items.stemHtml:
A 10-day-old girl is seen after her state newborn screen was reported as abnormal. She was born at term, weighs 3.4 kg (birth weight 3.3 kg), and is breastfeeding well with normal stools. Her examination is normal. The screening results are below.

TestResult
Immunoreactive trypsinogenElevated (above the screening cut-off)
CFTR variant panelOne pathogenic variant detected
Thyroid-stimulating hormoneNormal
Hemoglobin electrophoresisNormal

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Reassure the parents that she is a carrier only

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat the newborn screen at 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
A positive newborn screen for cystic fibrosis (raised immunoreactive trypsinogen, here with one CFTR variant) needs confirmation with a sweat chloride test at an accredited center: 60 mmol/L or more confirms CF, while intermediate values need further genetic and clinical evaluation.

Takeaway: positive CF newborn screen → sweat chloride test; one variant does not mean carrier only.

whyNot.A: Imaging is not diagnostic for CF and exposes her to radiation.
whyNot.B: One variant on a limited panel does not exclude a second, untested variant; CF has not been ruled out.
whyNot.C: Waiting delays diagnosis and nutritional care if she has CF.
whyNot.D: Treatment waits for a diagnosis; she has no malabsorption.

items.objective: Confirm a positive cystic fibrosis newborn screen with sweat chloride testing.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at 41 weeks after a labor complicated by fetal heart rate decelerations. The amniotic fluid is thick and green. At birth he is limp, apneic and has a heart rate of 80/min. He is placed under a radiant warmer, dried and positioned, and his mouth and nose are cleared with a bulb syringe. He remains apneic. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Intubation for tracheal suctioning before any ventilation

items.explanationHtml:
Under current neonatal resuscitation guidance, a non-vigorous infant with meconium-stained fluid is managed like any other: warm, dry, position, clear the airway, and if apneic or the heart rate is below 100/min, start positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute. Ventilation of the lungs is the most important step in newborn resuscitation.

Takeaway: meconium-exposed and apneic → ventilate; do not delay for routine tracheal suctioning.

whyNot.A: Compressions start when the heart rate stays below 60/min despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation.
whyNot.B: Free-flow oxygen does not help an apneic infant who needs ventilation.
whyNot.C: Epinephrine is given only when the heart rate remains below 60/min despite ventilation and compressions.
whyNot.D: Routine tracheal suctioning of non-vigorous meconium-exposed infants is no longer recommended because it delays ventilation; it is reserved for an obstructed airway.

items.objective: Apply current neonatal resuscitation steps to a non-vigorous infant with meconium-stained fluid.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at 29 weeks' gestation. Within an hour he has grunting, nasal flaring and intercostal retractions, and needs 40% oxygen. A chest x-ray shows low lung volumes with a diffuse fine granular pattern and air bronchograms. Deficient secretion by which of the following cells is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
This is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome: surfactant deficiency in a preterm lung causes diffuse microatelectasis (ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms). Surfactant, mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, is made and secreted by type II pneumocytes from lamellar bodies.

Takeaway: preterm + ground-glass lungs = surfactant deficiency from immature type II pneumocytes.

whyNot.A: Macrophages clear surfactant and particles; they do not secrete it.
whyNot.B: Club cells in bronchioles secrete protective proteins and detoxify, but are not the source of alveolar surfactant.
whyNot.C: Goblet cells secrete mucus in larger airways.
whyNot.D: Type I cells form the thin gas-exchange surface; they do not make surfactant.

items.objective: Identify type II pneumocytes as the source of surfactant in neonatal RDS.

items.stemHtml: Two alveoli of different sizes are connected by a common airway. Their walls have the same surface tension, and surfactant is absent. Which of the following best describes what happens?

options.label: A
options.html: Airflow stops because pressures equalize immediately

options.label: B
options.html: Both alveoli overdistend because compliance rises

options.label: C
options.html: Both alveoli remain stable because surface tension is equal

options.label: D
options.html: The larger alveolus empties into the smaller one

options.label: E
options.html: The smaller alveolus empties into the larger one

items.explanationHtml:
By the law of Laplace (P = 2T / r), with equal surface tension the smaller alveolus has the higher collapsing pressure, so it empties into the larger one. Surfactant prevents this by lowering surface tension more in small (compressed) alveoli, which keeps alveoli of different sizes stable at end-expiration.

Takeaway: without surfactant, small alveoli collapse into large ones (Laplace); surfactant equalizes them.

whyNot.A: Pressures cannot equalize while radii differ under equal tension.
whyNot.B: Loss of surfactant lowers compliance; it does not cause overdistension.
whyNot.C: Equal tension with unequal radii means unequal collapsing pressures, so they are not stable.
whyNot.D: The larger alveolus has the lower pressure, so air flows toward it, not out of it.

items.objective: Apply the law of Laplace to explain alveolar instability without surfactant.

items.stemHtml: A woman with type 1 diabetes and poor glycemic control during pregnancy delivers a 4.4-kg boy by cesarean delivery at 37 weeks. He develops grunting and retractions, and a chest x-ray shows diffuse ground-glass opacities. Which of the following best explains his lung disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Excess fetal cortisol from maternal hyperglycemia

options.label: C
options.html: Hypoglycemia depriving type II cells of energy

options.label: D
options.html: Macrosomia compressing the chest during delivery

options.label: E
options.html: Maternal antibodies crossing the placenta and damaging type II cells

items.explanationHtml:
Maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperglycemia and compensatory fetal hyperinsulinemia, which antagonizes the maturing effect of glucocorticoids on type II pneumocytes and delays surfactant synthesis. These infants can have RDS later in gestation than expected, even when large.

Takeaway: infant of a diabetic mother: big but surfactant-immature because insulin delays lung maturation.

whyNot.A: Cortisol speeds lung maturation; it would protect, not harm.
whyNot.C: The fetus of a poorly controlled diabetic mother is hyperglycemic, not hypoglycemic, before birth.
whyNot.D: Macrosomia causes birth trauma but not surfactant deficiency.
whyNot.E: There is no antibody-mediated mechanism; this is a metabolic effect.

items.objective: Explain delayed surfactant maturation in infants of diabetic mothers.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation is admitted in preterm labor with a cervix dilated to 3 cm. She receives two intramuscular injections 24 hours apart of a drug intended to reduce the risk of neonatal respiratory distress. Which of the following is the main mechanism of benefit?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased synthesis of surfactant by fetal type II pneumocytes

options.label: D
options.html: Relaxation of uterine smooth muscle to delay delivery

items.explanationHtml:
Two intramuscular doses 24 hours apart describe betamethasone. Glucocorticoids induce enzymes for phospholipid synthesis and the maturation of type II pneumocytes, increasing surfactant and structural maturity; they also reduce intraventricular hemorrhage and neonatal death.

Takeaway: antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation by boosting surfactant production.

whyNot.A: Ductal closure is a prostaglandin-related effect, unrelated to this drug's benefit.
whyNot.C: Magnesium sulfate (given before about 32 weeks) is the neuroprotective agent.
whyNot.D: That is the action of tocolytics, not the drug given for fetal lung maturity.
whyNot.E: Fetal breathing movements are not the target of antenatal corticosteroids.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism by which antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal RDS.

items.stemHtml: A newborn girl has severe respiratory distress immediately after birth. Her abdomen is sunken, breath sounds are absent on the left, and heart sounds are loudest to the right of the sternum. A chest x-ray shows gas-filled loops of bowel in the left hemithorax. Failure of which embryologic structure to develop properly is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
Bowel in the left chest with a scaphoid abdomen and a shifted mediastinum is congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The common posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect results from failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close the pericardioperitoneal canal, usually on the left. Compression of the lung during branching causes pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension, the main threats to life.

Takeaway: posterolateral (Bochdalek) diaphragmatic hernia = failed pleuroperitoneal membrane closure.

whyNot.A: Body wall muscle forms the peripheral rim; defects there are uncommon.
whyNot.B: The esophageal mesentery contributes the crura; it is not the usual site of failure.
whyNot.D: The septum transversum forms the central tendon; central defects are rare and not the usual posterolateral hernia.
whyNot.E: Defects of this septum cause tracheoesophageal fistula, not a diaphragmatic hernia.

items.objective: Relate congenital diaphragmatic hernia to its embryologic origin.

items.stemHtml: A newborn boy has excessive frothy oral secretions and coughs and turns blue during his first feed. His mother had polyhydramnios. A feeding tube cannot be advanced beyond 10 cm, and an x-ray shows the tube coiled in the upper chest; the stomach and bowel contain gas. Abnormal development of which structure is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Laryngotracheal groove closure at the larynx

items.explanationHtml:
A blind upper esophageal pouch (tube coils) with gas in the stomach means esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula, the most common type. It results from abnormal division of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum. Polyhydramnios reflects the fetus's inability to swallow amniotic fluid.

Takeaway: coiled tube + gas in the abdomen = esophageal atresia with distal TEF (faulty tracheoesophageal septum).

whyNot.A: Pancreatic bud defects cause annular pancreas, with bilious vomiting later, not this picture.
whyNot.B: A laryngeal cleft causes aspiration but the esophagus remains continuous, so a tube would pass.
whyNot.C: Pouch defects produce thymic, parathyroid or ear anomalies, not esophageal atresia.
whyNot.D: Failed duodenal recanalization causes duodenal atresia with a double-bubble, not a blind esophagus.

items.objective: Recognize the most common type of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula and its embryology.

items.stemHtml: A 13-year-old girl has had four episodes of left lower lobe pneumonia in 3 years. Between episodes she is well. A contrast-enhanced CT shows a heterogeneous mass in the posterior basal left lower lobe, contained within the normal visceral pleura, with no connection to the bronchial tree. An artery arising from the descending thoracic aorta supplies the mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Nonfunctioning lung tissue without a bronchial connection, supplied by a systemic artery from the aorta, is pulmonary sequestration. The intralobar type lies within normal pleura, favors the posterior basal segments and causes recurrent infection in older children; the extralobar type has its own pleura and systemic venous drainage.

Takeaway: lower-lobe mass + aortic arterial supply + no bronchial connection = pulmonary sequestration.

whyNot.A: CF bronchiectasis is diffuse and upper-lobe predominant and connects to the airways.
whyNot.B: Bronchogenic cysts are usually mediastinal and are not supplied by a systemic artery from the aorta.
whyNot.C: These connect to the airway and are supplied by the pulmonary artery.
whyNot.E: An AVM connects a pulmonary artery to a pulmonary vein; it is not supplied by the aorta.

items.objective: Diagnose pulmonary sequestration from its systemic arterial supply.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He has had a wet cough every day since childhood, chronic nasal discharge and repeated ear infections. His heart sounds are loudest in the right chest, and a chest x-ray shows the cardiac apex on the right and dilated, thick-walled bronchi. Semen analysis shows a normal sperm count with no motile sperm. A defect in which of the following is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme

options.label: D
options.html: Microtubule polymerization in the mitotic spindle

items.explanationHtml:
Bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, otitis, situs inversus and immotile sperm make up Kartagener syndrome, a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia. Defective axonemal dynein arms stop ciliary and flagellar bending; failure of embryonic nodal cilia randomizes left-right orientation, so about half of patients have situs inversus.

Takeaway: immotile sperm + bronchiectasis + situs inversus = dynein arm defect (primary ciliary dyskinesia).

whyNot.A: CF causes male infertility through absent vas deferens (azoospermia), not immotile sperm, and does not cause situs inversus.
whyNot.C: Kinesin moves cargo toward microtubule plus ends in axons; it does not power ciliary bending.
whyNot.D: Spindle defects would impair cell division broadly, not just ciliary motion.
whyNot.E: Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome.

items.objective: Link primary ciliary dyskinesia to axonemal dynein defects and its clinical features.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has a chest x-ray for a persistent cough. It shows a smooth, round 4-cm mass near the carina. CT shows a thin-walled, fluid-filled cyst in the middle mediastinum. The cyst is removed. Which of the following is most likely to be seen lining its wall?

options.label: A
options.html: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with cartilage and glands

options.label: D
options.html: Keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with hair follicles

options.label: E
options.html: Neoplastic spindle cells with nerve sheath differentiation

items.explanationHtml:
A thin-walled fluid-filled cyst near the carina in the middle mediastinum is a bronchogenic cyst, from abnormal budding of the ventral foregut. Its wall recapitulates the airway: ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, smooth muscle, cartilage and seromucous glands.

Takeaway: bronchogenic cyst = foregut bud with an airway-type wall (respiratory epithelium, cartilage).

whyNot.B: A pericardial cyst is lined by mesothelium and usually sits at the cardiophrenic angle.
whyNot.C: Gastric mucosa suggests an enteric duplication cyst, usually posterior, near the esophagus.
whyNot.D: Skin adnexa suggest a mature teratoma, an anterior mediastinal tumor.
whyNot.E: A nerve sheath tumor is solid and posterior mediastinal.

items.objective: Identify the histology of a bronchogenic cyst.

items.stemHtml: A 6-week-old boy has noisy breathing that began at 2 weeks of age. The high-pitched noise occurs only on inspiration, is louder when he lies on his back and when he feeds, and softens when he lies prone. He is gaining weight well. Which of the following best explains why the noise occurs during inspiration?

options.label: A
options.html: Airway smooth muscle constriction triggered by vagal reflexes

options.label: B
options.html: Expansion of the intrathoracic airways during inspiration

options.label: C
options.html: Extrathoracic airway pressure dropping below atmospheric

options.label: D
options.html: Increased airway resistance from mucus plugging

options.label: E
options.html: Increased elastic recoil of the lung during inspiration

items.explanationHtml:
This is laryngomalacia, the most common cause of stridor in infants. During inspiration, pressure inside the extrathoracic airway falls below atmospheric pressure, and floppy supraglottic tissues are drawn inward, narrowing the airway. In expiration the pressure is positive and they are pushed open. Intrathoracic floppy airways (tracheomalacia) behave the opposite way and cause expiratory noise.

Takeaway: extrathoracic dynamic obstruction → inspiratory stridor; intrathoracic → expiratory.

whyNot.A: Bronchospasm causes expiratory wheeze in the intrathoracic airways.
whyNot.B: Intrathoracic airways widen in inspiration; that cannot explain inspiratory narrowing.
whyNot.D: Mucus plugging affects both phases and would be associated with cough and infection.
whyNot.E: Recoil acts during expiration and affects intrathoracic airways.

items.objective: Explain why extrathoracic dynamic airway obstruction causes inspiratory stridor.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old girl has noisy breathing in both phases of respiration, frequent coughing and choking during bottle feeds, and two episodes of bronchiolitis. A barium esophagram shows indentations on both sides of the esophagus and a posterior indentation. CT angiography shows two aortic arches that join behind the esophagus and encircle the trachea and esophagus. Which of the following embryologic events most likely failed to occur?

options.label: B
options.html: Division of the truncus arteriosus by the aorticopulmonary septum

options.label: C
options.html: Formation of the left fourth arch artery

options.label: D
options.html: Regression of the distal right dorsal aorta

options.label: E
options.html: Regression of the right sixth arch artery

items.explanationHtml:
Normally the right dorsal aorta beyond the origin of the right subclavian artery regresses, leaving a left arch.
