When it persists, both fourth arches remain, forming a double aortic arch, the most common symptomatic vascular ring, which compresses the trachea (biphasic stridor, infections) and esophagus (feeding difficulty).

Takeaway: double aortic arch = persistent distal right dorsal aorta; a ring around trachea and esophagus.

whyNot.A: The ductus venosus is in the liver circulation and unrelated.
whyNot.B: Failure causes persistent truncus arteriosus, not a vascular ring.
whyNot.C: The left fourth arch normally forms the aortic arch; it is present here.
whyNot.E: Persistence of the right sixth arch gives a right-sided ductus, not a double arch.

items.objective: Explain the embryology of a double aortic arch.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman is receiving ABVD chemotherapy for stage II Hodgkin lymphoma. Before cycle 4 she reports a new dry cough and breathlessness climbing one flight of stairs. Temperature is normal. Fine bibasilar crackles are heard. DLCO has fallen from 92% to 61% of predicted. CT shows new bilateral subpleural reticulation. Infection has been excluded. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue the full regimen and repeat DLCO after the next cycle

options.label: B
options.html: Discontinue bleomycin and start a systemic glucocorticoid

options.label: D
options.html: Halve the dose for the next cycle

items.explanationHtml:
New cough, crackles, a fall in DLCO and reticulation during bleomycin therapy indicate bleomycin pneumonitis. The drug must be stopped permanently, and systemic glucocorticoids are generally given for symptomatic disease. The remaining chemotherapy continues without bleomycin (AVD), which preserves efficacy in most patients with Hodgkin lymphoma.

Takeaway: Bleomycin pneumonitis: stop the drug permanently and give glucocorticoids.

whyNot.A: Continuing exposes her to progressive, potentially fatal fibrosis.
whyNot.C: Infection has been excluded; antibiotics do not treat drug-induced pneumonitis.
whyNot.D: Dose reduction is not appropriate once symptomatic pneumonitis has developed.
whyNot.E: High inspired oxygen can worsen bleomycin lung injury; she is not hypoxemic.

items.objective: Manage bleomycin pulmonary toxicity during chemotherapy.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man is scheduled for elective inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia. Six years ago he was cured of a testicular germ cell tumor with chemotherapy that included bleomycin. He has no respiratory symptoms, and his pulmonary function is normal. Which of the following intraoperative measures most reduces his risk of postoperative respiratory failure?

options.label: D
options.html: Keeping the inspired oxygen fraction low

items.explanationHtml:
Previous bleomycin exposure sensitizes the lungs to oxygen-derived free radicals for years. High inspired oxygen during anesthesia has been linked to acute lung injury in these patients. The usual approach is to limit FiO2 to the lowest level that maintains acceptable saturation, use lung-protective ventilation and avoid fluid overload.

Takeaway: After bleomycin, keep FiO2 as low as safely possible during anesthesia.

whyNot.A: Volatile anesthetics are not specifically linked to bleomycin lung injury.
whyNot.B: Excess fluid increases the risk of pulmonary edema; restrained fluid is preferred.
whyNot.C: Steroids do not prevent oxygen-triggered bleomycin injury.
whyNot.E: High tidal volumes cause ventilator-induced lung injury and are avoided.

items.objective: Minimize inspired oxygen in patients previously treated with bleomycin.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man has taken amiodarone for 2 years for recurrent ventricular tachycardia. He has 6 weeks of worsening exertional dyspnea, dry cough and low-grade fever. SpO2 is 91% on room air. CT shows bilateral peripheral opacities and interstitial thickening. Echocardiography shows unchanged mildly reduced ejection fraction without volume overload. Bronchoscopy shows no infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Continue the drug and add an inhaled corticosteroid

options.label: D
options.html: Lower the dose and repeat CT in 3 months

options.label: E
options.html: Stop the drug and give systemic steroids

items.explanationHtml:
Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity is suggested by subacute cough, dyspnea, fever and new infiltrates in a patient taking the drug, after heart failure and infection are excluded. Treatment is to stop amiodarone, with systemic glucocorticoids for hypoxemic or extensive disease, usually tapered over months because the drug persists in tissue. A different strategy for his ventricular arrhythmia (eg, an ICD, catheter ablation or another antiarrhythmic) is needed.

Takeaway: Amiodarone lung toxicity: stop the drug and give steroids; expect slow resolution because of its long half-life.

whyNot.A: Antifibrotics are for progressive fibrosing ILD; this is an acute-subacute drug pneumonitis.
whyNot.B: Continuing the drug allows progression; inhaled steroids do not treat interstitial pneumonitis.
whyNot.C: Echocardiography shows no volume overload, so heart failure does not explain the opacities.
whyNot.D: Significant pneumonitis requires stopping the drug, not lowering the dose.

items.objective: Manage amiodarone pulmonary toxicity.

items.stemHtml:
An 81-year-old woman has 4 months of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. She has no fever. Fine bibasilar crackles are heard. Chest CT shows bilateral lower-lobe reticular opacities that were absent on a CT 2 years ago. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate is 38 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her medication list:

MedicationIndicationDuration
AmlodipineHypertension6 years
AtorvastatinHyperlipidemia6 years
LevothyroxineHypothyroidism10 years
Nitrofurantoin, nightlyPrevention of recurrent urinary tract infections18 months
OmeprazoleGastroesophageal reflux4 years

Which of these medications is most likely responsible for her lung disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Months to years of nitrofurantoin can cause chronic interstitial pneumonitis and fibrosis, typically in older women on long-term prophylaxis. Stopping the drug often leads to partial or full improvement; glucocorticoids are sometimes added. Long-term nitrofurantoin is best avoided in older adults, especially with reduced kidney function, because it is less effective and more toxic when filtration is low.

Takeaway: Chronic nitrofurantoin prophylaxis in older adults can cause pulmonary fibrosis; stop it.

whyNot.A: Amlodipine causes ankle edema and gingival hyperplasia, not interstitial fibrosis.
whyNot.B: Statins very rarely cause interstitial lung disease; long-term nitrofurantoin is a far more likely cause.
whyNot.C: Levothyroxine at replacement doses does not cause lung disease.
whyNot.E: Proton pump inhibitors are linked to pneumonia risk, not progressive fibrosis.

items.objective: Identify nitrofurantoin as a cause of chronic interstitial lung disease in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of lip and tongue swelling that resolved over 24 hours in the emergency department. He had no hives or itching, and no airway compromise. He has taken lisinopril for hypertension for 4 years. He has no other medical problems and no family history of swelling episodes. Blood pressure today is 148/92 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his antihypertensive therapy?

options.label: A
options.html: Add hydrochlorothiazide and halve the lisinopril dose

options.label: B
options.html: Continue lisinopril and add daily cetirizine

options.label: C
options.html: Continue lisinopril and prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector

items.explanationHtml:
Angioedema without urticaria in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor is bradykinin-mediated and can occur after years of uneventful use. The ACE inhibitor must be stopped permanently, and all ACE inhibitors (and sacubitril-valsartan) should be avoided. A drug from a different class, such as a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or a thiazide, controls his blood pressure without that risk. ARBs carry a small risk of recurrence and are used cautiously, if at all.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitor angioedema: stop the entire class permanently and switch to an unrelated antihypertensive.

whyNot.A: Any ongoing ACE inhibitor exposure carries the risk of recurrence, regardless of dose.
whyNot.B: Antihistamines do not prevent bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
whyNot.C: Epinephrine is unreliable for this type of angioedema, and keeping the drug risks a fatal laryngeal episode.
whyNot.E: All ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin; angioedema recurs with any of them.

items.objective: Change antihypertensive therapy after ACE inhibitor–associated angioedema.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man is found unresponsive in a public restroom with a syringe nearby. Respirations are 4/min, pulse is 58/min and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Pupils are 1 mm and reactive. Pulse oximetry is 78%. Bag-valve-mask ventilation is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Immediate endotracheal intubation before any drug

items.explanationHtml:
Coma, respiratory depression and miosis form the opioid toxidrome. After assisted ventilation, naloxone, a competitive μ-receptor antagonist, is given and titrated to adequate breathing rather than full wakefulness, to avoid precipitating abrupt withdrawal. Because naloxone's effect can wear off before a long-acting opioid's, he needs observation, and he should be offered take-home naloxone and treatment for opioid use disorder.

Takeaway: Opioid toxidrome with hypoventilation: ventilate, then give naloxone titrated to breathing.

whyNot.A: The drug was injected, and lavage would risk aspiration in an unprotected airway.
whyNot.B: Naloxone often restores breathing within minutes and can avoid intubation; ventilate with a bag-valve mask meanwhile.
whyNot.C: Checking glucose is reasonable, but it does not explain miosis with apnea; naloxone is the key treatment.
whyNot.D: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; pinpoint pupils and apnea point to an opioid, and flumazenil can provoke seizures.

items.objective: Treat opioid-induced respiratory depression with naloxone.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with a seizure disorder treated with clonazepam for many years is brought in after taking an unknown number of her tablets and a bottle of wine. She is drowsy but rousable to voice, protecting her airway, with respirations 12/min and SpO2 95% on room air. Pupils are 3 mm. Blood glucose is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Isolated benzodiazepine overdose, even with alcohol, usually causes sedation with preserved breathing and is managed supportively: airway monitoring, observation and treatment of co-ingestants. Flumazenil is generally avoided because it can provoke seizures, especially in chronic users and people with epilepsy. Assess for suicidal intent once she is awake.

Takeaway: Benzodiazepine overdose: supportive care; avoid flumazenil in chronic users and seizure disorders.

whyNot.A: Charcoal is risky in a drowsy patient and offers little benefit for a benzodiazepine taken hours earlier.
whyNot.B: She is rousable, protecting her airway and breathing adequately; intubation is not needed now.
whyNot.C: In long-term benzodiazepine users and patients with seizure disorders, flumazenil can precipitate withdrawal seizures that are hard to control.
whyNot.D: There is no opioid toxidrome; her breathing and pupils are normal.

items.objective: Choose supportive care over flumazenil in benzodiazepine overdose in a chronic user.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man has 6 days of cough, dyspnea, fever, nausea and diarrhea. He vapes cartridges containing tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) bought from an informal seller. Temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), respirations are 26/min and SpO2 is 89% on room air. The leukocyte count is 13,500/mm3 with 2% eosinophils. CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with subpleural sparing. Respiratory viral panel, COVID-19 test, blood cultures and urine Legionella antigen are negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows lipid-laden macrophages and no eosinophilia or organisms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
EVALI presents with respiratory, gastrointestinal and constitutional symptoms in people who vape, especially THC products adulterated with vitamin E acetate. CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities, often with subpleural sparing, and lavage may show lipid-laden macrophages. It is a diagnosis of exclusion after infection testing. Treatment is to stop vaping, give oxygen and systemic glucocorticoids for significant disease, and cover pneumonia empirically if it cannot be excluded.

Takeaway: Vaping THC + GI symptoms + bilateral ground-glass with negative infection workup = EVALI.

whyNot.A: Vaping can trigger it, but the lavage has no eosinophilia.
whyNot.B: Bilateral ground-glass with negative cultures and lipid-laden macrophages after THC vaping fits EVALI better.
whyNot.C: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis needs a repeated organic antigen exposure and typically shows lymphocytic lavage.
whyNot.D: Nothing suggests immunosuppression, and lavage showed no organisms.

items.objective: Diagnose e-cigarette or vaping product use–associated lung injury.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman with severe COPD comes to the emergency department with 2 days of increased dyspnea and purulent sputum. Her usual daytime PaCO2 is about 52 mm Hg. Paramedics gave oxygen at 15 L/min through a non-rebreather mask during transport. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable. SpO2 is 99%. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.24, PaCO2 84 mm Hg, PaO2 238 mm Hg and HCO3− 35 mEq/L. Which of the following most likely contributed most to her worsening acidosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Her PaCO2 has risen far above her baseline while her PaO2 is very high, producing acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (the bicarbonate of 35 mEq/L reflects chronic compensation). Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen in a CO2-retaining patient worsens V/Q matching and adds the Haldane effect, raising PaCO2. The exacerbation itself contributes, but the overshoot of oxygen is the avoidable cause.

Takeaway: SpO2 of 99% in a CO2 retainer is too high; it can worsen hypercapnia.

whyNot.B: A high PaCO<sub>2</sub> with high bicarbonate is a respiratory acidosis, not a lactic (metabolic) acidosis.
whyNot.C: Her bicarbonate reflects chronic renal compensation; the acute change is respiratory.
whyNot.D: A pneumothorax would lower saturation and cause unilateral findings; her oxygenation is excessive.
whyNot.E: Embolism causes hypoxemia and usually hypocapnia, not a PaO<sub>2</sub> above 200 mm Hg.

items.objective: Recognize oxygen-induced hypercapnia in a COPD exacerbation.

items.stemHtml: In the same patient, oxygen is changed to a 28% Venturi mask and she is started on nebulized bronchodilators, a systemic glucocorticoid and an antibiotic. Thirty minutes later SpO2 is 90%, but she remains drowsy and repeat arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.26 and PaCO2 80 mm Hg. She can protect her airway and has no facial trauma or vomiting. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35 with a high PaCO2) despite controlled oxygen and medical therapy is the main indication for noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation in a COPD exacerbation. NIV lowers PaCO2, reduces the need for intubation and improves survival. Recheck a blood gas within 1–2 hours; intubate if she worsens or cannot tolerate NIV.

Takeaway: COPD exacerbation with persistent respiratory acidosis despite controlled oxygen → noninvasive ventilation.

whyNot.A: Intubation is for NIV failure or contraindications (unable to protect the airway, arrest, vomiting); she has none yet.
whyNot.B: Respiratory stimulants are not standard care; ventilatory support is.
whyNot.C: Bicarbonate does not treat respiratory acidosis and can raise PaCO<sub>2</sub> further.
whyNot.E: Removing oxygen would cause dangerous hypoxemia; the target is 88–92%, not no oxygen.

items.objective: Start noninvasive ventilation for persistent hypercapnic acidosis in a COPD exacerbation.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man with Hodgkin lymphoma receives a combination chemotherapy regimen. After 4 cycles he has a dry cough and exertional dyspnea. Fine bibasilar crackles are heard. His diffusing capacity has fallen by 30% from baseline. CT shows subpleural reticular opacities at both bases. His blood counts are normal. The drug most likely responsible injures the lungs more than most other tissues mainly because of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Formation of a reactive metabolite by pulmonary cytochrome P450 enzymes

options.label: B
options.html: High concentration of folate-dependent enzymes in type II pneumocytes

options.label: C
options.html: Immune complexes formed between the drug and IgG in alveolar walls

options.label: D
options.html: Low activity of drug-inactivating enzymes in lung cells

options.label: E
options.html: Preferential uptake of the drug by alveolar macrophages through LDL receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Bleomycin (part of the ABVD regimen) chelates iron and generates oxygen free radicals that cut DNA. Most tissues detoxify it with bleomycin hydrolase, but lung and skin have little of this enzyme, so they accumulate damage: pneumonitis progressing to fibrosis, and skin hyperpigmentation. The drug causes little myelosuppression, which fits the normal blood counts.

Takeaway: Bleomycin targets lung and skin because they lack bleomycin hydrolase; it spares the marrow.

whyNot.A: Pulmonary bioactivation explains some toxins (eg, some solvents) but not this drug's selectivity.
whyNot.B: That describes a target of antifolates, which is not why this drug is lung-toxic.
whyNot.C: The injury is direct, oxidative and dose-related, not immune-complex mediated.
whyNot.E: Macrophage accumulation and phospholipidosis are features of amiodarone, not of this drug.

items.objective: Explain why bleomycin selectively injures the lung.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man who has taken an antiarrhythmic drug for 3 years for atrial fibrillation has 2 months of cough and dyspnea. He has blue-gray discoloration of sun-exposed skin. CT shows bilateral interstitial and patchy consolidative opacities, some with high attenuation. Bronchoalveolar lavage is performed. Which of the following findings in the lavage fluid is most characteristic of his drug toxicity?

options.label: A
options.html: Eosinophils making up 40% of the cells

options.label: B
options.html: Large numbers of neutrophils with gram-positive cocci in clusters

options.label: D
options.html: Milky fluid with PAS-positive acellular material

options.label: E
options.html: Progressively bloodier aliquots with hemosiderin-laden macrophages

items.explanationHtml:
Amiodarone is an iodine-rich, cationic amphiphilic drug that accumulates in tissues and inhibits lysosomal phospholipases, producing phospholipidosis. Alveolar macrophages filled with lamellar inclusions appear foamy. Foamy macrophages show exposure, not necessarily toxicity, but in a patient with new infiltrates they support amiodarone pulmonary toxicity. Its iodine content explains the high-attenuation lung and liver on CT.

Takeaway: Amiodarone lung: foamy, lipid-laden macrophages (phospholipidosis) and high-attenuation opacities.

whyNot.A: Marked BAL eosinophilia suggests eosinophilic pneumonia, which some drugs cause, but it is not the signature of this drug.
whyNot.B: This suggests bacterial pneumonia such as staphylococcal infection.
whyNot.D: This is pulmonary alveolar proteinosis from impaired surfactant clearance.
whyNot.E: This is diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.

items.objective: Recognize the histologic signature of amiodarone pulmonary toxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman develops a persistent dry, tickling cough 3 weeks after starting lisinopril for hypertension. Lung examination and chest radiograph are normal. Accumulation of which of the following substances most likely causes her cough?
items.explanationHtml:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme is the same enzyme as kininase II, which breaks down bradykinin and substance P. Inhibiting it raises these peptides in the airway, sensitizing cough receptors. The same mechanism underlies ACE inhibitor angioedema. Angiotensin receptor blockers leave bradykinin metabolism intact and rarely cause cough.

Takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema come from bradykinin; switch to an ARB for cough.

whyNot.A: Aldosterone secretion falls with ACE inhibition and has no effect on cough.
whyNot.B: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II formation.
whyNot.D: Histamine mediates allergic reactions; ACE does not degrade it.
whyNot.E: Leukotrienes drive aspirin-exacerbated asthma, not ACE inhibitor cough.

items.objective: Identify bradykinin accumulation as the cause of ACE inhibitor cough.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman with asthma and recurrent nasal polyps takes ibuprofen for a headache. Within 1 hour she develops nasal congestion, flushing and severe wheezing. Which of the following best explains her reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.html: Diversion of arachidonic acid toward cysteinyl leukotriene synthesis

options.label: C
options.html: IgE antibodies against ibuprofen bound to mast cells

options.label: D
options.html: Increased thromboxane A<sub>2</sub> production by platelets

items.explanationHtml:
Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease combines asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and reactions to COX-1 inhibitors. Blocking COX-1 removes prostaglandin E2, which normally restrains 5-lipoxygenase and mast cells, so arachidonic acid is shunted toward cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4), causing bronchoconstriction and nasal symptoms. Leukotriene modifiers help, and selective COX-2 inhibitors are usually tolerated.

Takeaway: Aspirin/NSAID-induced asthma is a leukotriene shunt, not IgE allergy.

whyNot.A: Beta-blockers cause bronchospasm this way; NSAIDs do not act on adrenergic receptors.
whyNot.C: Reactions occur with any COX-1 inhibitor, including chemically unrelated ones, so this is not a drug-specific IgE allergy.
whyNot.D: COX inhibition reduces thromboxane production.
whyNot.E: This is the mechanism of ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with asthma well controlled on an inhaled glucocorticoid is started on a medication for migraine prophylaxis. Two days later she has severe wheezing that responds poorly to her albuterol inhaler. Blockade of which of the following receptors most likely explains this reaction?
items.explanationHtml:
Propranolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, is used for migraine prophylaxis. Blocking β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle removes sympathetic bronchodilation and blunts the effect of β2 agonists such as albuterol, so bronchospasm can be severe. Nonselective beta-blockers, including timolol eye drops, should be avoided in asthma.

Takeaway: Nonselective beta-blockers can provoke refractory bronchospasm in asthma by blocking β2 receptors.

whyNot.A: Triptans are agonists at these receptors and treat, not prevent, migraine; they do not constrict airways.
whyNot.B: H<sub>1</sub> blockade does not cause bronchospasm.
whyNot.C: Blocking M3 receptors (eg, tiotropium) dilates the airways.
whyNot.D: Blocking α<sub>1</sub> receptors causes vasodilation and orthostasis, not bronchospasm.

items.objective: Explain beta-blocker–induced bronchospasm in asthma.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man is found unresponsive at home with an empty bottle of oxycodone tablets. Respirations are 5/min and shallow. His pupils are pinpoint. Pulse oximetry on room air is 84%. Which of the following sets of arterial blood gas findings is most likely before treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: pH high, PaCO<sub>2</sub> low, A–a gradient normal

options.label: B
options.html: pH low, PaCO<sub>2</sub> high, A–a gradient high

options.label: C
options.html: pH low, PaCO<sub>2</sub> high, A–a gradient normal

options.label: D
options.html: pH low, PaCO<sub>2</sub> low, A–a gradient high

options.label: E
options.html: pH normal, PaCO<sub>2</sub> high, A–a gradient normal

items.explanationHtml:
Opioids act on μ receptors in the brainstem to slow breathing and blunt the response to CO2. Alveolar ventilation falls, so PaCO2 rises acutely and pH falls. By the alveolar gas equation, a higher PACO2 lowers PAO2, and PaO2 falls with it, so the A–a gradient stays normal. Aspiration pneumonia would later widen the gradient.

Takeaway: Pure hypoventilation: high PaCO2, hypoxemia, normal A–a gradient.

whyNot.A: This is acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation (eg, anxiety, salicylates early).
whyNot.B: A widened gradient would require a parenchymal problem such as aspiration; pure hypoventilation keeps it normal.
whyNot.D: A low PaCO<sub>2</sub> means hyperventilation; this pattern fits metabolic acidosis with lung disease, not hypoventilation.
whyNot.E: A normal pH with high PaCO<sub>2</sub> means chronic compensation, which takes days.

items.objective: Predict the blood gas pattern of opioid-induced hypoventilation.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with severe COPD and chronic hypercapnia is brought to the emergency department with an exacerbation. He receives oxygen at 15 L/min through a non-rebreather mask. One hour later his SpO2 is 99%, he is drowsy, and his PaCO2 has risen from 58 to 79 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most important mechanism of the rise in PaCO2?

options.label: A
options.html: Absorption atelectasis causing a right-to-left shunt

options.label: B
options.html: Increased CO<sub>2</sub> production by oxygen metabolism

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction, worsening V/Q mismatch

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of the hypoxic stimulus to the peripheral chemoreceptors

items.explanationHtml:
In COPD, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli. High inspired oxygen relieves that vasoconstriction, so perfusion returns to low-V/Q units and physiological dead space rises; CO2 elimination falls. The Haldane effect adds to this: well-oxygenated hemoglobin carries less CO2, releasing it into the plasma. Loss of hypoxic drive plays a smaller role. Target SpO2 88–92% in patients at risk.

Takeaway: Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD is mainly worsened V/Q matching plus the Haldane effect.

whyNot.A: Shunt mainly lowers PaO<sub>2</sub>, which is high here; it does not explain a 20 mm Hg rise in PaCO<sub>2</sub>.
whyNot.B: CO<sub>2</sub> production depends on metabolic rate, which supplemental oxygen does not raise meaningfully.
whyNot.D: Reduced hypoxic drive contributes a little, but minute ventilation often falls only slightly; it is not the main mechanism.
whyNot.E: Oxygen does not constrict airways.

items.objective: Explain the mechanisms of oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after inhaling the contents of a small bottle of liquid sold as "room odorizer" at a party. He is anxious and has cyanosis of the lips and nail beds that does not improve with 100% oxygen. Pulse oximetry reads 85%. Arterial PaO2 is 410 mm Hg. Arterial blood is chocolate-brown. Which of the following best describes the action of the most appropriate antidote?

options.label: A
options.html: It binds the toxin in the gut to prevent further absorption

options.label: B
options.html: It displaces the toxin from hemoglobin by competitive binding

options.label: C
options.html: It donates sulfur to convert the toxin to a renally excreted form

options.label: D
options.html: It forms a stable complex with free iron for urinary excretion

options.label: E
options.html: It is reduced to a compound that converts ferric heme iron back to the ferrous state

items.explanationHtml:
Nitrite inhalants (poppers) oxidize hemoglobin iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+, forming methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. PaO2 stays high, pulse oximetry hovers near 85% and the blood is brown. Methylene blue is reduced by NADPH–methemoglobin reductase (which needs NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway) to leukomethylene blue, which reduces methemoglobin back to hemoglobin. It fails or causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

Takeaway: Nitrite inhalant → methemoglobinemia → methylene blue reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+.

whyNot.A: Activated charcoal binds ingested drugs; the toxin was inhaled and has already oxidized hemoglobin.
whyNot.B: Competitive displacement describes high-flow oxygen in carbon monoxide poisoning.
whyNot.C: Sodium thiosulfate detoxifies cyanide this way.
whyNot.D: Deferoxamine chelates iron in iron overdose.

items.objective: Describe the action of methylene blue in methemoglobinemia.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl uses a nicotine vaping device for the first time and develops palpitations, tremor and nausea. Her pulse is 112/min and blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. The receptor through which nicotine produces these effects is best described as which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: A Gq-coupled receptor that activates phospholipase C

options.label: B
options.html: A Gs-coupled receptor that raises cyclic AMP

options.label: D
options.html: A nuclear receptor that alters gene transcription

items.explanationHtml:
Nicotine is an agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, pentameric ligand-gated channels that let sodium and potassium (and some calcium) in. Stimulation of sympathetic ganglia and adrenal chromaffin cells releases catecholamines, causing tachycardia, hypertension and tremor; parasympathetic ganglionic stimulation and the area postrema explain nausea. In the brain, α4β2 receptors release dopamine, driving dependence.

Takeaway: Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors, ligand-gated cation channels in ganglia, adrenal medulla and brain.

whyNot.A: This describes α<sub>1</sub>-adrenergic and M<sub>1</sub>/M<sub>3</sub> muscarinic receptors.
whyNot.B: This describes β-adrenergic receptors; nicotine acts upstream at ganglia and the adrenal medulla.
whyNot.D: Steroid and thyroid hormones act on nuclear receptors with slow effects.
whyNot.E: Insulin and growth-factor receptors are tyrosine kinases; nicotine's receptor is an ion channel.

items.objective: Classify the nicotinic receptor and relate it to nicotine's acute effects.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken a once-weekly oral drug for 5 months. She now has 2 weeks of fever, dry cough and dyspnea. Chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows a lymphocytosis; stains and cultures, including for Pneumocystis, are negative. The drug most likely responsible acts mainly by inhibiting which of the following enzymes?
items.explanationHtml:
Methotrexate, taken once weekly for rheumatoid arthritis, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (and at low doses raises extracellular adenosine, which is anti-inflammatory). Methotrexate pneumonitis is a hypersensitivity reaction, independent of dose, usually in the first year, with fever, cough, ground-glass opacities and lymphocytic lavage. Infection must be excluded because these patients are immunosuppressed.

Takeaway: Methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor) can cause dose-independent hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

whyNot.A: Calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus are not standard once-weekly RA drugs.
whyNot.C: This is the target of leflunomide, which is taken daily and is more often linked to liver toxicity.
whyNot.D: This is the target of mycophenolate, which is not a first-line RA drug.
whyNot.E: JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib) are taken daily and are linked to infection and thrombosis rather than hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

items.objective: Identify methotrexate pneumonitis and the drug's mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 26 weeks' gestation required mechanical ventilation and high concentrations of supplemental oxygen for several weeks. At 8 weeks of age, retinal examination shows a demarcation ridge between the vascular and avascular retina with abnormal new vessels growing into the vitreous. Which of the following best explains the vessel growth?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct oxygen-induced proliferation of retinal endothelial cells

options.label: B
options.html: Glucose-driven pericyte loss from sorbitol accumulation

options.label: D
options.html: Immune complexes deposited in retinal capillaries

options.label: E
options.html: Raised intraocular pressure compressing choroidal vessels

items.explanationHtml:
In preterm infants, the peripheral retina is still vascularizing. High inspired oxygen suppresses VEGF and halts vessel growth (phase 1). When the infant returns to lower oxygen, the enlarged, avascular retina becomes hypoxic, VEGF surges and abnormal neovascularization grows into the vitreous (phase 2), risking retinal detachment. Careful oxygen targeting, screening and laser or anti-VEGF therapy reduce blindness.

Takeaway: Retinopathy of prematurity: oxygen suppresses VEGF, then relative hypoxia triggers VEGF-driven neovascularization.

whyNot.A: High oxygen suppresses retinal vessel growth; the new vessels appear later, when the retina is relatively hypoxic.
whyNot.B: This is a mechanism of diabetic retinopathy.
whyNot.D: Retinopathy of prematurity is not an immune-complex disease.
whyNot.E: Glaucoma damages the optic nerve; it does not cause peripheral retinal neovascularization.

items.objective: Explain the two-phase pathogenesis of retinopathy of prematurity.
